Plant sampling was conducted at the V6, silking (R1), grain filling (R3), and physiological maturity (R6) stages for maize, and at the V4, flowering (R2), pod filling (R5), and maturity (R8) stages for soybean. At each stage, three representative plants per plot were harvested for the determination of leaf area index (LAI, LI-3100C area meter), aboveground biomass (oven-dried at 75 °C to constant weight), and plant nitrogen concentration (Kjeldahl method). Chlorophyll content (SPAD-502) and chlorophyll fluorescence parameters (Fv/Fm, measured with a PAM-2500 fluorometer) were recorded on the youngest fully expanded leaves between 09:00 and 11:00 on clear days. At maturity, plants from a 2 m² quadrat in the center of each plot were harvested to determine grain yield (adjusted to 14% moisture), yield components (ears per plant, kernels per ear, 1000-grain weight for maize; pods per plant, seeds per pod, 100-seed weight for soybean), and the land equivalent ratio (LER). Soil samples (0–20 and 20–40 cm) were collected before sowing and after harvest for the determination of soil organic carbon, available nitrogen, and gravimetric water content. Soil water storage and crop water use were calculated using the water balance approach, and water-use efficiency (WUE) was expressed as grain yield per unit of evapotranspiration.

 Statistical Analysis

All data were checked for normality (Shapiro–Wilk test) and homogeneity of variance (Levene's test) before analysis. A linear mixed-effects model was fitted using the lme4 package in R (version 4.3.1), with water regime, cropping system, and their interaction as fixed effects, and year, replication (nested within year), and their interactions with the main-plot factor as random effects, since the water-regime effect was tested against the main-plot error. When significant effects were detected (P < 0.05), treatment means were separated using Tukey's HSD test at α = 0.05. The intercropping advantage was quantified using the LER, and the competitive ratio and aggressivity index were calculated to characterize interspecific competition under the two water regimes. Relationships among physiological traits, yield, and WUE were examined using Pearson correlation analysis and stepwise multiple regression. Principal component analysis was performed to visualize multivariate treatment differences. All analyses were conducted in R 4.3.1, with figures generated using ggplot2; results were considered significant at P < 0.05.

title: archaeology|Neolithic rice cultivation in the lower Yangtze region
text: The lower Yangtze region is a key center for the origins of rice agriculture in East Asia, yet the timing, pace, and ecological context of the transition from rice gathering to cultivation remain debated. This study synthesizes archaeobotanical, chronological, and environmental evidence from Neolithic sites across the lower Yangtze valley—including Shangshan, Kuahuqiao, Hemudu, and Majiabang cultural contexts—to reconstruct the trajectory of rice exploitation and cultivation between approximately 10,000 and 6,000 cal BP. Our analysis combines re-examination of macrobotanical remains (rice spikelets, grains, and husks) with published phytolith and starch records, supported by a Bayesian chronological framework. Results indicate that initial rice use during the Shangshan period (~10,000–8,500 cal BP) involved low-intensity exploitation of wild or incipiently domesticated populations in wetland margins, with morphologically wild rice dominating assemblages. Clear evidence for deliberate cultivation—including increased rice frequencies, larger grain size, and elevated proportions of domesticated-type spikelet bases—emerges during the Kuahuqiao period (~8,000–7,000 cal BP) and intensifies through the Hemudu and Majiabang periods, when rice becomes a staple associated with paddy-field management. These changes coincide with mid-Holocene sea-level stabilization, deltaic progradation, and the expansion of freshwater wetlands, which created labor-accessible and highly productive landscapes. We argue that rice cultivation in the region developed incrementally through a mosaic of human–plant–environment interactions rather than as a single domestication event. This synthesis refines current models of agricultural origins in East Asia and highlights the lower Yangtze as a locus of protracted, landscape-mediated neolithization.

title: archaeology|Neolithic rice cultivation in the lower Yangtze region
text:
The transition from foraging to farming represents one of the most consequential developments in human history, and the origins of rice agriculture in East Asia stand among its most significant chapters. The lower Yangtze region of eastern China, encompassing parts of modern Zhejiang, Jiangsu, Anhui, and Shanghai, is widely recognized as one of the primary centers of rice domestication and the earliest known locus of sustained wet rice cultivation anywhere in the world (Fuller et al. 2009; Zong et al. 2007). Understanding how, when, and why communities in this region came to depend on cultivated rice is therefore central not only to East Asian prehistory but to broader comparative debates about agricultural origins, the relationship between environmental change and subsistence intensification, and the social consequences of food production.

Early investigations at sites such as Hemudu in Zhejiang, excavated in the 1970s, brought the antiquity of rice farming in the region into sharp focus. Abundant rice remains, together with waterlogged wooden tools, pile-dwelling architecture, and rich faunal assemblages, were interpreted as evidence for a well-established rice-based economy by the fifth millennium BC (Chang 1986; Zhejiang Provincial Museum 1978). Subsequent work at Kuahuqiao,跨湖桥, pushed evidence for rice exploitation and possible management back toward the sixth millennium BC, while also revealing the complex, mixed foraging-cultivation strategies that preceded full agricultural commitment (Liu et al. 2007; Zong et al. 2007). More recently, systematic archaeobotanical and dating programs at sites including Shangshan, Hehuashan, and Tianluoshan have refined our understanding of the tempo and mode of domestication, documenting a protracted process in which morphological domestication traits, such as the shift toward non-shattering panicles and larger grains, accumulated gradually over millennia rather than appearing as a single event (Fuller et al. 2009; Fuller et al. 2011; Zheng et al. 2016).

These developments have been accompanied by important methodological advances. Systematic flotation has transformed the recovery of charred plant remains, while the analysis of rice spikelet bases has provided a more reliable proxy for domestication status than grain size or shape alone (Fuller et al. 2009). Phytolith and starch grain analyses have extended the record to sites and sediments where macroremains are scarce (Ma et al. 2018; Wu et al. 2014), and high-resolution radiocarbon chronologies, including Bayesian modeling of dated sequences, have sharpened the temporal framework considerably (Long et al. 2017; Ma et al. 2018). Stable isotope studies, though still limited for this region and period, offer additional avenues for investigating diet, mobility, and the role of rice relative to other foods (Lanehart et al. 2011). Together these approaches have complicated earlier narratives of a rapid Neolithic revolution and replaced them with a picture of gradual, regionally variable, and socially embedded plant management.

Environmental context has figured prominently in explanations of lower Yangtze rice cultivation. The region's monsoonal climate, extensive wetlands, and network of rivers and lakes provided the ecological setting in which rice and human communities co-evolved (Zong et al. 2007). Holocene sea-level change and associated shifts in coastal configuration, hydrology, and sedimentation profoundly shaped the landscapes available for habitation and cultivation, and several authors have argued that mid-Holocene environmental instability, including marine transgression and subsequent regression, structured patterns of settlement and subsistence (Innes et al. 2009; Zong et al. 2011). The relationship between rice cultivation and the spread of waterlogged, paddy-like field systems, documented at sites such as Caoxieshan and Chuodun, further highlights the entanglement of ecological management, labor investment, and agricultural practice (Qin et al. 2011; Cao et al. 2006).

Despite this progress, significant questions remain. The relative contributions of climatic forcing, demographic pressure, and social agency to the intensification of rice cultivation are debated; the degree to which early cultivation was wetland-based versus dryland or mixed is contested; and the social organization of early farming communities, including questions of labor cooperation, tenure, and the ritual dimensions of agricultural life, remains poorly understood (Fuller 2011; Liu and Chen 2012). Regional variability within the lower Yangtze, between coastal, lacustrine, and hilly sub-zones, has also been insufficiently integrated into synthetic accounts.

This paper addresses these issues by synthesizing recent archaeobotanical, chronological, and environmental evidence for Neolithic rice cultivation in the lower Yangtze region. Drawing on published datasets from key sites and new analyses of spikelet-base assemblages, we examine the timing and tempo of domestication, the ecological and social contexts of cultivation, and the implications of the lower Yangtze record for broader models of agricultural origins. In doing so, we aim to contribute to ongoing efforts to decentre narratives of rapid agricultural revolution in favor of accounts that recognize the long, uneven, and contingent pathways by which rice became a staple crop.

title: history|local militias and state power during the Song–Yuan transition
text:
Discussion

The evidence assembled here suggests that the relationship between local militias and state power during the Song–Yuan transition is best understood not as a simple oscillation between state monopoly on violence and its collapse, but as a prolonged negotiation over the terms of delegation. Three findings deserve emphasis.

First, the militias that proved most durable were those whose organizational horizons were already regional before 1276. The Xiangyang and Lianghuai cases show that where defense networks had crystallized around grain transport, salt routes, or cross-regional kinship alliances, local commanders could convert wartime authority into recognition from the Yuan state with relatively little disruption. By contrast, militias constituted primarily around single prefectures or urban defense tended to dissolve or be absorbed once the immediate threat passed. This pattern qualifies the common assumption that the Yuan simply dismantled Southern Song military structures; in several localities, what occurred was closer to a reclassification, whereby irregular forces were granted *tusi*-style or garrison designations that preserved local command hierarchies while subordinating them to the Mongol decimal system.

Second, the sources reveal a persistent gap between statutory and practical authority. The Yuan prohibition on private arms and unauthorized militia (*yibing*) was enforced unevenly, and enforcement correlated less with the letter of the law than with the fiscal and military needs of provincial administrations. Where a locality's militia could be taxed or conscripted, it was tolerated; where it could not, it was suppressed. This instrumental pattern suggests that Yuan state-building in the south operated through selective incorporation rather than uniform disarmament—a finding consistent with recent work on Mongol governance but extending it to the militia question specifically.

Third, and perhaps most tentatively, the transition appears to have accelerated the localization of military identity in ways that outlasted the dynasty itself. Several of the lineages documented here reappear in early Ming garrisons with claims to hereditary command. Whether this continuity reflects genuine institutional persistence or retrospective genealogical construction by Ming-era descendants is difficult to adjudicate with the sources available; the lineage registers were compiled or revised in the fifteenth century, and their reliability for thirteenth-century events is uneven.

Several limitations circumscribe these conclusions. The sample is drawn disproportionately from Fujian, Jiangxi, and the Huai region, reflecting the survival of local gazetteers and genealogies rather than any claim to representativeness. Northern China, where the transition proceeded under different military-administrative conditions, is largely absent. Moreover, the Yuan-era documents that would allow us to see militia–state negotiation from the administrative side—provincial memorials, garrison rosters—survive only fragmentarily, and our reconstruction leans heavily on retrospective sources whose authors had their own reasons to emphasize either loyalist resistance or smooth incorporation.

Conclusion

Taken together, the evidence points toward a model of the Song–Yuan transition in which local militias functioned less as obstacles to state power than as its connective tissue—flexible, locally legitimated intermediaries through which first Song and then Yuan authorities projected authority into terrain they could not administer directly. The Yuan did not so much conquer Southern Song society as bargain with the armed structures already embedded in it, and those structures in turn extracted recognition, tax exemptions, and hereditary privilege in exchange for pacification and local order.

This has implications beyond the period. It suggests that the conventional divide between "local society" and "the state" obscures the extent to which military organization in this era was itself a zone of exchange, in which both parties made claims and both made concessions. The persistence of militia lineages into the Ming further implies that the transition's institutional legacy was longer than the conventional 1279 caesura suggests. Future work with provincial archives and a more systematic northern comparison would help establish whether the pattern described here is a southern peculiarity or a more general dynamic of conquest-era governance.

title: education|the effects of formative assessment on secondary school mathematics
text:
The Effects of Formative Assessment on Secondary School Mathematics

Abstract

Formative assessment has attracted considerable attention in mathematics education as a means of improving student learning rather than merely measuring it. This paper examines the effects of formative assessment on secondary school students' mathematics achievement, motivation, and self-regulation. Drawing on theoretical perspectives and empirical studies, it argues that formative assessment, when implemented with clarity of learning intentions, effective feedback, and opportunities for self- and peer-assessment, produces meaningful gains in conceptual understanding and student engagement. The paper also considers implementation challenges, including time constraints, teacher assessment literacy, and the risk of superficial practice, and concludes that formative assessment is most effective when embedded systematically in classroom culture rather than applied as an isolated technique.

1. Introduction

Mathematics is frequently reported as a subject in which secondary school students experience anxiety, disengagement, and persistent achievement gaps. Traditional assessment regimes, dominated by summative tests and grades, tend to inform students of their failure without offering a route to improvement. In response, researchers and practitioners have increasingly turned to formative assessment—the ongoing process of eliciting evidence about learning and using it to adapt teaching and learning. Black and Wiliam's influential review (1998) estimated effect sizes of 0.4 to 0.7 for formative assessment interventions, placing them among the most cost-effective educational strategies available. However, the translation of these findings into secondary mathematics classrooms remains uneven, and questions persist about which components matter most and under what conditions. This paper reviews the theoretical foundations and empirical evidence concerning formative assessment in secondary mathematics, analyses its effects on achievement and affective outcomes, and discusses the conditions required for successful implementation.

2. Theoretical Foundations

Formative assessment is grounded in constructivist and sociocultural learning theories. From a constructivist perspective, learners build mathematical understanding by connecting new ideas to existing schemas; formative assessment provides the diagnostic information needed to identify misconceptions and gaps. From a sociocultural perspective, learning is mediated by interaction, and feedback functions as a scaffold within the learner's zone of proximal development. Sadler's (1989) influential formulation identified three conditions for effective formative assessment: learners must understand the standard of quality being aimed at, compare their current performance with that standard, and take action to close the gap. Hattie and Timperley (2007) further distinguished feedback about the task, the process, and self-regulation, showing that process- and self-regulation-level feedback is generally more powerful than praise or purely evaluative comments. These frameworks imply that formative assessment is not a test format but a pedagogical cycle of eliciting, interpreting, and responding to evidence.

3. Effects on Mathematics Achievement

Empirical evidence suggests that formative assessment improves mathematics achievement, particularly when it targets conceptual understanding rather than procedural fluency alone. Classroom techniques such as diagnostic questioning, exit tickets, mini-whiteboard responses, and carefully designed hinge-point questions allow teachers to detect misconceptions in real time and adjust instruction accordingly. Studies of mathematics classrooms using these approaches report improved performance on transfer tasks and reduced gaps between high- and low-achieving students, since struggling learners receive more immediate and targeted support. A key mechanism is the shift from judging answers to interpreting reasoning: when teachers ask students to explain their methods, they gain access to the mathematical thinking behind errors. Meta-analyses generally support modest to moderate positive effects, with variability attributable to implementation quality rather than to the approach itself.

4. Effects on Motivation and Self-Regulation

Formative assessment also influences affective and metacognitive outcomes. When assessment is framed as information for improvement rather than judgment of ability, students are more likely to adopt mastery goals and to persist after errors. Feedback that is specific, timely, and actionable supports a growth mindset by attributing success to strategy and effort. Self-assessment and peer-assessment, central components of formative practice, develop students' capacity to monitor their own mathematical work—an essential skill for independent problem solving. However, effects on motivation are conditional: if formative assessment is reduced to frequent quizzing and grading, it can increase anxiety and reinforce performance-oriented goals. The distinction between assessment *for* learning and assessment *as* frequent testing is therefore crucial.

5. Implementation Challenges

Several obstacles limit the effectiveness of formative assessment in secondary mathematics. First, curriculum coverage pressures encourage teachers to prioritize pace over responsive teaching, making it difficult to pause and reteach. Second, many teachers lack training in interpreting student responses and designing high-quality feedback, and may default to evaluative comments. Third, large classes and limited time constrain individual dialogue. Fourth, school accountability systems that emphasize summative results can undermine formative priorities. Finally, superficial adoption—for example, using exit tickets without adjusting subsequent instruction—produces little benefit. Successful implementation requires sustained professional development, collaborative planning, and leadership support that values diagnostic teaching.

6. Conclusion

Formative assessment offers a coherent and evidence-supported approach to improving secondary school mathematics education. Its effects operate through clearer learning intentions, responsive teaching, and feedback that helps students close the gap between current and desired performance. The evidence indicates positive effects on achievement, particularly conceptual understanding, as well as on motivation and self-regulation, although these outcomes depend heavily on implementation quality. Formative assessment should therefore be understood not as an add-on technique but as an integral part of classroom culture, supported by teacher professional learning and coherent assessment policy. Future research should examine long-term effects and the conditions under which formative assessment most benefits low-achieving students in mathematics.

References

Black, P., & Wiliam, D. (1998). Assessment and classroom learning. *Assessment in Education*, 5(1), 7–74.

Hattie, J., & Timperley, H. (2007). The power of feedback. *Review of Educational Research*, 77(1), 81–112.

Sadler, D. R. (1989). Formative assessment and the design of instructional systems. *Instructional Science*, 18(2), 119–144.

title: accounting|earnings management around seasoned equity offerings
text:
Methodology

 Data Sources and Sample Construction

This study draws on multiple data sources to examine earnings management behavior around seasoned equity offerings (SEOs). Financial statement data are obtained from Compustat North America (annual file), stock return and price data from the Center for Research in Security Prices (CRSP), and SEO issuance records from the Securities Data Company (SDC) Global New Issues database. Analyst forecast data, used in supplementary tests of forecast-based earnings benchmarks, are collected from the Institutional Brokers' Estimate System (I/B/E/S). Governance and ownership variables are drawn from BoardEx and Thomson Reuters (Refinitiv) ownership files.

The initial SEO sample consists of all U.S. public firms conducting firm-commitment seasoned equity offerings between January 2000 and December 2019. Following prior literature (e.g., Rangan, 1998; Teoh, Welch, & Wong, 1998), I apply the following filters: (1) exclude financial firms (SIC codes 6000–6999) and utilities (SIC 4900–4999) because of their regulated accounting and capital structures; (2) exclude closed-end funds, REITs, and unit offerings; (3) require the issuer to be listed on the NYSE, AMEX, or NASDAQ with available CRSP return data; (4) require sufficient Compustat data to estimate discretionary accruals, specifically at least ten observations in the estimation period; and (5) exclude firms involved in mergers, acquisitions, or major restructuring during the estimation window to avoid confounding effects on accruals. After these screens, the final sample comprises 1,148 SEOs by 962 unique firms. All continuous variables are winsorized at the 1st and 99th percentiles to mitigate the influence of outliers.

 Measurement of Earnings Management

Earnings management is measured using discretionary accruals estimated via the modified Jones (1991) model, as refined by Dechow, Sloan, and Sweeney (1995). Total accruals are computed as the difference between net income before extraordinary items and cash flows from operations, scaled by lagged total assets. For each firm-year, the following cross-sectional regression is estimated within two-digit SIC industry groups with at least ten observations:

TA_it/A_i,t−1 = α₀(1/A_i,t−1) + α₁(ΔREV_it/A_i,t−1) + α₂(PPE_it/A_i,t−1) + ε_it

where ΔREV is the change in revenues and PPE is gross property, plant, and equipment. Discretionary accruals (DA) are the residuals from this model, with the change in receivables subtracted from ΔREV in the prediction period (the modified Jones specification). As a robustness check, I also estimate performance-matched discretionary accruals following Kothari, Leone, and Wasley (2005), matching each SEO firm-year to a non-SEO firm with the closest return-on-assets in the same industry and year. Earnings management is measured over a three-year window: the fiscal year preceding the offering (year −1), the offering year (year 0), and the year following (year +1), with pre-SEO accruals benchmarked against a pre-issuance period (years −3 and −2) and a post-issuance period (years +2 and +3).

 Empirical Design

The analysis proceeds in three stages. First, I document the time-series pattern of discretionary accruals around SEOs using univariate comparisons of means and medians (t-tests and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests) across event-relative years. Second, I estimate pooled OLS regressions of discretionary accruals on event-year indicators, firm characteristics (size, leverage, market-to-book, profitability, and cash flow volatility), and industry and year fixed effects, with standard errors clustered at the firm level. Third, I examine cross-sectional variation in pre-SEO earnings management conditional on governance quality (board independence, institutional ownership), analyst coverage, and underwriter reputation, and I relate pre-SEO discretionary accruals to post-issuance outcomes—including stock return performance, operating performance (ROA), and the likelihood of subsequent restatements—to assess the economic consequences of accrual manipulation. Endogeneity concerns are addressed through propensity-score matching of SEO firms to non-issuing benchmark firms and, in supplementary tests, a difference-in-differences specification exploiting the 2003 Regulation FD and Sarbanes-Oxley disclosure environment as an exogenous shock to reporting discretion.

title: management|remote work and team innovation in technology companies
text:
Remote work has become a defining feature of modern technology companies, yet its implications for team innovation remain insufficiently understood. Drawing on media synchronicity theory and the input–process–output framework, this study examines how the extent of remote work affects team innovation in technology firms and investigates the mediating roles of knowledge sharing and team communication quality, as well as the moderating role of team virtuality management practices. Data were collected through a two-wave survey of 187 product development teams nested within 42 technology companies, supplemented by supervisor ratings of team innovation. Multilevel regression and structural equation modeling were used to test the hypothesized relationships. The results reveal an inverted U-shaped relationship between the extent of remote work and team innovation: moderate levels of remote work enhance innovation by combining the flexibility and focused time afforded by remote arrangements with the spontaneous interaction and informal knowledge exchange enabled by on-site work, whereas very low or very high levels of remote work diminish innovation outcomes. Knowledge sharing and team communication quality partially mediate this curvilinear relationship. Furthermore, team virtuality management practices—including structured asynchronous communication norms, deliberate in-person collaboration rituals, and clear coordination protocols—positively moderate the relationship, shifting the innovation optimum toward higher levels of remote work. These findings extend remote work research beyond individual-level outcomes to team-level innovation and offer practical guidance for technology leaders seeking to design hybrid work arrangements that preserve the social and communicative foundations of team creativity.

*Keywords:* remote work, team innovation, knowledge sharing, communication quality, virtual teams, technology companies

title: nursing|nurse staffing levels and patient falls in acute care
text:
Patient falls represent one of the most persistent and consequential adverse events in acute care hospitals, contributing substantially to preventable patient harm, extended length of stay, and increased healthcare costs (Cox et al., 2015). International estimates suggest that falls affect between 3 and 5 per 1,000 patient bed days in acute settings, with approximately one-quarter to one-third of falls resulting in injury, including fractures, subdural haematomas, and soft tissue damage (Bouldin et al., 2013). Beyond physical injury, falls are associated with psychological sequelae such as fear of falling, reduced mobility, and diminished quality of life, as well as significant financial burden; the average incremental cost attributable to a fall with injury in acute care has been estimated at several thousand dollars per episode (Morello et al., 2015). Falls are also increasingly regarded as a nurse-sensitive indicator, reflecting the extent to which nursing care structures and processes influence patient outcomes (Dunton et al., 2004). Consequently, understanding modifiable determinants of fall risk, particularly those related to the organisation and delivery of nursing care, is a priority for health services research and quality improvement.

Among the structural determinants of care quality, nurse staffing has received sustained empirical attention. A large body of international evidence, synthesised in systematic reviews and cross-national studies, demonstrates that lower nurse staffing levels and higher patient-to-nurse ratios are associated with adverse outcomes including increased mortality, failure-to-rescue, medication errors, and patient dissatisfaction (Aiken et al., 2014; Kane et al., 2007). The theoretical mechanisms linking staffing to outcomes are well described: inadequate staffing constrains the time available for surveillance, assessment, and timely intervention, and may lead to task prioritisation in which preventive care, such as toileting assistance, mobility support, and environmental safety checks, is deferred (Schubert et al., 2008). Because falls prevention is fundamentally dependent on proactive nursing surveillance and assistance with ambulation and elimination, it is plausible that staffing levels influence fall occurrence. However, the empirical literature on this specific relationship is less consistent than for other nurse-sensitive outcomes, and the direction and magnitude of association remain debated.

Findings regarding nurse staffing and falls have been mixed. Several observational studies have reported that lower staffing or higher patient-to-nurse ratios are associated with increased fall rates (Dunton et al., 2004; Yang et al., 2004), and some have identified staffing as an independent predictor after adjustment for patient acuity and unit characteristics. In contrast, other studies have found no significant association, or even an inverse relationship, whereby higher staffing was linked to greater fall detection and reporting rather than increased occurrence (Staggs & Dunton, 2014). These inconsistencies may reflect methodological heterogeneity, including variation in staffing measures (nurse hours per patient day versus patient-to-nurse ratios versus skill mix), differing fall case definitions and reporting practices, and inadequate adjustment for confounding by patient acuity and unit type (Lake et al., 2010). The reliance on administrative or aggregated data in many studies has also limited the ability to capture the dynamic, shift-level relationship between staffing and falls, since falls are temporally clustered and staffing fluctuates across shifts and days of the week.

Recent methodological advances have begun to address these limitations. Studies using shift-level or day-level staffing data, including nursing hours, registered nurse proportions, and overtime, have examined temporal associations with fall incidence and have reported associations that vary by unit type, with stronger effects observed in medical and surgical units than in intensive care settings (Patrician et al., 2011). There is also growing recognition that skill mix, teamwork, and the availability of unlicensed assistive personnel may moderate the staffing-falls relationship, and that the effectiveness of falls prevention depends not only on the quantity but also on the composition and deployment of the nursing workforce (Twigg et al., 2016). Furthermore, the COVID-19 pandemic has intensified concerns about staffing adequacy and its consequences for patient safety, underscoring the policy relevance of this question.

Despite this accumulating evidence, important gaps remain. Few studies have simultaneously examined multiple dimensions of staffing, incorporated patient-level fall risk factors, and accounted for the clustering of patients within units and hospitals. Moreover, much of the evidence derives from the United States and Europe, limiting generalisability to other health systems. The aim of this study was therefore to examine the association between nurse staffing levels and patient falls in acute care settings, using detailed staffing and incident data while adjusting for patient and unit characteristics. Clarifying this relationship is essential for informing nurse staffing policy, resource allocation, and the design of falls prevention strategies, and for strengthening the evidence base supporting falls as a nurse-sensitive outcome.

title: political science|electoral reform and party fragmentation in Latin America
text:
Literature Review: Electoral Reform and Party Fragmentation in Latin America

The relationship between electoral institutions and party system fragmentation has long been a central concern in comparative politics, and Latin America has served as a critical laboratory for testing competing theoretical claims. Scholars broadly agree that district magnitude, electoral formula, and the structure of the ballot shape the number of parties competing and winning seats, yet the region's experience reveals important qualifications to Duvergerian expectations. This review synthesizes the literature on how electoral rules affect party fragmentation in Latin America, the feedback effects between fragmentation and subsequent reform, and the methodological debates that structure the field.

The foundational claim that proportional representation with large district magnitudes multiplies parties while plurality rules constrain them (Duverger 1954) has been extensively tested in the region. Mainwaring (1993) demonstrated that Brazilian open-list PR with high district magnitude and weak party organization produced extreme fragmentation and indiscipline, showing that the mechanical effects of electoral rules are mediated by the strength of party institutions. Similarly, Jones (1995) found that district magnitude and malapportionment jointly shaped the number of parties in Argentine provincial legislatures, while Cox (1997) refined the argument by showing that the strategic entry of parties depends on the interaction between district magnitude and the effective number of presidential candidates, a finding with particular resonance in Latin America's presidential systems.

A second strand of literature examines the unintended consequences of reform. The wave of reforms in the 1980s and 1990s, often undertaken to strengthen governability, sometimes produced paradoxical outcomes. Nohlen (2004) documented how reforms intended to reduce fragmentation, such as the introduction of thresholds or mixed systems, frequently generated new parties or encouraged strategic splitting. In Venezuela, the shift from a highly institutionalized two-party system to a fragmented multiparty system occurred without fundamental changes to the electoral formula, prompting scholars to look beyond electoral rules altogether (Morgan 2011). This work highlights that fragmentation is not solely a mechanical product of rules but also reflects the erosion of party-society linkages and the personalization of politics.

A third body of scholarship emphasizes the endogenous relationship between fragmentation and reform. Fragmented legislatures make reform coalitions difficult to assemble, while dominant parties facing electoral decline may pursue reforms that inadvertently accelerate fragmentation. Shugart and Wattenberg (2001) argued that mixed-member systems create incentives for strategic behavior that can either consolidate or fragment party systems depending on the balance between nominal and list tiers, and Latin American cases such as Bolivia and Mexico have been used to test these propositions. Bolivia's mixed system, combined with a distinctive presidential runoff mechanism, produced a party system that oscillated between fragmentation and concentration across electoral cycles (Mayorga 2017). These findings suggest that the causal arrow runs in both directions, complicating static institutional accounts.

Methodologically, the literature has moved from cross-sectional correlations toward dynamic and subnational designs. Birch (2003) cautioned against inferring causal effects from cross-national variation alone, noting that informal institutions and historical legacies confound the relationship between rules and fragmentation. Recent work has exploited subnational variation in district magnitude and reform timing to identify effects more credibly, finding that the impact of rules is conditional on the strength of territorial cleavages and the presence of established party labels (Gervasoni 2018). Comparative studies of Andean countries have further shown that the same formal rules can produce different levels of fragmentation depending on the degree of party system institutionalization (Sánchez 2009).

In sum, the literature has moved beyond a simple Duvergerian framework to a more contingent understanding in which electoral rules interact with party organization, presidentialism, and historical legacies to shape fragmentation. Yet gaps remain: few studies systematically model the reciprocal relationship between fragmentation and reform over time, and the region's recent experiments with parity and alternation mechanisms have yet to be integrated into fragmentation theory. Future research would benefit from dynamic panel designs and from attention to how informal electoral practices mediate formal rule changes.

References

Birch, S. 2003. Electoral Systems and Political Transformation in Post-Communist Europe. Basingstoke: Palgrave.

Cox, G. W. 1997. Making Votes Count: Strategic Coordination in the World's Electoral Systems. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.

Duverger, M. 1954. Political Parties: Their Organization and Activity in the Modern State. London: Methuen.

Gervasoni, C. 2018. Hybrid Regimes within Democracies: Fiscal Federalism and Subnational Rentier States. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.

Jones, M. P. 1995. Electoral Laws and the Survival of Presidential Democracies. Notre Dame: University of Notre Dame Press.

Mainwaring, S. 1993. "Brazilian Party Underdevelopment in Comparative Perspective." Political Science Quarterly 107(4): 677-707.

Mayorga, F. 2017. "Bolivia's Electoral System and Party System Dynamics." Latin American Politics and Society 59(2): 45-68.

Morgan, J. 2011. Bankrupt Representation and Party System Collapse. University Park: Penn State University Press.

Nohlen, D. 2004. Sistemas electorales y partidos políticos. Mexico City: Fondo de Cultura Económica.

Sánchez, O. 2009. "Party System Institutionalization in the Andes." Journal of Politics in Latin America 1(2): 3-30.

Shugart, M. S., and M. P. Wattenberg, eds. 2001. Mixed-Member Electoral Systems: The Best of Both Worlds? Oxford: Oxford University Press.

title: architecture|adaptive reuse of industrial buildings in post-socialist cities
text:
Adaptive Reuse of Industrial Buildings in Post-Socialist Cities

Abstract

The transition from state socialism to market economies in Central and Eastern Europe left behind extensive industrial landscapes, many of which became obsolete within a remarkably short period. This paper examines the adaptive reuse of industrial buildings in post-socialist cities, arguing that these structures constitute a distinctive category of heritage whose transformation demands approaches sensitive to both their material qualities and their contested symbolic meanings. Drawing on theoretical frameworks from architectural conservation and urban studies, and illustrated through selected examples from cities such as Łódź, Tallinn, and Leipzig, the paper identifies three recurring strategies of intervention—museumisation, creative clustering, and commercial conversion—and evaluates their respective contributions and limitations. It concludes that successful adaptive reuse in this context depends less on stylistic choices than on the capacity of projects to negotiate between the erasure of socialist-era associations and the preservation of collective memory.

1. Introduction

The post-socialist city presents a condition for which Western conservation theory was largely unprepared. Following 1989, the rapid deindustrialisation of Central and Eastern Europe rendered vast tracts of factories, warehouses, and workers' facilities redundant. Unlike the gradual obsolescence experienced in Western Europe, this process was compressed into a decade, producing what scholars have termed an "industrial wasteland" at the heart of many urban areas.

Adaptive reuse—the process of giving obsolete buildings new programmes while retaining significant portions of their fabric—has become the dominant response. Yet the literature on adaptive reuse has developed primarily through Western case studies, where industrial heritage is understood as a source of nostalgic authenticity. In post-socialist cities, by contrast, industrial architecture carries more ambivalent associations: it is simultaneously a testament to rapid modernisation, a symbol of political coercion, and a repository of working-class memory. This paper asks how adaptive reuse can operate responsibly within this doubled condition.

2. Theoretical Framework: Heritage, Memory, and the Industrial Past

Adaptive reuse occupies an unstable position between conservation and development. The Burra Charter's emphasis on retaining cultural significance provides one useful anchor, but significance itself is precisely what is disputed in post-socialist contexts. Architectural theorists have long noted that industrial buildings possess a distinctive "spatial generosity"—large floor plates, high ceilings, robust structures—that makes them unusually adaptable. This flexibility is both an opportunity and a risk: the very qualities that permit conversion also permit the erasure of the building's historical identity.

A second body of literature concerns memory. Post-socialist societies have engaged in what some scholars describe as a "settling of accounts" with the past, often expressed architecturally through demolition or radical alteration. Industrial buildings complicate this impulse because they are less directly associated with political power than monuments or party buildings; their demolition is rarely ideologically motivated, yet their transformation nonetheless shapes how the socialist period is remembered.

3. Strategies of Intervention

*3.1 Museumisation*

The most conservative strategy treats industrial buildings as heritage in the conventional sense, stabilising the fabric and inserting interpretative programmes. Manufaktura in Łódź exemplifies a hybrid approach: the former textile factory of Izrael Poznański was converted into a cultural and commercial complex in 2006, retaining the brick facades and spatial volumes while introducing retail, museums, and public space. The result is commercially successful but has been criticised for sanitising the labour history it ostensibly commemorates.

*3.2 Creative Clustering*

A second strategy repurposes industrial sites as cultural production spaces. The Telliskivi Creative City in Tallinn, a former railway industrial complex, hosts studios, galleries, and independent businesses. This model generates genuine cultural activity and preserves the informal character of the industrial fabric, but it also participates in gentrification processes that displace the very populations whose labour the buildings once housed.

*3.3 Commercial Conversion*

The third and most widespread strategy converts industrial structures into offices, housing, or retail. Leipzig's Baumwollspinnerei, a former cotton mill, now combines galleries with commercial tenants, demonstrating the financial viability of conversion at scale. Yet commercial conversion tends to privilege exchange value over cultural significance, and the resulting spaces are often indistinguishable from generic contemporary architecture.

4. Discussion: Negotiating Memory

Across these strategies, a common tension emerges between the erasure and the preservation of the socialist past. Successful projects tend to share certain characteristics: they retain legible traces of industrial use—cranes, machinery, structural systems—and they incorporate interpretative elements that acknowledge, rather than suppress, the political context of production. Conversely, projects that treat industrial form as mere aesthetic packaging risk producing what might be called "memory without content," in which the shell survives but the history does not.

5. Conclusion

Adaptive reuse of industrial buildings in post-socialist cities is not merely a technical problem of conversion but a cultural practice of memory work. The three strategies identified here—museumisation, creative clustering, and commercial conversion—each offer partial solutions, and no single model can be universally recommended. What matters is the degree to which projects engage honestly with the contested meanings of their buildings. Future research should attend to the perspectives of former workers and local communities, whose voices are frequently absent from the design and interpretation of reused industrial sites.

References

(Note: A formal reference list would be included here, e.g., works by Lorens, Klasik, and others on post-socialist urban transformation; the Burra Charter; and studies of industrial heritage in Central and Eastern Europe.)

title: agronomy|intercropping maize and soybean under drought stress
text:
Methodology

 Experimental Site and Design

The study was conducted over two consecutive growing seasons (2022 and 2023) at the Experimental Farm of [University/Institution] (latitude 34°18′ N, longitude 108°05′ E; 520 m above sea level). The site has a warm temperate semi-humid climate with a mean annual precipitation of 580 mm—approximately 60% of which falls during the maize growing season—and a mean annual temperature of 13.2°C. The soil is a loam (Eutric Cambisol) with 1.42 g cm⁻³ bulk density, pH 7.8, 12.4 g kg⁻¹ organic matter, 0.82 g kg⁻¹ total nitrogen, 18.6 mg kg⁻¹ available phosphorus, and 142 mg kg⁻¹ available potassium in the 0–20 cm layer. Prior to the experiment, the field had been under continuous maize monoculture for at least five years. Weather data, including daily precipitation, temperature, and solar radiation, were obtained from an on-site automatic weather station (HOBO U30, Onset, USA).

The experiment employed a randomized complete block design with four treatments and four replicates (16 plots, each 6 m × 5 m). Treatments comprised: (i) sole maize (SM), (ii) sole soybean (SS), (iii) maize–soybean intercropping (MS), and (iv) maize–soybean intercropping under drought stress (MS-D). A drought-stressed sole maize treatment (SM-D) was included as a stress reference. Intercropping followed a 2:2 row arrangement (two maize rows alternating with two soybean rows), with a plant density of 6.0 plants m⁻² for maize and 18 plants m⁻² for soybean in both sole and intercropped systems. Drought stress was imposed from the sixth leaf stage (V6) to physiological maturity using rainout shelters (3 m × 5 m steel frames covered with transparent polyethylene) that excluded natural rainfall, supplemented by deficit irrigation (50% of full evapotranspiration, applied weekly via drip lines). Non-stressed plots received full irrigation to maintain soil moisture at 70–80% of field capacity, monitored with ECH₂O soil moisture probes (Decagon Devices, USA) at 10, 20, and 40 cm depths. All plots received standard basal fertilization (120 kg N ha⁻¹, 60 kg P₂O₅ ha⁻¹, 75 kg K₂O ha⁻¹) and were kept weed-free by hand.

 Data Collection and Sample Analysis

Data were collected on plant growth, physiological traits, yield components, and resource-use efficiency. At the V6, R1 (silking), and R6 (physiological maturity) stages, three representative plants per plot were destructively sampled to determine leaf area index (LI-3100C area meter, LI-COR, USA), aboveground biomass (oven-dried at 75°C to constant weight), and root biomass (soil cores to 60 cm depth, washed over a 0.5 mm sieve). Chlorophyll content was measured with a SPAD-502 meter (Minolta, Japan) and canopy temperature with an infrared thermometer (Fluke TI400, USA) at three positions per plot. Photosynthetic rate, stomatal conductance, and transpiration were measured on the uppermost fully expanded leaf using a LI-6800 portable photosynthesis system (LI-COR, USA) between 09:00 and 11:00 on clear days. Soil moisture content was determined gravimetrically every 10 days to calibrate continuous probe readings.

At maturity, plants from a 2 m² central area of each plot were harvested to determine grain yield (adjusted to 14% moisture), yield components (ears per plant, kernels per ear, 1000-grain weight for maize; pods per plant, seeds per pod, 100-seed weight for soybean), and harvest index. Land equivalent ratio (LER) was calculated as the sum of the partial LERs of the two component crops. Water use efficiency (WUE) was calculated as grain yield divided by seasonal evapotranspiration, estimated from soil water balance using probe and precipitation/irrigation records.

 Statistical Analysis

Data were analyzed using R version 4.3.2 (R Core Team, 2023). Treatment effects on all measured variables were tested with linear mixed-effects models using the lme4 package, with treatment as a fixed effect and block and year as random effects; when year × treatment interactions were non-significant, data were pooled across seasons. Normality and homoscedasticity were verified using Shapiro–Wilk and Levene tests, and log transformations were applied where necessary. Post-hoc separation of means was performed using Tukey's HSD test at α = 0.05. Two-way analysis of variance was used to assess the main and interactive effects of cropping system (sole vs. intercrop) and water regime (well-watered vs. drought). Relationships among physiological traits and yield were examined using Pearson correlation coefficients and stepwise multiple regression. Results are presented as means ± standard error.

title: art history|patronage and workshop practice in Ming dynasty court painting
text: This article examines the relationship between imperial patronage and workshop practice in Ming dynasty (1368–1644) court painting, arguing that the structural conditions of court employment profoundly shaped artistic production. Drawing on painted works, archival records, and colophons, it challenges the persistent historiographic divide between the professional workshops of the early Ming and the scholar-amateur aesthetics later championed by literati critics. The study first analyzes the institutional frameworks through which emperors commissioned painting—most notably the Renzhi dian and Wuying dian workshops—and demonstrates how court painters such as Bian Wenjin and Shang Xi operated within collaborative hierarchies that governed drafting, execution, and finishing. Close visual analysis of large-scale ceremonial and auspicious subjects, including dragon-and-phoenix compositions and imperial portraiture, reveals standardized motifs, shared brush conventions, and division of labor that point to workshop coordination rather than individual authorship. The article further considers how later sixteenth-century emperors, particularly the Jiajing emperor, redirected patronage toward Daoist subjects, prompting shifts in workshop organization and specialization. By reconstructing the social and material conditions of court painting—including painters' hereditary status, ranks, and mobility between court and commercial spheres—this study reframes Ming court works as products of institutional practice rather than mere reflections of imperial ideology. It concludes that attention to patronage structures and workshop dynamics offers a more nuanced account of stylistic change and artistic agency at the Ming court, complicating narratives that privilege literati autonomy over courtly collaboration.

title: law|data protection obligations of cross-border e-commerce platforms
text:
The rapid expansion of cross-border electronic commerce has produced a class of commercial actors whose operations are, by design, jurisdictionally dispersed. Platforms that mediate the sale of goods and services between merchants and consumers across national borders routinely process personal data in multiple legal systems simultaneously: account and identity data are collected at registration, payment and address data are transferred to facilitate fulfilment, behavioural and transactional data are analysed to power recommendation engines and fraud detection, and data are shared with logistics providers, payment intermediaries and marketing partners scattered across continents. This architecture of distributed data processing places cross-border e-commerce platforms at the centre of one of the most contested questions in contemporary information law: how, and according to whose rules, should personal data be protected when commercial activity does not respect territorial boundaries?

The legal landscape governing this question is characterised less by the absence of regulation than by its proliferation. Since the entry into force of the General Data Protection Regulation, the European Union has asserted a broad territorial reach over processing activities connected to the offering of goods or services to, or the monitoring of, individuals within the Union (Article 3(2) GDPR). The Court of Justice of the European Union has reinforced this extraterritorial ambition in its case law, most notably in Google Spain, which established that search engine operators may be obliged to remove links from results displayed to European users, and in subsequent decisions clarifying the conditions under which non-establishment controllers fall within the Regulation's scope (CJEU 2014; Kuner 2020). Comparable, if differently calibrated, regimes have emerged elsewhere: China's Personal Information Protection Law, the Brazilian Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados, India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, and a growing cohort of comprehensive statutes across Asia, Latin America and Africa have each adopted their own definitions of personal data, their own lawful bases for processing, their own rules on cross-border transfers, and their own enforcement machinery (Greenleaf 2023). The result is a fragmented global framework in which a single platform's data processing operation may be subject to a dozen or more overlapping and sometimes conflicting obligations.

This fragmentation generates distinctive compliance problems for cross-border e-commerce platforms. The first is the problem of applicable law: determining which regime governs a given processing operation requires an assessment of establishment, targeting, monitoring and the location of data subjects, and the criteria used to make that assessment differ materially between regimes (Svantesson 2017). The second is the problem of transfer regulation: platforms that centralise data processing in regional hubs must navigate export restriction regimes that range from the European adequacy and standard contractual clause model, through the Chinese security assessment and standard contract mechanisms, to the more permissive but increasingly conditional approaches adopted in other jurisdictions (Kuner 2020; Zhao and others 2022). The third is the problem of allocation: where a platform operates through subsidiaries, local agents and third-party service providers, the attribution of controller and processor responsibilities is frequently ambiguous, and the contractual instruments used to allocate those responsibilities must satisfy multiple legal systems at once (Article 29 Working Party 2017). The fourth is the problem of enforcement: supervisory authorities increasingly cooperate through mechanisms such as the GDPR's consistency mechanism and one-stop-shop, but cross-border enforcement against platforms without local establishment remains uneven, and the risk of divergent regulatory outcomes for identical conduct is substantial (CJEU 2014; Bennett and Raab 2020).

Scholarship on platform regulation has begun to address these issues, but much of the existing literature examines data protection, consumer protection and e-commerce regulation in isolation from one another. Studies of platform liability tend to focus on intermediary responsibility for illegal content or unsafe products rather than on the data protection obligations that attach to the platform's own processing activities (Busch 2021). Conversely, data protection scholarship has devoted considerable attention to the extraterritorial scope of the GDPR and to transfer mechanisms, but has engaged less systematically with the specific operational realities of cross-border retail platforms, whose data flows are shaped by payment processing, logistics, customs clearance and marketplace intermediation in ways that differ from those of social media or search providers (Kuner 2020; Svantesson 2017). The result is a gap in the literature: there is as yet no comprehensive account of how the full set of data protection obligations — lawful basis, transparency, data minimisation, security, transfer restrictions, and accountability — operates in practice for cross-border e-commerce platforms, nor of how those platforms can reconcile divergent obligations across the major regulatory regimes to which they are subject.

This paper addresses that gap. It argues that the data protection obligations of cross-border e-commerce platforms cannot be understood through a single jurisdictional lens, and that effective compliance requires a layered approach in which platform operators map their processing activities against the most demanding applicable regimes and design governance structures capable of accommodating regulatory divergence. Drawing on a comparative analysis of the GDPR, the PIPL and selected other regimes, together with an examination of platform business models and data flows, the paper develops a framework for identifying and allocating data protection obligations across the platform ecosystem. The analysis proceeds in four parts. Part II sets out the regulatory landscape and the criteria for territorial application. Part III examines the specific obligations that arise across the platform's data lifecycle, from collection through transfer to retention and deletion. Part IV analyses the allocation of responsibility among platforms, merchants and service providers, and the contractual and technical mechanisms available to manage it. Part V considers enforcement risk and the prospects for regulatory convergence, before the paper concludes with recommendations for platform operators and for policymakers.

title: history|the role of Venetian merchants in the fourteenth-century spice trade
text:
The Role of Venetian Merchants in the Fourteenth-Century Spice Trade: A Historiographical Review

The fourteenth-century spice trade has long occupied a central place in the economic history of medieval Europe, and within that historiography Venetian merchants have functioned as both subject and synecdoche: to study the pepper, ginger, cinnamon and clove that moved from the Levant to the lagoon is, in much of the literature, to study Venice itself. Yet the scholarly consensus on what exactly Venetian merchants did, and how decisive their role really was, has shifted considerably over the past half-century. This review traces four overlapping bodies of scholarship: the classic institutional and commercial studies that established the Venetian "commercial revolution"; the quantitative and price-history tradition; the revisionist work that provincialised Venice within a wider Mediterranean and Mamluk framework; and the recent turn toward merchant culture, networks and materiality.

The foundational layer remains the institutional history of the late thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. Lane (1973) and, later, Lane and Mueller (1985) portrayed Venetian commerce as a sophisticated machine of state-supported galley convoys, the mude, whose fixed sailing schedules to Alexandria, Beirut and Constantinople gave Venetian merchants a structural advantage in the distribution of Eastern aromatics. This account dovetailed with Lopez's (1976) broader narrative of a medieval commercial revolution in which Italians, and Venetians above all, substituted rational accounting, maritime insurance and negotiable credit instruments for the personal and itinerant commerce of earlier centuries. On this view the Venetian merchant was less a travelling adventurer than a sedentary investor operating through commissions, bills of exchange and family partnerships such as the corner (Lane 1973; Lopez 1976).

A second strand is quantitative. The punctual publication of notarial and customs records, above all the Venetian documentary series edited by Thomas and others (Thomas 2004), permitted historians to reconstruct cargo manifests, freight rates and pepper prices with unusual precision. The resulting price series underpinned the influential argument that Venetian merchants functioned as arbitrageurs between Mamluk Alexandria and the markets of the Adriatic and Germany, capturing margins through superior information and control of shipping rather than through monopoly (Thomas 2004; Goldberg 2005). Goldberg's (2005) comparison of Venetian and Genoese pepper prices is particularly instructive: it demonstrates that Venice's edge lay less in purchasing power at Alexandria than in the reliability and frequency of its return voyages, a conclusion that qualified earlier assumptions of Venetian commercial supremacy.

The third and most contentious body of work is revisionist. Ashtor (1976), working from Geniza and Mamluk sources, argued that the fourteenth century witnessed a relative decline in Italian access to Eastern spices, driven by Mamluk fiscal policy and by the diversion of trade through the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf. His account challenged the Venetian-centred narrative by relocating agency to Cairo and to the Karimi merchants. Subsequent scholarship has softened but not dissolved this challenge: Apellániz (2011) documents the persistence of Venetian-Alexandrian exchange well into the fifteenth century, while Jacoby (2005) shows that Venetian merchants in Constantinople and the Black Sea functioned as intermediaries in a genuinely multi-polar network rather than as the sole gatekeepers of Europe's spice supply. Genoese competition, emphasised by Balard (1995), further qualifies any picture of Venetian monopoly.

Finally, a newer cultural and social history has reframed the merchant not as a price-taking rational actor but as a member of confraternities, a patron of art and a bearer of practical knowledge. Mack (2002) reconstructs Venetian mercantile self-fashioning through wills and devotional bequests, and the material-culture literature on spices as markers of status (Freedman 2008) insists that consumption, not merely carriage, shaped the trade. These studies remind us that the "role" of Venetian merchants was simultaneously economic, institutional and cultural.

Taken together, the literature has moved from a triumphalist account of Venetian organisational genius toward a more contingent picture: Venetian merchants were indispensable but not omnipotent brokers, whose advantage rested on shipping regularity, credit and diaspora networks rather than on exclusive control of supply. The most pressing gap remains the systematic integration of Mamluk fiscal records with Venetian notarial data, a task begun but far from complete (Apellániz 2011; Thomas 2004).

References

Apellániz, F. (2011) 'Venetian trading networks in the medieval Mediterranean', Journal of Interdisciplinary History, 42(2), pp. 201–223.

Ashtor, E. (1976) A Social and Economic History of the Near East in the Middle Ages. Berkeley: University of California Press.

Balard, M. (1995) 'Genoese and Venetian commercial rivalry in the fourteenth century', in Mediterranean Studies Association, Proceedings. Malta, pp. 45–62.

Freedman, P. (2008) Out of the East: Spices and the Medieval Imagination. New Haven: Yale University Press.

Goldberg, J. (2005) 'Pepper prices and shipping cycles: Venice and Genoa compared', Economic History Review, 58(3), pp. 489–514.

Jacoby, D. (2005) 'Venetian commercial expansion in the Eastern Mediterranean', in Laiou, A. (ed.) The Economic History of Byzantium. Washington, DC: Dumbarton Oaks, pp. 113–138.

Lane, F. C. (1973) Venice: A Maritime Republic. Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press.

Lane, F. C. and Mueller, R. C. (1985) Money and Banking in Medieval and Renaissance Venice. Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press.

Lopez, R. S. (1976) The Commercial Revolution of the Middle Ages, 950–1350. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.

Mack, C. E. (2002) Art and Commerce in Venetian Merchant Society. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.

Thomas, G. (2004) 'Venetian customs records and the Levant trade, 1300–1400', Mediterranean Historical Review, 19(1), pp. 77–98.

title: linguistics|evidential markers in spoken Tibetan dialects
text:
Discussion

The distributional patterns reported above suggest that evidentiality in the spoken Tibetan varieties examined here is best analysed as a system organised around the interaction of two dimensions: the speaker's access to the described situation (direct perceptual, inferential, or hearsay) and the speaker's stance toward the reliability of that access. This two-dimensional treatment departs from accounts that model the Tibetan system as a simple paradigm of three or four mutually exclusive evidential categories (DeLancey 1986; Tournadre 1996; Garrett 2001). In our data, the inferential marker *thæ* and the hearsay marker *zero* were not in complementary distribution in the way a strict paradigm account would predict: in 23 of the 187 tokens of *thæ* in the Lhasa corpus, the marker co-occurred with a reduced form of the hearsay particle, yielding a composite form that speakers consistently glossed as 'apparently, so I hear'. We interpret this as evidence that the two dimensions can be marked simultaneously, and that the composite form encodes a specific epistemic stance—an inference drawn from reported evidence—rather than a simple category blend. This finding is consistent with, though not directly predicted by, the hierarchical account proposed by Aikhenvald (2004: 68–72) for languages with intersecting evidential and epistemic systems.

A second finding concerns dialect variation. The Amdo varieties in our sample showed a markedly higher frequency of the direct perceptual marker *hdug* in narrative contexts (41% of all evidential tokens, against 18% in the Central varieties), and our Amdo consultants accepted *hdug* in reported speech contexts where Central speakers rejected it outright. We are cautious about over-interpreting this: the Amdo sample is smaller (four speakers, two communities) and the elicitation task was not designed to probe reported speech systematically. It may be that the difference reflects genre conventions in the narrative task rather than a grammatical difference between varieties, since the Amdo narratives in our corpus were consistently more richly anchored in the speaker's perceptual field. A targeted study using matched narrative prompts would be needed to disentangle these possibilities.

The acquisition data, though preliminary, point in an interesting direction. Our two child participants (aged 3;4 and 4;1) used *hdug* and *song* productively from the earliest recording sessions, but did not produce *thæ* until well after the age at which adult-like use of the other markers was established. This asymmetry is difficult to explain on a purely semantic account, since *thæ* is arguably the least marked inferential category; we suggest, tentatively, that the delay may be pragmatic rather than semantic, reflecting the later development of the discourse contexts (conjecture, narrative evaluation) in which inferential marking is licensed. This hypothesis is speculative and rests on a very small sample; we present it primarily to motivate further work.

Several limitations should be borne in mind. Our corpus, while larger than those used in most previous work on Tibetan evidentiality, is skewed toward male speakers over 40 in the Central varieties, and the elicitation component relied heavily on translation from Chinese, which may have primed particular evidential choices. The composite *thæ* + hearsay form, in particular, was rare enough (23 tokens) that our characterisation of its function should be treated as provisional. Finally, our transcription conventions collapsed some phonological distinctions that may prove relevant; the reduced hearsay particle, in particular, was transcribed uniformly despite noticeable phonetic variation across speakers.

Conclusion

The evidence presented here supports a two-dimensional analysis of evidential marking in spoken Tibetan, in which access type and epistemic stance are marked independently and can co-occur. This account accommodates the composite forms that a strict paradigm analysis leaves unaccounted for, and it aligns the Tibetan data with cross-linguistic work on intersecting evidential-epistemic systems. At the same time, the dialect differences we observed—particularly the greater permeability of *hdug* in Amdo—caution against treating "Tibetan evidentiality" as a single homogeneous system. The acquisition asymmetry between *thæ* and the direct markers, if it holds up in larger samples, would suggest that the pragmatic conditions on inferential marking are acquired later than the semantic categories themselves, a possibility with implications for the broader debate on the semantics-pragmatics interface in evidential systems. We regard the present study as establishing the descriptive groundwork for these questions rather than settling them; matched-prompt elicitation across a wider dialect sample, and longitudinal acquisition data from a larger cohort of children, are the obvious next steps.

title: history|grain prices and famine relief in eighteenth-century Qing China
text:
Here is a methodology section for a history study on grain prices and famine relief in eighteenth-century Qing China.

---

 Methodology

This study employs a mixed-methods approach, integrating quantitative analysis of historical price data with qualitative analysis of archival records to investigate the relationship between grain price volatility and the efficacy of famine relief systems in eighteenth-century Qing China (c. 1700-1799). The research design is structured around three core components: data sources, sample selection, and analytical strategy.

Data Sources

The primary quantitative dataset is derived from the acclaimed "Qing Grain Price Database," a digitized compilation of monthly grain price reports submitted by provincial officials to the central government. These "palace memorials" (奏折, *zouzhe*) and routine reports (题本, *tiben*) were a cornerstone of Qing governance, providing the emperor with systematic information on local economic conditions. The database contains over one million price observations for major grains—predominantly rice, wheat, millet, and sorghum—across various prefectures and counties. These reports typically recorded prices in silver taels per *shi* (a unit of volume, approximately 103 liters), offering a high-resolution view of market fluctuations. To supplement this, we utilize the *Qing Veritable Records* (清实录, *Qing Shilu*), which chronicle imperial edicts, court deliberations, and reports on relief measures, and the *Gongzhongdang* (宫中档, Palace Archives), which contain detailed memorials from provincial governors and granary officials. These qualitative sources provide crucial context on the timing, scale, and nature of famine relief operations, including the distribution of grain from the ever-normal granaries (常平仓, *changping cang*), tax remissions, and direct monetary aid.

Sample

The study defines its temporal scope as the "long eighteenth century," from 1700 to 1799, a period encompassing the prosperous High Qing era and the beginning of its subsequent fiscal and administrative challenges. Geographically, the sample focuses on five core provinces that were both major grain producers and frequently subject to significant environmental stress: Zhili, Shandong, Henan, Jiangnan (specifically Jiangsu and Anhui), and Hubei. This selection allows for a comparative analysis between the politically central North China Plain and the economically vital Yangtze River region. From the vast Qing Grain Price Database, we extracted a purposive sample of monthly price series for key prefectural markets within these provinces. The selection criteria for a prefecture's inclusion were data continuity (a minimum of 80% of monthly observations present for a given decade) and its status as a provincial or regional administrative center. This yielded a final dataset of 25 prefectures, providing a robust and representative sample of price dynamics across our target regions. For the qualitative analysis, we systematically sampled memorials and edicts from the *Qing Shilu* and *Gongzhongdang* that explicitly mention famine, grain price surges, or relief distribution within our selected provinces, ensuring chronological and geographical coverage.

Analysis

The analytical strategy proceeds in two stages. First, a quantitative analysis of the grain price data is conducted using descriptive statistics and time-series methods. We calculate annual and seasonal price volatility, identify periods of extreme price spikes (defined as prices exceeding two standard deviations above the ten-year moving average), and map the spatial diffusion of these spikes. This allows us to pinpoint the timing and location of market crises. Second, we conduct a qualitative, comparative analysis of the archival records. We correlate the identified price spikes with documented relief interventions. For each major crisis, we analyze the imperial and provincial responses, focusing on the speed of reaction, the scale of relief (e.g., quantity of grain released, number of recipients), and the mechanisms employed (e.g., granary sales, inter-provincial grain transfers). By triangulating the quantitative evidence of market distress with the qualitative evidence of state action, this study aims to move beyond a simple correlation and build a nuanced understanding of the feedback loop between market signals and state intervention, ultimately assessing the responsiveness and effectiveness of the Qing famine relief apparatus in the face of eighteenth-century economic and environmental pressures.

title: economics|minimum wage increases and employment in small retail firms
text:
This study examines the employment effects of minimum wage increases on small retail firms, a sector characterized by thin profit margins, limited pricing power, and a high concentration of low-wage workers. Using establishment-level data from the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages merged with state-level minimum wage variations between 2010 and 2023, we exploit staggered policy changes across states and counties to identify causal effects. Our empirical strategy employs a difference-in-differences design with event-study specifications, allowing us to trace dynamic employment responses and test for pre-trends. We find that a 10 percent increase in the minimum wage reduces employment in small retail firms (fewer than 50 employees) by approximately 1.8 percent within two years, with effects concentrated among firms with fewer than 20 employees and in counties with lower median incomes. Larger retail establishments show no statistically significant employment response. We also document heterogeneous effects across subsectors: grocery and general merchandise stores exhibit the largest employment declines, while specialty retail shows muted responses, consistent with differences in labor cost shares and demand elasticity. Firms respond to wage increases through reduced hiring, shortened hours, and modest increases in part-time positions rather than layoffs alone. Our findings suggest that minimum wage policies impose measurable adjustment costs on the smallest retail employers, informing ongoing policy debates about the trade-off between wage floors and small business viability.

*JEL classification: J23, J38, L81*

*Keywords: minimum wage, employment, small firms, retail, difference-in-differences*

title: anthropology|ritual exchange and kinship in a highland Papua New Guinea village
text:
The study of ritual exchange in Melanesia has long occupied a central place in anthropological theory, serving as a privileged window onto the articulation of kinship, political authority, and cosmological reproduction. Since the foundational contributions of Malinowski (1922) and Mauss (1925), anthropologists have recognized that the circulation of valuables is never merely economic but is saturated with obligations, histories, and meanings that constitute social persons and relations. In the highlands of Papua New Guinea, these insights have been developed through a rich ethnographic tradition examining how exchange systems such as the moka (Strathern 1971), the tee (Meggitt 1974), and various forms of bridewealth and affinal prestation (A. Strathern 1972; Josephides 1985) simultaneously create and express the relational fabric of clan-based societies. This paper contributes to that tradition by examining the relationship between ritual exchange and kinship in a highland village, arguing that exchange practices are not simply epiphenomenal expressions of pre-existing kin structures but are themselves generative of kinship, authority, and historical consciousness.

The theoretical stakes of this argument are considerable. Early structural-functionalist accounts tended to treat exchange as a mechanism for maintaining social equilibrium, with kinship providing the underlying grid of rights and obligations that exchange merely activated (Fortes 1969). Subsequent approaches, influenced by practice theory and feminist anthropology, challenged this static picture by attending to the strategic, interested, and often contested dimensions of exchange (Bourdieu 1977; Weiner 1976).
