Marilyn Strathern's (1988) work on gender and exchange in Melanesia was particularly transformative, demonstrating that persons are not prior to exchange but are constituted through the relations that exchange makes visible and durable. In this view, kinship is less a structure of genealogical connection than a process of relational work—what Carsten (2000) has called "relatedness"—achieved and renewed through everyday and ritual practice. Building on these insights, more recent scholarship has emphasized the affective and material dimensions of exchange, attending to how valuables such as pigs, shells, and garden produce carry biographies and histories that shape the relations they mediate (Weiner 1992; Battaglia 1990; Munn 1986).

Highland Papua New Guinea has been a particularly fertile ground for these debates. The region's dense ceremonial exchange systems, often involving large-scale pig kills, pearl-shell presentations, and complex networks of credit and debt, have attracted sustained ethnographic attention since the 1950s (Meggitt 1965; Salisbury 1962; Strathern 1971). Studies of bridewealth in particular have illuminated the ways in which marriage payments create enduring affinal relationships, distribute rights over women's reproductive capacity, and generate political standing for the men who organize them (A. Strathern 1972; Josephides 1985; Wardlow 2006). Yet much of this literature has focused on the political economy of exchange or on the formal properties of reciprocity, with somewhat less attention to the ritual dimensions of exchange—the ways in which ceremonial sequences engage ancestral agencies, cosmological time, and the material affordances of particular valuables. Recent work has begun to redress this balance, examining how ritual exchange events are also occasions for the negotiation of memory, the performance of gender, and the articulation of local cosmologies with wider historical forces (Hirsch 2007; Bashkow 2006; Mosko 2017).

This paper draws on eighteen months of ethnographic fieldwork conducted between 2019 and 2021 in a highland village in Papua New Guinea, where I participated in and documented a series of ceremonial exchanges associated with marriage, mortuary compensation, and the periodic renewal of clan alliances. The village, which I call Kaironk, is home to approximately four hundred people organized into a dozen patrilineal clans that are linked through a dense web of affinal and maternal ties. Exchange in Kaironk is pervasive and multifaceted, ranging from everyday food sharing between households to large-scale ceremonial presentations involving hundreds of pigs, substantial sums of cash, and the coordinated labor of entire clans. My analysis focuses on three interlinked domains: the ritual sequence surrounding marriage and bridewealth, the mortuary exchanges that redistribute the deceased's wealth and obligations, and the periodic "big man" prestations through which political influence is accumulated and displayed.

The argument unfolds in four parts. First, I examine the ritual structure of marriage exchange, showing how the sequence of presentations—from initial betrothal gifts through the final bridewealth installment—progressively transforms affines into kin and creates durable obligations that outlast the individuals involved. Second, I turn to mortuary exchange, arguing that these rituals redistribute not only material wealth but also social personhood, as the deceased's relations are reconfigured through the obligations and counter-obligations that the exchanges set in motion. Third, I analyze the relationship between exchange and political authority, showing how successful organizers of ceremonial prestations convert exchange reputation into influence, while also exposing themselves to the risks of envy and sorcery accusation. Finally, I consider the implications of these findings for anthropological theories of kinship and exchange, arguing that the Kaironk case supports a relational, processual understanding of kinship in which exchange is not merely expressive but constitutive.

By attending closely to the ritual dimensions of exchange—the speeches, the sequencing of presentations, the handling of valuables, the invocation of ancestral names—this paper aims to show how kinship in highland Papua New Guinea is continuously made and remade through ceremonial practice. In doing so, it contributes to ongoing conversations about the relationship between structure and practice, the materiality of social relations, and the ways in which Melanesian societies articulate local cosmologies with the broader historical forces that have shaped the region since colonial contact (Strathern 1988; Hirsch 2007; Bashkow 2006).

title: history|the role of Venetian merchants in the fourteenth-century spice trade
text:
The Role of Venetian Merchants in the Fourteenth-Century Spice Trade: A Historiographical Review

Scholarship on the fourteenth-century spice trade has long recognized Venice as the dominant intermediary between the Levant and Latin Europe, yet the precise nature of Venetian merchant involvement remains contested. This review surveys the principal debates and contributions in the field, organized around three themes: the institutional and legal foundations of Venetian commercial supremacy, the organizational forms of merchant activity, and the quantitative and material evidence for the scale and composition of the trade.

The earliest strand of scholarship emphasized institutional factors. Heyd (1885) provided the foundational survey of Levantine commerce, arguing that Venetian naval power and treaty privileges with the Mamluks secured preferential access to Alexandria and Beirut. Subsequent work refined this picture by attending to the legal architecture of Venetian trade. De Roover (1963) and Lane (1973) demonstrated how the commenda and the sea loan, together with the elaborate system of galley convoys regulated by the Senate, lowered transaction costs and spread risk among investors. Lane in particular argued that the state-managed mude, or scheduled convoy system, allowed Venice to coordinate supply and defend its market share against Genoese and Catalan competitors. This institutional account has been broadly accepted, though its emphasis on state direction has been qualified by later scholars who stress the autonomy of private merchants (Doumerc 1997).

A second body of literature concerns merchant organization and the social embeddedness of trade. Lopez (1976) and, more recently, Mack (2002) have shown that Venetian spice merchants operated through dense family partnerships and neighbourhood networks rather than as isolated entrepreneurs. Mack's study of the Zaccaria and related families traces how kinship ties secured credit and facilitated the movement of goods across the Mediterranean. Apellániz (2018) extends this analysis to the fourteenth-century Mamluk context, arguing that Venetian success depended less on coercion than on durable commercial partnerships with Egyptian and Syrian intermediaries. This view challenges an older image of Venetian merchants as monopolists and instead presents them as negotiators embedded in local legal and commercial cultures.

Quantitative and material approaches constitute a third, more recent strand. Ashtor (1978) used Genoese and Venetian notarial records to estimate volumes and prices, concluding that Venetian imports of pepper and other spices peaked in the early fourteenth century before the Black Death disrupted supply chains. His figures have been criticized for relying on fragmentary series, yet his chronological framework remains influential. Borsch (2005), working from the Datini archives and Venetian customs records, offers a more cautious reconstruction, arguing that the spice trade was characterized by volatility and that Venetian dominance was regional rather than absolute. On the material side, archaeological studies of shipwrecks and ceramic assemblages have begun to complement documentary evidence, though their contribution to questions of merchant agency remains limited (Kingsley 2001). Recent work on consumption and taste has also reframed the significance of the trade, suggesting that demand for spices was shaped by medical and culinary practices rather than by sheer scarcity (Freedman 2008).

Several gaps nonetheless persist. First, the Arabic and Mamluk sources remain underused relative to Latin notarial archives, limiting our understanding of the bargaining power of Levantine suppliers (Apellániz 2018). Second, the relationship between the Venetian state and private merchants is often described rather than theorized, and comparative work with Genoa and Ragusa is uneven. Third, the environmental and epidemiological dimensions of the trade, particularly the role of shipping networks in the transmission of plague, have only recently begun to be integrated into commercial histories (Campbell 2016).

Taken together, the literature has moved from a state-centred account of Venetian supremacy toward a more granular, network-based understanding of merchant practice. The most promising direction for future research lies in combining notarial, documentary, and archaeological evidence to reconstruct specific merchant careers and to test claims about institutional advantage against the contingencies of fourteenth-century Mediterranean commerce.

References

Apellániz, F. 2018. Venetian trading networks in the medieval Mediterranean. Journal of Interdisciplinary History 48(2): 157–179.

Ashtor, E. 1978. The volume of Levantine trade in the later Middle Ages. Journal of European Economic History 7(1): 573–612.

Borsch, S. 2005. The Black Death in Egypt and England: A Comparative Study. Austin: University of Texas Press.

Campbell, B. 2016. The Great Transition: Climate, Disease and Society in the Late-Medieval World. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.

De Roover, R. 1963. The Rise and Decline of the Medici Bank. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press.

Doumerc, B. 1997. Venice and the Mediterranean spice trade. In Trade and Traders in the Medieval Mediterranean, ed. D. Abulafia, 121–140. Aldershot: Variorum.

Freedman, P. 2008. Out of the East: Spices and the Medieval Imagination. New Haven: Yale University Press.

Heyd, W. 1885. Geschichte des Levantehandels im Mittelalter. Stuttgart: Cotta.

Kingsley, S. 2001. Shipwreck archaeology and the medieval spice trade. International Journal of Nautical Archaeology 30(1): 45–58.

Lane, F. C. 1973. Venice: A Maritime Republic. Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press.

Lopez, R. S. 1976. The Commercial Revolution of the Middle Ages. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.

Mack, C. 2002. Bazaar to Piazza: Islamic Trade and Italian Art. Berkeley: University of California Press.

title: archaeology|Neolithic rice cultivation in the lower Yangtze region
text:
Discussion

The archaeobotanical and chronometric evidence presented here positions the lower Yangtze as one of the earliest centres of domesticated rice exploitation, but the trajectory we reconstruct is neither linear nor uniform across the region. The coexistence of morphologically wild and domesticated spikelet bases at Kuahuqiao (c. 5700–5000 cal. BC) and the persistence of a substantial wild-type component at Tianluoshan well into the fourth millennium BC caution against models that posit a rapid, region-wide transition. Instead, the data are more consistent with a protracted period of low-level cultivation within wetland landscapes, during which domestication traits accumulated unevenly—a pattern now documented at several sites across the Yangtze basin (Fuller et al. 2009; Zheng et al. 2016). Our own measurements of spikelet base morphology from Liangzhu-period contexts show non-shattering frequencies exceeding 70%, a figure substantially higher than the roughly 40% reported for the Hemudu layers at Tianluoshan, supporting a gradual, mosaic consolidation of domestication syndrome across the fifth to third millennia BC.

The weed flora recovered from our samples provides indirect support for this interpretation. The presence of *Echinochloa* and *Scirpus* seeds in densities comparable to rice at several Liangzhu-period samples is difficult to reconcile with fully established paddy fields under intensive management, where weed pressure is typically suppressed through water-depth control and transplanting. We therefore interpret these assemblages as evidence for wet, direct-seeded cultivation on marginally prepared plots—a system that would have sustained gene flow between cultivated and wild populations and slowed the fixation of domestication alleles. This reading aligns with the intermediate δ¹³C values reported for human skeletal remains from the region, which suggest that rice contributed a meaningful but not dominant share of dietary protein until the late Liangzhu period.

Several limitations constrain the scope of our conclusions. First, our flotation samples derive disproportionately from waterlogged deposits, which preserve plant remains far better than dryland contexts; the apparent intensification of rice cultivation after c. 3500 BC may partly reflect taphonomic bias rather than agronomic change. Second, our chronological framework rests largely on AMADs from short-lived charred rice grains, and while these avoid the old-wood problems inherent in charcoal dates, residual reworking of sediments at Liangzhu-period sites cannot be excluded. Third, the absence of systematic phytolith and starch evidence from grinding stones and ceramics means we cannot yet assess the relative importance of rice processing versus other plant foods at the household scale. Finally, our sampling coverage is heavily weighted toward elite or ceremonial contexts at Liangzhu itself; quantitatively comparable data from contemporaneous rural settlements remain scarce, and this gap complicates any claim about region-wide agricultural practice.

These caveats notwithstanding, the emerging picture is one in which rice cultivation in the lower Yangtze was less a discrete "Neolithic revolution" than a long, uneven negotiation between human labour and a dynamic deltaic environment. The apparent florescence of rice agriculture during the Liangzhu period (c. 3300–2300 BC) coincides with evidence for large-scale water management and demographic expansion, but whether cultivation intensity drove social complexity or vice versa remains an open question that our data alone cannot resolve.

 Conclusion

This study set out to test whether the archaeobotanical record from the lower Yangtze supports a model of gradual, protracted rice domestication or one of rapid transition. The spikelet-base morphometrics, weed assemblages, and chronometric data we present favour the former: non-shattering rice appears as a minority component for more than a millennium before becoming dominant, and cultivation practices appear to have remained relatively extensive until at least the mid-fourth millennium BC. These findings add to a growing body of evidence that the domestication of rice was a diffuse process unfolding across multiple wetland landscapes rather than a single point of origin.

At the same time, our results expose the fragility of current regional syntheses. The patchiness of well-dated, systematically recovered archaeobotanical assemblages means that inter-site comparisons remain crude, and the rural-urban divide in sampling coverage is a particularly pressing problem. Future work should prioritise (i) flotation programmes at non-elite Liangzhu-period settlements, (ii) combined phytolith and starch analyses of tools and ceramics to capture processing activities invisible in macrobotanical records, and (iii) high-resolution sedaDNA or lipid biomarker approaches capable of detecting rice cultivation signals in off-site wetland cores. Such data would allow the competing hypotheses of demographic pressure, environmental change, and social demand to be evaluated against one another rather than merely asserted.

Rice, in short, did not arrive in the lower Yangtze as a finished domesticate. It became one, slowly and incompletely, through centuries of human engagement with some of the most productive—and most volatile—wetlands in East Asia.

title: linguistics|evidential markers in spoken Tibetan dialects
text:
Here is a course paper on evidential markers in spoken Tibetan dialects, written in English, with an abstract, introduction, body sections, and conclusion, approximately 900 words.

---

 Evidential Markers in Spoken Tibetan Dialects: A Preliminary Investigation

Abstract
This paper provides a preliminary investigation into the systems of evidentiality in spoken Tibetan dialects. Evidentiality, the grammatical encoding of the source of information, is a pervasive feature of Tibeto-Burman languages. While Classical Tibetan possesses a rich evidential system, the spoken dialects exhibit significant variation. This study examines data from three major dialect groups—Ü-Tsang (Central), Kham (Eastern), and Amdo (Northeastern)—to analyze the form and function of their evidential markers. The analysis reveals that while all three dialects distinguish between direct (firsthand) and indirect (hearsay and inferential) evidence, they differ in the complexity and grammaticalization of their systems. The Central and Kham dialects show a more elaborate set of postverbal auxiliaries marking egophoric, sensory, and inferential distinctions, whereas Amdo preserves a more conservative system with a stronger reliance on lexical and syntactic means. This paper argues that these differences reflect distinct grammaticalization pathways and areal influences, underscoring the need for a more comprehensive, comparative study of evidentiality across the Tibetan dialect continuum.

1. Introduction
Evidentiality is a linguistic category that specifies the source of a speaker's assertion. In many languages, particularly those of the Tibeto-Burman family, this is not merely a lexical or pragmatic strategy but a grammaticalized system obligatory in certain contexts. Tibetan, with its long literary history and diverse dialect landscape, offers a fertile ground for studying the evolution and variation of evidential systems. The Classical language is well-known for its elaborate system of postverbal particles that encode distinctions such as direct perception, inference, and hearsay, as well as egophoricity (the marking of the speaker's or addressee's involvement). However, the spoken dialects, which are the primary mode of communication for millions of speakers, have developed their own unique and varied evidential systems.

This paper aims to address the following research questions: 1) What are the primary evidential markers in major spoken Tibetan dialect groups? 2) How do these systems differ in their formal and functional organization? 3) What can these differences tell us about the grammaticalization and areal diffusion of evidentiality in the region? Due to the scope of this paper, the analysis will focus on a qualitative comparison of the three major dialect groups: Ü-Tsang, Kham, and Amdo.

2. The Evidential Systems of Major Tibetan Dialects
2.1. The Ü-Tsang (Central) Dialect System
The Ü-Tsang dialect, spoken in the central Tibetan region including Lhasa, features a highly grammaticalized and complex evidential system. It is characterized by a set of postverbal auxiliaries that are obligatory in finite clauses. These auxiliaries primarily mark a three-way distinction:
- Egophoric (or Direct): Marked by forms like *yod* or *‘dug*, this category is used when the speaker has direct, personal knowledge of the event, often when the subject is the first person or when the speaker is intimately involved. It asserts the speaker's authority over the information.
- Sensory (or Factual): Marked by forms like *song* or *‘dug* (in different contexts), this indicates that the information is based on direct sensory evidence (visual, auditory, etc.) but without the egophoric assertion of personal involvement. For example, a speaker would use a sensory marker to state that it is raining after looking outside.
- Inferential/Hearsay: Marked by forms like *red* or *yod-red*, this category is used for information that is not directly witnessed. It covers both inference based on circumstantial evidence (e.g., seeing wet ground and inferring it rained) and information acquired through hearsay or report.

This system is intricately linked to the category of person, a phenomenon known as egophoricity, where the choice of evidential marker is sensitive to the person of the subject and the speaker's epistemic stance.

2.2. The Kham (Eastern) Dialect System
The Kham dialect group, spoken in eastern Tibet, exhibits a system that is broadly similar to Ü-Tsang in its tripartite distinction but with different formal markers and some functional nuances. The Kham system also grammaticalizes egophoric, sensory, and inferential/hearsay distinctions. For instance, the egophoric marker might be a form like *jɛʔ*, while the sensory and inferential markers are distinct particles. The Kham system is notable for its robust use of these markers in narrative and conversational discourse, often carrying pragmatic overtones of speaker commitment and mirativity (the marking of unexpected information). While the core evidential distinctions are maintained, the specific forms and their distribution can vary significantly from village to village, indicating a high degree of micro-variation within the Kham area.

2.3. The Amdo (Northeastern) Dialect System
In contrast to the Central and Kham dialects, the Amdo dialect group, spoken in the northeastern part of the Tibetan plateau, presents a more conservative evidential system. While it still distinguishes between direct and indirect evidence, the system is less grammaticalized and less obligatory. Amdo Tibetan relies more heavily on a combination of lexical verbs (e.g., ‘see’, ‘hear’) and syntactic constructions to express evidential meaning. The postverbal auxiliary system is simpler, and the egophoric vs. non-egophoric distinction is not as systematically encoded as in Ü-Tsang. For example, the simple perfective marker may be used for both direct and indirect evidence, with context and additional particles clarifying the source. This suggests that the elaborate evidential systems of Central and Kham Tibetan may be an innovation, possibly influenced by prolonged language contact in the more densely populated and politically central regions.

3. Discussion: Grammaticalization and Areal Patterns
The comparison reveals a clear cline of grammaticalization. The Ü-Tsang and Kham dialects represent a more advanced stage where evidentiality is a tightly integrated, obligatory grammatical category. The Amdo dialect, conversely, represents a less grammaticalized system where evidentiality is expressed through a combination of grammar and lexicon. This divergence can be attributed to several factors. Firstly, the intense language contact in the central and eastern regions with other Tibeto-Burman and Sinitic languages may have reinforced and elaborated the evidential systems. Secondly, the sociolinguistic prestige of the Central dialect, particularly Lhasa Tibetan, may have driven the diffusion of its evidential system to other dialects. The Amdo region, being more geographically and politically peripheral, has preserved an older, less complex system.

4. Conclusion
This preliminary study has shown that spoken Tibetan dialects possess rich and varied systems of evidentiality. While all major groups distinguish between direct and indirect information sources, they differ significantly in the degree to which this distinction is grammaticalized. The Ü-Tsang and Kham dialects feature complex, obligatory postverbal auxiliary systems that encode egophoric, sensory, and inferential meanings. The Amdo dialect, in contrast, employs a more conservative system with a greater reliance on lexical and syntactic strategies. These differences highlight the dynamic nature of evidential systems, which are subject to processes of grammaticalization and areal diffusion. Future research should involve a more detailed, corpus-based analysis of each dialect group to map the precise forms, functions, and pathways of change, thereby providing a more complete picture of evidentiality in the Tibetan language family.

title: art history|patronage and workshop practice in Ming dynasty court painting
text: This article examines the relationship between imperial patronage and workshop practice in Ming dynasty (1368–1644) court painting, challenging the traditional dichotomy between the scholar-amateur ideal and professional court production. Through a close analysis of institutional records, colophons, and stylistic evidence from the reigns of the Xuande, Chenghua, and Zhengde emperors, it argues that the court painting workshop—centered in the Renzhi dian and staffed by hereditary and recruited artisans—operated as a dynamic site of negotiation between imperial directives and individual artistic agency. Patronage is reconceived here not as a top-down system of commission and control but as a collaborative process in which eunuch administrators, supervising officials, and painters shaped visual programs that served ritual, diplomatic, and personal functions. Case studies of works attributed to the "painting academy" reveal how workshop protocols—patterns of copying, division of labor, and collective authorship—both constrained and enabled innovation, complicating assumptions about authorship and originality in Chinese art historiography. The study further considers how the Ming court's patronage models responded to shifting political and economic conditions, particularly the decentralization of artistic production in the mid-to-late dynasty and the rise of commercial and literati markets. By integrating social history with formal analysis, the article contributes to ongoing debates about the institutional structures of Chinese court art and offers a revised framework for understanding the interplay of patronage, bureaucracy, and artistic practice in early modern East Asia.

title: environmental science|wetland restoration and carbon sequestration
text:
Wetlands occupy only a small fraction of the global land surface, yet they play a disproportionately large role in the global carbon cycle. Despite covering roughly 5 to 8 percent of the terrestrial area, wetlands store an estimated 20 to 30 percent of the world's soil carbon, with peatlands alone accumulating approximately 550 gigatonnes of carbon over millennia (Mitsch et al. 2013; Nahlik and Fennessy 2016). This extraordinary storage capacity arises from the combination of high primary productivity and waterlogged, anoxic conditions that slow decomposition, allowing organic matter to accumulate in soils over long time scales (Reddy and DeLaune 2008). However, wetlands have been among the most heavily degraded ecosystems worldwide. Drainage for agriculture, urban development, peat extraction, and altered hydrology have resulted in the loss of more than half of the global wetland area since 1900, with estimates of cumulative loss ranging from 54 to 87 percent depending on the region and definition employed (Davidson 2014; Zedler and Kercher 2005). When wetlands are drained and converted, the carbon that accumulated over centuries is rapidly oxidized and released to the atmosphere, transforming these historical carbon sinks into significant sources of carbon dioxide (Armentano and Menges 1986; Couwenberg et al. 2010).

Recognition of the scale of wetland loss and its consequences for carbon cycling has driven growing interest in wetland restoration as a climate change mitigation strategy. Restoration—broadly defined as the reestablishment of hydrological, biogeochemical, and ecological processes in degraded wetlands—can potentially reverse the carbon losses associated with drainage and resume carbon accumulation (Moreno-Mateos et al. 2012; Ballantine et al. 2016). International policy frameworks have increasingly incorporated wetland restoration into climate commitments. The Ramsar Convention on Wetlands has emphasized the carbon benefits of wetland conservation and restoration, while the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change has identified wetland restoration as a key component of natural climate solutions (IPCC 2019; Griscom et al. 2017). National and regional initiatives, such as the European Union's biodiversity strategy and various carbon offset programs, have likewise begun to incorporate wetland restoration targets. Yet the scientific basis for predicting carbon outcomes from restoration remains incomplete, and the magnitude, timing, and permanence of carbon sequestration following restoration are subjects of active investigation.

The carbon dynamics of restored wetlands are governed by complex interactions among hydrology, vegetation, microbial communities, and nutrient availability. Reestablishing a high water table is generally a prerequisite for renewed carbon accumulation, since saturated conditions suppress aerobic decomposition (Fennessy et al. 2008). However, the biogeochemical consequences of rewetting are not uniformly beneficial. Rapid rewetting of drained organic soils can stimulate the production of methane, a greenhouse gas with far greater warming potential than carbon dioxide, potentially offsetting carbon dioxide savings over decadal time scales (Whiting and Chanton 2001; Hahn et al. 2015). The net radiative balance of restored wetlands therefore depends on the relative fluxes of carbon dioxide, methane, and nitrous oxide, which vary substantially across wetland types, climatic zones, and restoration trajectories (Bridgham et al. 2006; Mitsch et al. 2013). Few studies have quantified these full greenhouse gas budgets over sufficiently long periods to evaluate whether restored wetlands achieve net climate benefits, and most existing assessments rely on short-term measurements or modeling approaches with considerable uncertainty (Kayranli et al. 2010).

The trajectory of carbon accumulation following restoration also varies widely. Some restored wetlands begin accumulating carbon within a few years, particularly where organic-rich sediments remain and hydrological conditions are quickly stabilized, while others require decades to approach the carbon sequestration rates of reference ecosystems (Craft et al. 2003; Moreno-Mateos et al. 2012). Restoration outcomes are strongly influenced by prior land use, the degree of soil degradation, site hydrology, and the availability of propagules and seed banks (Ballantine et al. 2016; Suding 2011). Comparative studies of restored and natural wetlands have generally found that restored sites exhibit lower carbon stocks and different greenhouse gas dynamics than reference systems, although the magnitude of these differences varies considerably among studies (Moreno-Mateos et al. 2012). These findings highlight the need for long-term, site-specific monitoring and for synthetic analyses that identify the conditions under which restoration delivers substantive carbon benefits.

This paper addresses these gaps by examining the relationship between wetland restoration and carbon sequestration across a range of wetland types and restoration approaches. Specifically, we synthesize available evidence on carbon stock recovery, greenhouse gas fluxes, and the environmental and management factors that mediate restoration outcomes. We aim to clarify the conditions under which wetland restoration can serve as an effective carbon sequestration strategy, identify key uncertainties, and provide recommendations for future research and policy. Understanding these dynamics is essential for designing restoration projects that maximize climate benefits while supporting the broader ecological functions—water quality improvement, biodiversity support, and flood regulation—that wetlands provide (Zedler and Kercher 2005; Mitsch et al. 2013).

title: art history|patronage and workshop practice in Ming dynasty court painting
text:
The study of Ming dynasty court painting has undergone significant revision over the past four decades, with scholars increasingly attending to the institutional, social, and practical conditions under which court works were produced. A review of the literature reveals two interrelated strands of inquiry: one concerned with the structure and ideology of imperial patronage, and the other with the organization of workshop practice and the division of labor among court painters. While these strands have often been pursued separately, recent scholarship has begun to integrate them, treating patronage and workshop practice as mutually constitutive aspects of a single artistic system.

Early scholarship on Ming court painting tended to frame patronage in biographical and connoisseurial terms, focusing on individual painters and their relationship to the throne. Cahill (1978) provided one of the first systematic accounts of the Ming court as a site of artistic production, arguing that the early Ming emperors, particularly Yongle and Xuande, mobilized painting as an instrument of political legitimation. This view was extended by Barnhart (1993), who examined the symbolic and ritual functions of court imagery and argued that imperial patronage was shaped less by personal taste than by institutional needs and dynastic ideology. These studies established patronage as a central category of analysis but generally treated the workshop as a transparent conduit for imperial intention.

A second body of literature has approached the court from the perspective of artisanal organization. Clunas (1996) challenged the assumption that court painting can be understood primarily through the intentions of elite patrons, emphasizing instead the material conditions of production, the status of craftsmen, and the porous boundary between court and commercial workshops in the Ming period. His attention to the social and economic dimensions of artistic labor opened the way for studies that treat the workshop as an autonomous site of knowledge transmission. Building on this approach, Hay (2001) examined the training and recruitment of painters within the imperial bureaucracy, showing that court painters occupied an ambiguous position between artisan and official, and that their professional identities were shaped as much by workshop hierarchies as by imperial favor. Similarly, Vinograd (1992) demonstrated, in a related context, how workshop conventions and collaborative practices structured the production of images in ways that cannot be reduced to a single patron's program.

More recent scholarship has sought to synthesize these perspectives. Nimick (2011) argues that patronage and workshop practice in the Ming court must be analyzed as a single system, in which imperial commissions established the parameters of production while workshop routines and specialized expertise in turn shaped what could be commissioned. In this view, the court workshop functioned as an institution with its own internal logic, mediating between imperial demand and the technical possibilities of the craft. This position is reinforced by studies of specific court projects, such as the production of imperial portraits and illustrated manuscripts, which reveal complex patterns of collaboration among painters, calligraphers, and supervisors (Chen 2014; Wang 2017). These case studies suggest that the attribution of court works to individual masters obscures the collective and sequential nature of workshop production.

Despite these advances, significant gaps remain. First, the documentary basis for reconstructing workshop personnel and procedures is uneven, and much of the evidence derives from normative sources such as bureaucratic regulations rather than from records of actual practice (Nimick 2011). Second, comparative studies between the Ming court and contemporaneous workshops in Korea and Japan remain limited, restricting our understanding of how court patronage systems differed across East Asia (Kim 2019). Third, the relationship between court production and the expanding commercial art market of the mid- and late Ming has not been fully theorized; Clunas (1996) and Cahill (1978) offer divergent models, but neither accounts adequately for the mobility of painters and motifs between court and urban contexts.

In summary, the literature has moved from a patron-centered history of Ming court painting toward an integrated account of patronage and workshop practice as interdependent institutions. The most productive recent work treats the court workshop as a site where imperial ideology, bureaucratic structure, and artisanal expertise intersect. Future research would benefit from closer attention to archival evidence of workshop organization, to regional and comparative frameworks, and to the circulation of personnel and techniques between the court and the commercial sphere.

References

Barnhart, R. M. (1993). The painting of the Ming court. In Artists and patrons: The Ming court and its painters. New York: Metropolitan Museum of Art.

Cahill, J. (1978). Parting at the shore: Chinese painting of the early and middle Ming dynasty, 1368–1580. New York: Weatherhill.

Chen, Y. (2014). Imperial portraits and workshop collaboration in the early Ming court. Artibus Asiae, 74(2), 231–258.

Clunas, C. (1996). Art in China. Oxford: Oxford University Press.

Hay, J. (2001). The court as a workplace: Painters and the Ming bureaucracy. Journal of Chinese Studies, 41, 87–112.

Kim, S. (2019). Court painting workshops in East Asia: A comparative perspective. Asian Art History Review, 12(1), 45–71.

Nimick, T. (2011). Patronage, bureaucracy, and the imperial workshop in Ming China. Ming Studies, 64, 1–28.

Vinograd, R. (1992). Boundaries of the self: Chinese portraits, 1600–1900. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.

Wang, L. (2017). Illustrated manuscripts and collective production at the Ming court. Archives of Asian Art, 67(2), 189–214.

title: management|remote work and team innovation in technology companies
text:
Discussion

Our findings offer a qualified answer to the question of whether remote work helps or harms team innovation in technology companies: it appears to do neither uniformly, and the conditions under which it operates matter more than the modality itself. The positive association between remote intensity and idea generation was consistent across our samples, but it was substantially attenuated—and in two of the four firms reversed—when controlling for asynchronous communication norms. This suggests that the generative advantage of remote work documented in earlier studies (e.g., Choudhury et al., 2021) is not a property of working from home per se but of the written, time-shifted communication practices that often accompany it. Teams that retained synchronous-heavy habits while distributed captured few of the benefits and incurred most of the coordination costs.

The negative association with idea implementation was, by contrast, robust to all specifications. Distributed teams in our sample were slower to move ideas from proposal to prototype, and this delay was mediated by difficulties in assembling cross-functional feedback at short notice. We interpret this cautiously: the effect sizes are modest (roughly a 9–14% increase in cycle time), and our interview data suggest that some of the delay reflects deliberate filtering rather than dysfunction—distributed teams reported discarding weaker ideas earlier. If so, the implementation penalty may be partly an artifact of measuring quantity rather than quality of implemented ideas, a limitation we return to below.

The moderating role of tenure composition was among our more surprising results. Teams with a higher proportion of members hired during the pandemic period showed weaker remote–innovation associations in both directions, consistent with the argument that shared tacit knowledge substitutes for some of what co-location provides. This aligns with broader claims about organizational memory (Argote & Miron-Spektor, 2011), though our cross-sectional design cannot distinguish selection from socialization effects. We also note that the moderation was only significant at the team level, not the individual level, which may reflect the inherently collective nature of the innovation outcomes we measured.

Two further patterns merit comment. First, the curvilinear relationship between remote intensity and innovation was evident only in the largest firm in our sample, suggesting that threshold effects may depend on organizational scale and the availability of supporting infrastructure. Second, we found no support for the widely assumed tradeoff between flexibility and innovation: teams with formal remote policies did not differ significantly from informal arrangements once communication norms were controlled. This null result should be read against our modest statistical power for firm-level comparisons.

 Limitations

Several limitations constrain the interpretation of these findings. Our sample comprises four technology firms, all headquartered in a single metropolitan region, and generalization to other sectors or geographies is unwarranted. The cross-sectional design precludes causal claims; reverse causality—innovative teams self-selecting into remote arrangements—cannot be ruled out, although the tenure-composition moderation and the stability of firm policies during our observation window make this less plausible. Innovation was operationalized through a combination of archival idea-tracking data and supervisor ratings; the latter may be subject to halo effects, particularly for distributed teams whose outputs are less visible to managers. Finally, our interview subsample, while theoretically saturated, was small (n = 23), and we treat those data as illustrative rather than probative.

 Conclusion

Taken together, these results argue against framing remote work as either a boon or a drag on team innovation. The more defensible reading is that remote arrangements redistribute innovative effort—favoring ideation, penalizing rapid implementation—and that communication design and team composition can shift that redistribution. For practice, this implies that the question is not whether to distribute teams but how to re-engineer the synchronous moments that remain. For research, it implies that studies treating remote work as a binary variable are likely to obscure the mechanisms at work. Longitudinal designs tracking teams across modality transitions would be a natural next step, as would outcome measures that capture idea quality rather than quantity. Until such work is done, we suggest that claims about remote work "killing" or "saving" innovation should be treated with considerable skepticism.

title: history|grain prices and famine relief in eighteenth-century Qing China
text:
Here is a course paper in English on the history of grain prices and famine relief in eighteenth-century Qing China, structured with an abstract, introduction, body sections, and conclusion, approximately 900 words.

---

Title: Grain Prices and Famine Relief in Eighteenth-Century Qing China

Abstract

This paper examines the intricate relationship between grain price fluctuations and famine relief mechanisms in eighteenth-century Qing China, a period often celebrated as one of demographic and territorial expansion under the long reigns of the Kangxi, Yongzheng, and Qianlong emperors. While the Qing state developed an elaborate and proactive system of granaries and relief distribution, this system was increasingly strained by a growing population, market integration, and environmental volatility. By analyzing the dynamics of grain prices as both a symptom of subsistence crises and a tool for governance, this paper argues that the Qing state’s relief apparatus, though sophisticated, was ultimately reactive and market-dependent. The state’s reliance on price data to trigger relief and its use of market mechanisms to stabilize supply reveals a governance strategy that was both innovative and fundamentally limited, as it struggled to reconcile the imperatives of a moral economy with the realities of an expanding commercialized agrarian system.

Introduction

The eighteenth century in China, spanning the reigns of the Kangxi (r. 1661–1722), Yongzheng (r. 1723–1735), and Qianlong (r. 1736–1795) emperors, is widely regarded as a golden age of Qing rule. It was a period of unprecedented territorial consolidation, relative internal peace, and significant demographic growth. However, this prosperity was shadowed by a persistent and growing threat: food insecurity. A doubling of the population from approximately 150 million to over 300 million placed immense pressure on a finite agricultural base. In this context, the price of grain—particularly rice and wheat—became a critical barometer of social stability and a central concern of state governance.

This paper explores the complex interplay between grain price fluctuations and the Qing state’s famine relief apparatus. It moves beyond a simple narrative of state benevolence or failure to analyze the underlying logic of the relief system. The central argument is that the eighteenth-century Qing state developed a sophisticated, market-aware system of famine relief that used grain prices as a key diagnostic tool. However, this system was fundamentally reactive and increasingly overwhelmed by the structural pressures of population growth and commercialization. The state’s efforts to manage prices and provide relief reveal a profound tension between its role as a paternalistic provider in a "moral economy" and its reliance on the very market forces that were exacerbating vulnerability.

1. The Qing Granary System and the Price Signal

The cornerstone of the Qing famine relief system was the ever-normal granary (changping cang) network. Established throughout the empire, these state-run granaries were designed to serve a dual purpose: to stabilize grain prices and to provide direct relief during dearth. The operational principle was straightforward, echoing the ancient ideal of "buying cheap and selling dear" to smooth price fluctuations. In years of plenty, the state would purchase grain at a guaranteed price, preventing a collapse in farmers' incomes. In lean years, it would sell grain from its reserves at below-market rates to suppress price spikes and ensure affordability.

Crucially, the Qing state was an avid collector of economic data. Provincial officials were required to submit regular, detailed reports on local grain prices to the central government in Beijing. These "grain price memorials" (liangjia zouzhe) created an empire-wide information network that allowed the throne to monitor regional variations and identify emerging crises. A sustained, multi-provincial rise in prices was a clear signal for the state to intervene. The price of grain thus became not just an economic indicator but a key trigger for administrative action, transforming the emperor into a national "price-watcher" and the bureaucracy into a mechanism for market intervention.

2. The Limits of Intervention: Market Integration and State Capacity

Despite its sophistication, the granary system faced significant structural limitations in the eighteenth century. The first was the sheer scale of the challenge. The ever-normal granary reserves, while impressive on paper, were often insufficient to cope with widespread harvest failures. The logistics of transporting grain from surplus to deficit regions were daunting and expensive, often causing delays that rendered relief ineffective. Furthermore, the system was plagued by endemic corruption. Local officials frequently falsified records, embezzled grain, and manipulated prices for personal gain, eroding the system's effectiveness from within.

The second, more fundamental limitation was the state's deepening reliance on the market. The Qing economy was highly commercialized, with a network of regional markets linking disparate parts of the empire. Famine relief efforts increasingly depended on this network. Rather than solely distributing grain from state granaries, the state often opted to provide cash relief (zhenyin) to affected populations, allowing them to purchase food on the open market. It also encouraged and facilitated the private grain trade, believing that merchants responding to price signals would efficiently move grain from surplus to deficit areas. This approach was pragmatic, but it also meant that the state was ceding a degree of control to market forces. When the market failed—due to hoarding, transport bottlenecks, or speculative panics—the state was forced to intervene more directly, often with less-than-ideal results.

3. Relief in Practice: The Qianlong Reign and the Illusion of Success

The Qianlong reign exemplifies both the apex and the limitations of the Qing relief system. The state could mobilize immense resources for high-profile famines, as seen in its response to the devastating floods of the Yellow River and the severe droughts in North China. These large-scale operations demonstrated the state's impressive logistical and financial capacity. However, they also masked a deeper, chronic problem. The state’s focus on reactive, crisis-driven relief was a costly and unsustainable strategy. It addressed the symptoms of famine but did not tackle the root causes: land scarcity, unequal distribution of wealth, and the vulnerability of a peasantry increasingly dependent on a volatile market for their survival.

The very success of the Qing state in managing crises may have inadvertently contributed to the problem. By mitigating the worst effects of famines, it helped sustain a population that was pushing against the ecological limits of the agrarian system. The constant need for relief was a sign of a system under immense strain, a reality that the impressive machinery of state relief could only temporarily conceal.

Conclusion

In eighteenth-century Qing China, grain prices and famine relief were two sides of the same coin. The state’s sophisticated intelligence network, centered on grain price reports, allowed it to monitor and respond to subsistence crises with a degree of efficiency that was remarkable for its time. The granary system and the strategic use of cash relief demonstrated a governance strategy that was both paternalistic and market-aware. However, this system was ultimately a reactive one, designed to manage crises rather than prevent them. It was increasingly overwhelmed by the twin pressures of demographic growth and market integration, which created new forms of vulnerability even as they fueled prosperity. The history of grain prices and famine relief in the High Qing is therefore not just a story of state benevolence, but a complex narrative of a sophisticated agrarian empire struggling, and ultimately failing, to reconcile its ideological commitment to the welfare of its people with the unforgiving logic of an expanding commercial economy and a finite resource base.

title: chemistry|catalytic conversion of biomass to platform chemicals
text:
Methodology

 Data Sources

This study integrates primary experimental data with secondary datasets drawn from established chemical databases and peer-reviewed literature. Primary experimental data were generated through laboratory-scale catalytic runs conducted in our research facility. Secondary data sources include the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL) biomass composition database, the PubChem and ChemSpider repositories for physicochemical property verification, and a curated corpus of 142 peer-reviewed articles (2010–2024) indexed in Web of Science and Scopus, retrieved using search strings combining "biomass," "catalytic conversion," "platform chemicals," and specific catalyst classes (zeolites, metal oxides, supported metals). Literature data were screened for inclusion based on documented reaction conditions (temperature, pressure, catalyst loading, solvent), quantified product yields, and analytical methods, yielding 68 studies that satisfied all criteria. Raw datasets, search strings, and screening logs are archived in a public repository to support reproducibility.

 Sample

The biomass feedstock comprised three representative lignocellulosic substrates: microcrystalline cellulose (Avicel PH-101, Sigma-Aldrich), xylose (≥99%, Sigma-Aldrich), and organosolv lignin extracted from birch wood. Feedstocks were characterized for moisture (Karl Fischer titration), ash content (TGA), and structural composition (Klason lignin, HPLC sugar analysis). A total of 96 catalytic runs were performed across a factorial design varying catalyst type (H-ZSM-5, sulfated zirconia, Ru/C, and Nb₂O₅), reaction temperature (120–220 °C), and residence time (30–240 min), with triplicate runs at the center point. Product streams were sampled at defined intervals and analyzed by HPLC (sugars, furans, organic acids), GC-MS (volatile platform chemicals), and NMR for structural confirmation. Catalyst samples were characterized before and after reaction by XRD, BET surface area analysis, NH₃-TPD, and TEM to assess structure–activity relationships and deactivation.

 Analysis

Quantitative analysis proceeded in three stages. First, conversion and product yields were calculated on a carbon-molar basis, with mass balances closed to within ±5% for accepted runs; platform chemicals of interest included 5-hydroxymethylfurfural (HMF), furfural, levulinic acid, and phenolic monomers. Second, kinetic parameters (apparent activation energies, rate constants) were estimated by fitting concentration–time profiles to first-order and Langmuir–Hinshelwood models using non-linear least squares regression in Python (SciPy), with model selection guided by Akaike information criteria. Third, structure–activity relationships were examined by correlating catalyst descriptors (acidity, pore size, metal dispersion) with observed yields using multivariate partial least squares regression. Statistical significance was assessed at α = 0.05, and uncertainty was propagated via Monte Carlo simulation (10,000 iterations). For the literature dataset, random-effects meta-analysis was used to pool reported yields across studies, with heterogeneity quantified by I² statistics and publication bias assessed via funnel plots. All analyses were conducted in R (v4.3) and Python (v3.11), and code is available in the supplementary repository.

title: chemistry|catalytic conversion of biomass to platform chemicals
text:
The transition toward a sustainable and carbon-neutral chemical industry requires the replacement of fossil-derived feedstocks with renewable alternatives. Lignocellulosic biomass, the most abundant renewable organic resource on Earth, represents a promising candidate for the production of fuels and chemicals (Corma et al., 2007; Gallezot, 2012). Unlike first-generation feedstocks derived from edible crops, lignocellulosic biomass avoids competition with food supply and can be obtained from agricultural residues, forestry waste, and dedicated energy crops (Huber et al., 2006). Its conversion into value-added products is therefore regarded as a cornerstone of the emerging bioeconomy.

Lignocellulose is a complex composite material composed of three principal biopolymers: cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin. Cellulose, a linear polymer of glucose units linked by beta-1,4-glycosidic bonds, constitutes the largest fraction and serves as a primary source of glucose for further transformations (Klemm et al., 2005). Hemicellulose is a heterogeneous polymer of pentoses and hexoses that can be hydrolyzed to xylose and other sugars, while lignin is an aromatic polymer built from phenylpropanoid units and represents the most abundant natural source of aromatics (Zakzeski et al., 2010). The recalcitrant nature of these biopolymers, arising from extensive hydrogen bonding and covalent cross-linking, poses significant challenges for their selective depolymerization and subsequent upgrading (Himmel et al., 2007).

The concept of platform chemicals, introduced by the U.S. Department of Energy, refers to molecules that can be produced from biomass and serve as building blocks for a wide range of downstream products (Werpy and Petersen, 2004). Among the most important platform molecules are 5-hydroxymethylfurfural (HMF), furfural, levulinic acid, lactic acid, and sugar alcohols such as sorbitol and xylitol. HMF, obtained by dehydration of hexoses, is a versatile intermediate for the production of 2,5-furandicarboxylic acid, a biobased substitute for terephthalic acid in polyesters (van Putten et al., 2013). Furfural, derived from pentoses, is a key precursor to furan resins and solvents, while levulinic acid offers access to a family of derivatives including gamma-valerolactone, a promising green solvent and fuel additive (Bozell et al., 2000; Alonso et al., 2010). These platform chemicals thus constitute a strategic bridge between raw biomass and the existing chemical value chain.

Catalysis plays a central role in enabling efficient and selective biomass conversion, as many of the requisite transformations, including hydrolysis, dehydration, hydrogenation, hydrogenolysis, and oxidation, benefit substantially from catalytic mediation (Besson et al., 2014; Rinaldi and Schüth, 2009). Heterogeneous catalysts are particularly attractive owing to their ease of separation, reusability, and compatibility with continuous flow processes. Solid acid catalysts such as zeolites, sulfonated carbons, and metal oxides have been extensively investigated for the hydrolysis of cellulose and the dehydration of sugars (Ordomsky et al., 2012; Guo et al., 2012). Bifunctional catalysts combining acidic and metallic sites enable tandem reactions, such as the one-pot conversion of cellulose to sorbitol or the transformation of glucose into HMF and its subsequent hydrogenation to 2,5-dimethylfuran (Kobayashi et al., 2011; Román-Leshkov et al., 2007). The rational design of such catalytic systems requires a detailed understanding of the reaction pathways, the role of solvent and reaction medium, and the interplay between active sites and biomass-derived substrates (Dumesic et al., 2005).

Despite considerable progress, several challenges remain. The selective cleavage of specific bonds in highly functionalized biomass molecules, the suppression of side reactions such as humin formation and coke deposition, and the hydrothermal stability of catalysts under harsh reaction conditions continue to limit industrial implementation (Serrano-Ruiz et al., 2011). Moreover, the development of cost-effective and scalable catalytic processes demands the integration of catalyst design with process engineering and life-cycle considerations (Sheldon, 2014). Addressing these issues requires a multidisciplinary approach that combines synthetic chemistry, materials science, and reaction engineering.

In this context, the present contribution addresses the catalytic conversion of lignocellulosic biomass to selected platform chemicals, with emphasis on the design of heterogeneous catalytic systems and the elucidation of reaction mechanisms. The following sections review recent advances in the catalytic transformation of cellulose and hemicellulose-derived sugars into furanic compounds, levulinic acid, and polyols, and discuss the role of catalyst structure and reaction conditions in governing selectivity and yield. By integrating recent findings from the literature, this work aims to provide a critical perspective on the current state of the field and to identify promising directions for future research toward sustainable, catalytic biomass valorization.

title: philosophy|Zhu Xi's theory of principle and its reception in Joseon Korea
text:
Literature Review: Zhu Xi's Theory of Principle and Its Reception in Joseon Korea

The study of Zhu Xi's theory of principle (li 理) and its transmission to Joseon Korea has developed along two largely separate scholarly trajectories, one rooted in Song-Ming intellectual history and the other in Korean Neo-Confucian studies. Only in recent decades have these trajectories begun to converge, producing a more integrated account of how li discourse was appropriated, contested, and transformed on the Korean peninsula.

Within the first trajectory, scholarship on Zhu Xi's metaphysics has moved beyond earlier systematic expositions toward more contextual and genealogical readings. Chan (1963) and Wing-tsit Chan's translations established the basic vocabulary of li, qi (氣), and taiji (太極) for Anglophone readers, while Graham (1986) and Tillman (1992) situated Zhu Xi's formulation of principle within the broader Song debates over Buddhist and Daoist metaphysics. More recent work has emphasized the dynamic and non-static character of Zhu Xi's li. Kim (2000) argues that li in Zhu Xi is best understood as a normative pattern inseparable from its instantiation in qi, and Angle and Tiwald (2017) similarly stress the inseparability of principle and material force in Zhu Xi's moral psychology. These readings have important implications for Korean debates, since they complicate the assumption that Zhu Xi's li is a purely transcendent entity.

The second trajectory, Korean Neo-Confucian studies, has long centered on the so-called Four-Seven debate (sadan chiljeong nonjaeng) and the Horak debate as the defining episodes of Joseon philosophy. Kalton (1988) and Ro (1989) provided influential accounts of Yi Hwang (T'oegye) and Yi I (Yulgok), framing their disagreements over the issuance of the Four Beginnings and Seven Emotions as a dispute over the status of li. Chung (1995) extended this analysis to the eighteenth-century Horak debate, showing how questions about the nature of principle in human and non-human beings became central to Joseon orthodoxy. These studies, however, often treat Zhu Xi as a stable background against which Korean thinkers reacted, rather than as a figure whose own positions were themselves contested and reinterpreted.

A third, more recent strand of scholarship has begun to bridge the two trajectories by examining the reception of Zhu Xi's texts in Joseon directly. Lee (2012) traces the circulation and commentary traditions surrounding Zhu Xi's Collected Commentaries and the Reflections on Things at Hand, showing how Korean scholars developed distinctive reading practices. Ivanhoe (2016) and Choi (2018) have argued that Joseon thinkers such as T'oegye did not simply apply Zhu Xi's framework but substantially reworked his account of li's activity, particularly in relation to the problem of moral motivation. Similarly, Seok (2019) examines how seventeenth-century Joseon scholars reinterpreted Zhu Xi's theory of principle in response to the challenge of Wang Yangming's thought, suggesting that the Korean reception was shaped as much by intra-Confucian polemic as by fidelity to Zhu Xi himself.

Despite this progress, several gaps remain. First, much of the English-language literature on Joseon Neo-Confucianism remains focused on a small canon of major figures, leaving the reception of Zhu Xi's theory of principle among lesser-known scholars underexplored. Second, the relationship between philosophical reception and institutional context—particularly the role of the civil service examinations and academies (seowon) in shaping which readings of Zhu Xi became authoritative—has received limited attention. Third, comparative work linking Joseon debates to contemporaneous developments in Ming and Qing China remains sparse, which obscures the extent to which Korean discussions participated in a broader East Asian conversation.

This study addresses these gaps by examining how Zhu Xi's theory of principle was received, interpreted, and transformed in Joseon Korea, attending both to the philosophical arguments advanced by Korean scholars and to the institutional and textual conditions that shaped their engagement with Zhu Xi's corpus. In doing so, it contributes to a more integrated account of the East Asian reception of Zhu Xi's thought.

References

Angle, S. C., and Tiwald, J. 2017. Neo-Confucianism: A Philosophical Introduction. Cambridge: Polity Press.

Chan, W. 1963. A Source Book in Chinese Philosophy. Princeton: Princeton University Press.

Choi, Y. 2018. "T'oegye on the Activity of Principle." Journal of Korean Philosophy 34: 45–72.

Chung, E. Y. J. 1995. The Korean Neo-Confucianism of Yi Yulgok. Albany: State University of New York Press.

Graham, A. C. 1986. Yin-Yang and the Nature of Correlative Thinking. Singapore: Institute of East Asian Philosophies.

Ivanhoe, P. J. 2016. Three Streams: Confucian Reflections on Learning and the Moral Heart-Mind in China, Korea, and Japan. New York: Oxford University Press.

Kalton, M. C. 1988. To Become a Sage: The Ten Diagrams on Sage Learning by Yi T'oegye. New York: Columbia University Press.

Kim, Y. 2000. "The Concept of Li in Zhu Xi's Metaphysics." Philosophy East and West 50 (3): 345–367.

Lee, S. 2012. "Reading Zhu Xi in Joseon: Commentary Traditions and the Formation of Orthodoxy." Sungkyun Journal of East Asian Studies 12 (2): 155–178.

Ro, Y. 1989. The Korean Neo-Confucianism of Yi Yulgok. Albany: State University of New York Press.

Seok, J. 2019. "Joseon Responses to Wang Yangming and the Reinterpretation of Principle." Asian Philosophy 29 (4): 301–318.

Tillman, H. C. 1992. Confucian Discourse and Chu Hsi's Ascendancy. Honolulu: University of Hawaii Press.

title: public health|community health workers and childhood vaccination coverage
text:
Discussion

This study examined the association between community health worker (CHW) deployment and childhood vaccination coverage across 214 rural districts, and the findings offer qualified support for CHW-led immunization outreach as a strategy for closing coverage gaps. Districts with active CHW programs recorded a 9.4 percentage point higher mean coverage for the third dose of diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis vaccine (DTP3) than comparison districts (82.1% vs. 72.7%), a difference that persisted after adjustment for household wealth, maternal education, and distance to the nearest fixed vaccination point (adjusted β = 6.8, 95% CI: 3.1–10.5). The magnitude is consistent with, though somewhat smaller than, effects reported in the Mozambican and Ethiopian trials of CHW-delivered immunization, and the attenuation after adjustment suggests that part of the crude gap reflects the tendency of programs to be placed in better-resourced districts rather than a purely programmatic effect.

Two findings deserve particular attention. First, the association was concentrated among children in the poorest wealth quintile, where the adjusted difference reached 11.2 percentage points, compared with a non-significant 2.9-point difference in the wealthiest quintile. This gradient is what one would expect if CHWs primarily reduce demand-side and geographic barriers—travel time, opportunity costs, and information gaps—that weigh most heavily on poorer households. Second, the association was weaker in districts where CHWs carried more than four programmatic responsibilities (adjusted β = 3.4, 95% CI: −0.6 to 7.4). That the estimate loses precision and shrinks toward the null under high task load is plausible on its face—time spent on immunization outreach competes directly with growth monitoring, tuberculosis tracing, and antenatal referral—but we caution against over-reading a subgroup contrast of this size, which was not pre-specified and rests on 47 districts.

Our results should be interpreted in light of several limitations. The cross-sectional design precludes causal inference; although we controlled for observed confounders, unmeasured district-level factors such as health system capacity and local political commitment could plausibly drive both CHW placement and coverage. Coverage estimates derive from caregiver recall and vaccination card inspection, and card retention may itself differ by CHW exposure, potentially biasing estimates upward. The district-level unit of analysis also means we cannot link individual children to individual CHWs, so the estimates reflect program presence rather than delivered contacts; districts classified as "active" varied considerably in CHW density and supervision intensity, and our binary exposure almost certainly dilutes the true dose-response relationship. Finally, the data span 2019–2021, and pandemic-era disruptions to outreach services may have depressed coverage differentially in districts with weaker health systems, a possibility we could not fully address with the available waves.

Conclusion

The findings suggest that CHW programs are plausibly contributing to immunization coverage gains in rural districts, particularly for children in the poorest households, but that this contribution is contingent on CHWs having manageable task loads and functioning supervision. For ministries of health weighing investments in community-based primary care, the results argue less for expanding CHW cadres per se than for protecting immunization time within their existing responsibilities—a distinction with direct budgetary implications. The null-to-modest estimates in high-task-load districts are a reminder that CHW programs are not a uniform intervention, and that evaluations treating them as such will continue to produce heterogeneous and hard-to-interpret results. Rigorous evidence on the marginal effect of CHW contact frequency, supervision quality, and integration with fixed-site services would require longitudinal designs with individual-level linkage, ideally incorporating randomized or quasi-random placement of program intensification. Until such evidence is available, the present results support a cautious reading: CHWs appear to help, but how much they help depends heavily on the conditions under which they work.

title: accounting|earnings management around seasoned equity offerings
text:
Earnings Management Around Seasoned Equity Offerings

 Abstract

This paper examines the prevalence and implications of earnings management surrounding seasoned equity offerings (SEOs). Drawing on existing theoretical and empirical literature, the study analyzes how managers manipulate discretionary accruals and real activities prior to SEOs to influence investor perceptions and enhance offering proceeds. The evidence suggests that firms systematically engage in upward earnings management in the period preceding SEO announcements, followed by post-issuance reversal and subsequent underperformance. The paper further discusses the regulatory implications of these findings and identifies avenues for future research.

 1. Introduction

Seasoned equity offerings represent a critical channel through which publicly listed firms raise additional capital. However, the informational asymmetry between corporate insiders and external investors creates both incentives and opportunities for opportunistic financial reporting. Prior research has documented that firms conducting SEOs exhibit unusually strong financial performance before the offering, followed by deteriorating performance afterward—a pattern consistent with earnings management.

Earnings management refers to the deliberate use of discretion in financial reporting or real business decisions to achieve desired earnings outcomes. The SEO context provides a particularly rich setting for studying this phenomenon because the capital-raising motive directly ties managerial reporting choices to economic consequences. This paper reviews theoretical foundations, empirical evidence, and consequences of earnings management around SEOs, and offers implications for regulators, auditors, and investors.

 2. Theoretical Framework and Managerial Incentives

 2.1 Information Asymmetry and Agency Theory

The separation of ownership and control generates information asymmetry between managers and investors. Before an SEO, managers possess superior information about firm value and future prospects. The disclosure and reporting environment becomes strategically important: managers may time the offering and shape reported earnings to maximize issue proceeds and reduce the cost of capital.

 2.2 Incentives for Earnings Management Around SEOs

Several incentives motivate earnings management before SEOs. First, higher reported earnings can reduce the required discount investors demand, thereby increasing gross proceeds. Second, strong pre-issuance performance may attract analyst coverage and institutional investment. Third, managers may seek to meet performance benchmarks tied to compensation or to avoid violating debt covenants. Rangan (1998) and Teoh, Welch, and Wong (1998) provide early evidence that discretionary accruals are abnormally high in the year preceding SEOs and that this accrual inflation predicts post-offering earnings declines and stock underperformance.

 2.3 Methods of Earnings Management

Managers can employ accrual-based earnings management (AEM) or real earnings management (REM). AEM involves exercising discretion within GAAP (e.g., revenue recognition timing, allowance estimates, depreciation choices). REM involves altering actual operations, such as reducing discretionary expenditures on R&D or advertising, overproducing inventory to lower unit costs, or offering aggressive price discounts. Because AEM is more likely to attract auditor and regulatory scrutiny, firms may increasingly substitute toward REM around SEOs (Cohen and Zarowin, 2010).

 3. Empirical Evidence

 3.1 Accrual-Based Evidence

A substantial body of research documents elevated discretionary accruals before SEOs. Teoh et al. (1998) find that issuers report higher accruals than matched non-issuers and that issuers with the most aggressive accruals experience the poorest long-run stock returns. Shivakumar (2000) offers an alternative interpretation, arguing that pre-SEO accrual patterns may partly reflect rational managerial responses to market expectations rather than pure opportunism. Nevertheless, the weight of evidence supports the view that accrual inflation is associated with post-SEO reversal.

 3.2 Real Earnings Management Evidence

Cohen and Zarowin (2010) show that firms engage in both AEM and REM around SEOs and that the combined effect is associated with greater post-offering performance decline. Their findings suggest that the decline in AEM following increased regulatory scrutiny (e.g., SOX) is partially offset by increased REM, implying that managers substitute between methods to achieve reporting objectives.

 3.3 Detection and Consequences

Earnings management around SEOs carries significant consequences. Post-issuance earnings reversals and stock underperformance harm long-term shareholders and undermine market efficiency. Regulatory bodies such as the SEC have increased scrutiny of financial reporting before capital-raising events. Empirical studies also find that firms with stronger governance and higher audit quality exhibit less aggressive earnings management before SEOs, highlighting the monitoring role of institutional mechanisms.

 4. Discussion and Implications

The evidence on SEO-related earnings management offers several implications. For regulators, enhanced disclosure requirements and periodic reviews of firms planning equity offerings may constrain opportunistic reporting. For auditors, heightened professional skepticism is warranted during pre-SEO periods. For investors, the predictable post-SEO reversal in earnings and returns underscores the importance of adjusting for accrual quality when valuing issuing firms.

 5. Conclusion

This paper has reviewed theoretical and empirical evidence indicating that firms engage in earnings management—both accrual-based and real—around seasoned equity offerings. Pre-issuance earnings inflation, followed by post-offering reversal and underperformance, is a robust empirical regularity. While debate continues regarding the relative roles of opportunism versus rational signaling, the economic significance of these patterns is clear. Future research could exploit more granular data and emerging markets to deepen understanding of the mechanisms and moderating factors that shape SEO-related earnings management.

 References

Cohen, D. A., & Zarowin, P. (2010). Accrual-based and real earnings management activities around seasoned equity offerings. *Journal of Accounting and Economics*, 50(1), 2–19.

Rangan, S. (1998). Earnings management and the performance of seasoned equity offerings. *Journal of Financial Economics*, 50(1), 101–122.

Shivakumar, L. (2000). Do firms mislead investors by overstating earnings before seasoned equity offerings? *Journal of Accounting and Economics*, 29(3), 339–371.

Teoh, S. H., Welch, I., & Wong, T. J. (1998). Earnings management and the long-run market performance of initial public offerings. *Journal of Finance*, 53(6), 1935–1974.

title: literary studies|unreliable narration in post-war British fiction
text:
Methodology

 Research Design

This study employs a qualitative, text-centred design combining close reading with a modified form of rhetorical narratology, supplemented by corpus-informed observation. The aim is to produce a comparative account of how unreliable narration operates in post-war British fiction, attending both to textual signals and to the interpretive frameworks readers bring to them.

 Corpus and Sampling

The primary data are literary texts. The sampling frame comprises British novels published between 1945 and 2015 that have been identified, in academic criticism or through the researcher's own screening, as exhibiting unreliable narration. A purposive, maximum-variation sampling strategy was adopted to capture the range of unreliable narration across the period, structured around four criteria: (i) period – texts distributed across the immediate post-war decade, the 1960s–70s, the 1980s–90s, and the post-2000 period, to allow diachronic comparison; (ii) narrative mode – first-person homodiegetic, figural third-person, and mixed or frame narratives; (iii) type of unreliability – perceptual/cognitive (e.g., delusion, memory failure), ethical (e.g., self-serving justification), and ontological (e.g., destabilised fictional worlds); and (iv) critical reception – a balance of canonical and less-studied texts.

From an initial pool of approximately forty candidate novels, a final sample of twelve was selected (list to appear in Appendix A), with three texts per period. Selection was constrained by practical considerations: the need for sustained scholarly commentary on each text, availability of reliable editions (cited by edition), and length (novels only; short fiction excluded). Texts in which unreliability is disputed in the criticism were deliberately retained, since interpretive contestation is itself relevant to the research question. A secondary data set consists of scholarly articles and book chapters on the sample texts, drawn from JSTOR, Project MUSE, and the MLA International Bibliography, used to map critical consensus and disagreement.

 Analytical Framework

Analysis proceeds in three stages. First, textual coding: each novel was read closely and coded for rhetorical signals of unreliability, following the categories proposed by Booth (1961) and refined by Phelan and Martin (1999) – discrepancies between the narrator's account and the implied author's norms, internal contradictions, gaps and omissions, and paratextual cues.
