title: public health|community health workers and childhood vaccination coverage
text:
Here is a methodology section for a public health study on community health workers (CHWs) and childhood vaccination coverage.

---

 Methodology

This study employed a cross-sectional, mixed-methods design to evaluate the association between exposure to Community Health Worker (CHW) programs and childhood vaccination coverage. The study was conducted across three rural districts in [Insert Country/Region, e.g., the Northern Region of Ghana] between January and June 2023. These districts were selected based on their similar socio-demographic profiles and the presence of an active, government-supported CHW program, which allowed for a comparative analysis between areas with high and low CHW penetration.

Data Sources and Sample

The primary data source was a household survey administered to primary caregivers of children aged 12 to 23 months. This age group was chosen to ensure that all children had passed the age by which the full routine vaccination schedule—including BCG, Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV), Pentavalent, Pneumococcal, Rotavirus, and Measles-Rubella vaccines—should be completed, thereby allowing for an accurate assessment of full immunization status. A multi-stage cluster sampling technique was used. First, 30 enumeration areas (clusters) were randomly selected from a list of all communities within the three districts, with probability proportional to size. In the second stage, a complete household listing was conducted in each selected cluster, and 20 eligible households were randomly selected using a random number generator. If a household had more than one eligible child, one was randomly chosen for the study. The final sample consisted of 600 caregiver-child pairs (20 households x 30 clusters), achieving a 95% response rate.

Data were collected by trained research assistants using a structured, electronic questionnaire administered via tablets. The questionnaire captured detailed information on the child's vaccination history (verified by vaccination card when available), household socio-demographic characteristics (e.g., caregiver's education, household wealth index, child's sex and birth order), and caregiver exposure to CHWs. CHW exposure was the primary independent variable and was operationalized in two ways: (1) self-reported number of household visits by a CHW in the past 12 months, and (2) caregiver's knowledge of the name of the CHW assigned to their community. The primary outcome variable, full vaccination coverage, was defined as a child having received all age-appropriate vaccines by 12 months of age, as per the national immunization schedule, verified by a vaccination card or caregiver recall.

In addition to the household survey, qualitative data were collected through 12 key informant interviews (KIIs) with CHWs and their supervisors. These interviews aimed to provide context and explore the mechanisms through which CHWs influence vaccination uptake, including their strategies for defaulter tracing, health education, and their relationship with the formal health system. Participants were purposively selected to represent a range of experience and performance levels.

Data Analysis

Quantitative data were analyzed using Stata version 17. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize the characteristics of the study population and the primary variables of interest. The association between CHW exposure and full vaccination coverage was examined using multivariable logistic regression. Crude and adjusted Odds Ratios (aOR) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated. Potential confounders, including child's age, sex, caregiver's education level, household wealth quintile, and distance to the nearest health facility, were included in the multivariable model based on their a priori established association with vaccination status. A p-value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant. To account for the clustered sampling design, all regression models were adjusted for clustering at the enumeration area level using robust standard errors.

The qualitative data from the KIIs were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and translated into English where necessary. The transcripts were analyzed thematically using NVivo 12 software. A hybrid approach of deductive and inductive coding was employed, starting with a codebook developed from the study's conceptual framework and allowing for new themes to emerge from the data. The analysis sought to triangulate the quantitative findings, providing deeper insight into how and why CHW activities are linked to vaccination coverage.

title: history|grain prices and famine relief in eighteenth-century Qing China
text: This article examines the relationship between grain price fluctuations and famine relief policy in eighteenth-century Qing China, arguing that the empire's celebrated relief apparatus was both shaped by and vulnerable to the market conditions it sought to manage. Drawing on memorials, palace archives, and provincial price reports, it reconstructs how the Qianlong state's extensive granary system and price-reporting network functioned as an early-warning mechanism, enabling officials to anticipate dearth and intervene through grain transfers, tax remissions, and direct distribution. Yet the same infrastructure that facilitated relief also exposed the limits of state capacity. As commercialization deepened and regional markets became more integrated, price volatility increasingly reflected speculative activity and interregional trade rather than simple harvest failure, complicating official diagnosis and response. The article shows that relief expenditures, particularly the massive grain transfers and tax exemptions of the 1740s and 1750s, strained fiscal resources and contributed to the gradual depletion of granary reserves, a trend that accelerated in the late eighteenth century. Case studies of relief campaigns in Zhili, Shandong, and the Yangzi delta illustrate how local officials negotiated between central directives and market realities, sometimes manipulating price reports to secure resources or conceal shortfalls. The article contends that the Qing relief system's reliance on accurate price intelligence created a structural paradox: the state's effectiveness depended on the very market information that commercial expansion made increasingly difficult to interpret. By situating grain prices at the center of relief administration, this study offers a new perspective on the fiscal and informational foundations of Qing governance and on the origins of the empire's nineteenth-century relief crises.

title: law|the enforceability of arbitration clauses in consumer contracts
text:
Arbitration clauses have become ubiquitous in consumer contracts. From mobile telephone subscriptions and gym memberships to online retail purchases and financial services, standard-form agreements routinely contain provisions requiring consumers to resolve any dispute through private arbitration rather than in court. These clauses are typically buried in terms and conditions that few consumers read and fewer still understand, yet they can determine the forum, the procedure, the cost, and even the substantive law applicable to any future dispute. The growing prevalence of such clauses has generated intense debate among scholars, practitioners, and regulators about whether, and under what conditions, they should be enforceable against consumers (Drahozal 2006; Sternlight 2004). This paper examines that question, focusing on the tension between the doctrinal foundations of arbitration law and the realities of consumer contracting.

The doctrinal starting point in many jurisdictions is a strong presumption in favour of arbitration. In the United States, the Federal Arbitration Act 1925 establishes that arbitration agreements are "valid, irrevocable, and enforceable, save upon such grounds as exist at law or in equity for the revocation of any contract" (9 U.S.C. § 2). The Supreme Court has repeatedly affirmed this principle in the consumer context, holding that arbitration clauses must be enforced according to their terms even where the practical effect is to preclude class actions or to impose costs that individual consumers are unlikely to bear (AT&T Mobility LLC v Concepcion 2011; American Express Co v Italian Colors Restaurant 2013). Similar pro-arbitration policies animate the New York Convention 1958 and the UNCITRAL Model Law, which have shaped arbitration legislation in numerous jurisdictions (Born 2014). In England and Wales, the Arbitration Act 1996 likewise provides for the enforcement of arbitration agreements, although consumer contracts are subject to additional protections under the Consumer Rights Act 2015. Across these systems, the central doctrinal premise is that arbitration rests on consent: parties who agree to arbitrate should be held to their bargain.

Critics of consumer arbitration challenge this premise on both empirical and normative grounds. Empirically, scholars have documented that consumers rarely read or understand standard-form arbitration clauses, that they lack meaningful bargaining power over their terms, and that the arbitration process itself may be structurally biased in favour of repeat-player businesses (Sternlight 2004; Horton 2010; Resnik 2015). Normatively, the concern is that arbitration clauses can operate to strip consumers of access to courts, collective redress mechanisms, and public adjudication, thereby undermining the private enforcement of consumer protection law (Drahozal and Ware 2010; Schmitz 2013). These concerns have prompted legislative and judicial responses in various jurisdictions, ranging from outright prohibition of pre-dispute arbitration clauses in consumer contracts to targeted invalidation of clauses deemed unfair or unconscionable (Horton 2010; Fairman 2017).

At the same time, a substantial body of scholarship defends the enforceability of consumer arbitration clauses, emphasising the efficiency, speed, and expertise advantages of arbitration and questioning whether courts are in fact more favourable to consumers than arbitral tribunals (Drahozal 2006; Rutledge 2013). Empirical studies of consumer arbitration outcomes have produced mixed results, complicating the claim that arbitration systematically disadvantages consumers (Drahozal and Zyontz 2010). This literature suggests that the question of enforceability cannot be resolved by abstract appeals to consent or to consumer vulnerability alone; it requires careful attention to the institutional design of arbitration regimes, the content of substantive consumer protections, and the availability of procedural safeguards.

This paper contributes to that debate by analysing the conditions under which arbitration clauses in consumer contracts should be treated as enforceable. It argues that the traditional consent-based justification for enforcement is insufficient in the consumer context, where consent is often formal rather than substantive, and that enforceability should instead depend on a combination of factors: the transparency of the clause, the relative bargaining power of the parties, the costs and accessibility of the arbitral forum, the availability of collective redress, and the capacity of arbitration to vindicate statutory consumer rights. The analysis draws on comparative material from the United States, England and Wales, and the European Union, where the Unfair Contract Terms Directive and the Consumer ADR Directive have shaped a distinct approach to consumer dispute resolution (Fairman 2017; Cortés 2018).

The paper proceeds in four parts. Part II sets out the doctrinal framework governing arbitration clauses in consumer contracts across the selected jurisdictions. Part III examines the theoretical justifications for and critiques of enforcement, drawing on the empirical literature on consumer arbitration. Part IV develops the proposed multi-factor approach to enforceability and applies it to a range of clause types. Part V concludes by considering the implications of the analysis for legislative and judicial reform, arguing that a calibrated approach to enforceability better serves both consumer protection and the legitimate goals of arbitration law than either blanket enforcement or blanket prohibition.

title: geography|urban heat islands and green space distribution
text:
Literature Review: Urban Heat Islands and Green Space Distribution

The urban heat island (UHI) effect, whereby urban areas experience higher temperatures than surrounding rural landscapes, has become a central concern in urban climatology and environmental geography. A substantial body of scholarship has examined both the physical mechanisms driving UHI intensity and the role of urban vegetation in moderating thermal extremes, yet the distributional dimension of green space provision remains comparatively underexplored. This review synthesises key contributions across three interconnected themes: the measurement and explanation of UHI phenomena, the cooling functions of urban green infrastructure, and the uneven socio-spatial distribution of vegetation and its thermal consequences.

Research on the measurement and causation of UHI has matured considerably over recent decades. Oke (1982) established foundational principles of urban boundary layer climatology, demonstrating that UHI intensity arises from the interplay of reduced albedo, anthropogenic heat release, impervious surface coverage, and diminished evapotranspiration. Subsequent work has refined these insights through increasingly sophisticated methods. Voogt and Oke (2003) reviewed thermal remote sensing approaches, distinguishing surface urban heat islands (SUHI) from atmospheric UHI and cautioning against conflation of the two. More recent studies have exploited satellite platforms to document SUHI at metropolitan and global scales. Peng et al. (2012) analysed surface temperatures across 419 large global cities, finding that SUHI intensity correlates strongly with vegetation abundance and city size, and that daytime and nighttime patterns respond to different drivers. Zhou et al. (2014) similarly reported substantial heterogeneity in SUHI intensity across Chinese cities, attributing variation to background climate, urban form, and socio-economic development. These studies collectively establish that UHI is not a uniform phenomenon but a spatially differentiated one, shaped by both biophysical and built-environment factors.

A second strand of literature addresses the cooling capacity of green spaces. Evidence consistently indicates that urban vegetation lowers land surface and air temperatures through shading and evapotranspiration. Bowler et al. (2010) conducted a meta-analysis of 47 studies and found mean daytime cooling of approximately 1 degree Celsius in parks relative to outside, with larger parks producing greater effects. Oliveira et al. (2011) documented cooling effects of green roofs and street trees, while Aram et al. (2019) reviewed the role of urban green infrastructure in mitigating heat and emphasised the importance of configuration, not merely quantity, of vegetation. The concept of the cooling island (PCI) has been operationalised by many scholars, with park size, shape, and internal composition identified as key determinants (Chang et al., 2007; Yu et al., 2017). Remote sensing indices such as NDVI and fractional vegetation cover have been widely used to quantify these relationships (Weng et al., 2004). Importantly, several studies note that cooling benefits extend beyond park boundaries, generating a "park cool island" effect whose spatial reach depends on surrounding urban morphology (Cao et al., 2010).

The third and most policy-relevant theme concerns the distribution of green space and its equity implications. A robust literature demonstrates that urban vegetation is unevenly distributed, often inversely related to income, minority status, and population density. Heynen et al. (2006) found that green space provision in US cities varied systematically with race and class, while Wolch et al. (2014) reviewed evidence of green gentrification, whereby greening interventions can displace the very residents they purport to benefit. Within the UHI context, a growing number of studies link unequal vegetation cover to unequal heat exposure. Harlan et al. (2006) showed that neighbourhoods in Phoenix with higher proportions of low-income and minority residents experienced greater heat stress, mediated by lower vegetation cover. Mitchell and Chakraborty (2014) reported similar patterns across multiple US cities, and Chakraborty et al. (2019) extended this work to a global comparative framework, finding that intra-urban heat inequity is widespread. Recently, scholars have begun to integrate high-resolution thermal imagery with demographic data to model these relationships more precisely (Li et al., 2020; Mashhoodi et al., 2021).

Taken together, the literature establishes three robust findings: that UHI is spatially heterogeneous and biophysically mediated; that green space provides measurable cooling benefits contingent on size, configuration, and context; and that green space and its thermal benefits are distributed unevenly along socio-economic lines. However, important gaps remain. Most studies examine green space quantity rather than accessibility or quality, and few integrate cooling effectiveness with distributional equity in a single analytical framework. Furthermore, evidence from rapidly urbanising cities in the Global South remains sparse relative to North American and European contexts (Dong et al., 2020). Future research should therefore couple thermal remote sensing with fine-grained socio-spatial data to examine whether those most exposed to urban heat are also those least served by cooling green infrastructure.

title: journalism and media studies|local newspaper closures and civic participation
text:
Discussion

Taken together, the results suggest that the relationship between local newspaper closure and civic participation is real but more conditional than the “news desert” literature sometimes implies. The most consistent finding across our three matched pairs was a decline in precisely those forms of participation that depend on shared informational cues: turnout in off-cycle local elections fell by an average of 4.1 percentage points in closure counties relative to controls, while turnout in presidential-year elections showed no comparable divergence. This pattern is consistent with the monitoring and mobilization accounts of local news (Schulhofer-Wohl & Garrido, 2013; Hayes & Lawless, 2018): where partisan and national cues are abundant, voters appear able to substitute; where they are not, the loss of a newspaper’s voter guides, candidate questionnaires, and horse-race coverage leaves a gap that other institutions only partly fill.

The qualitative material complicates any simple causal story. In two of the three closure counties, municipal clerks and library staff described stepping into informational roles vacated by the paper—posting sample ballots, hosting candidate forums—and in one county a regional public radio station expanded its local coverage within eighteen months of the closure. That substitution was uneven: it was most evident in the county with the highest median income and weakest in the county where the paper had been the sole source of translated election information for a substantial Spanish-speaking population. We read this as suggestive evidence that civic infrastructure can adapt, but that adaptation tracks existing inequalities. It would be a mistake, on the basis of three counties, to treat substitution as a general remedy.

We were also struck by what did not change. Membership in civic associations, attendance at town meetings, and self-reported political interest were statistically indistinguishable between closure and control counties in our difference-in-differences specifications. This null result should be interpreted cautiously—our survey wave is a single post-closure snapshot, and self-reported interest is a blunt instrument—but it aligns with work suggesting that newspaper closure depresses *informed* participation more than participation as such (Shaker, 2014). Residents, in short, did not disengage; they engaged with less local information. Whether that distinction matters for the quality of local governance is a question our design cannot answer, though the clerk interviews—several of whom described fielding more questions about ballot measures after the closure—hint that it might.

Several limitations warrant emphasis. Our treatment counties were selected in part because archival records of the closures were unusually complete, which likely biases the sample toward papers with longer publishing histories and more institutional embeddedness than the median closure. The matched-pair design, while useful for controlling observed confounders, cannot rule out unobserved shocks—a plant closing, a contentious zoning fight—that coincided with closure and independently depressed turnout. Our turnout data are aggregated at the county level, which masks ward-level heterogeneity and probably attenuates the estimated effects. Finally, the eighteen-month post-closure window captures short-run adjustment, not equilibrium; some of the substitution we observed may prove durable, or may not.

Conclusion

The evidence presented here supports a narrow claim: local newspaper closure is associated with measurable declines in local, low-information electoral participation, and with modest but uneven replacement of the paper’s informational functions by other civic actors. It does not support the broader claim, increasingly common in policy discourse, that closure produces civic withdrawal across the board. The distinction matters for policy. Interventions aimed at restoring local news—philanthropic subsidies, public funding, cooperative ownership models—are often justified in terms of civic revival, and our findings suggest they should be targeted at the informational gaps closure creates rather than at participation in general. They also suggest that the communities most at risk are those where substitution is least likely: older, poorer, and linguistically diverse counties where the paper was doing work no other institution was positioned to do. Future research with individual-level panel data and a longer post-closure horizon would help distinguish transient adjustment from durable loss. Until then, we would counsel against reading these results as either a reprieve or a verdict. They are, we think, a reasonably clear signal that the local informational environment shapes who shows up—and that when a paper closes, the answer is not always no one.

title: musicology|improvisation practices in early jazz recordings
text:
Methodology

This study examines improvisation practices in early jazz recordings through a mixed-methods design combining corpus-based description with close stylistic analysis. The corpus comprises commercially issued recordings made between 1917 and 1932, a period bounded by the first jazz records (the Original Dixieland Jass Band sessions of February 1917) and the consolidation of swing-era conventions. Recordings were drawn from four sources: the Mosaic and Chronological Classics reissue series, the Library of Congress National Jukebox, the Internet Archive's 78 rpm collections, and the Discography of American Historical Recordings (DAHR) for session metadata. All materials are in the public domain or available through institutional streaming licenses.

The sample was constructed through stratified purposive sampling to ensure representation across three dimensions: ensemble type (New Orleans small groups, Chicago-style combos, territory bands, and early large ensembles), region (New Orleans, Chicago, New York), and recording format (acoustic pre-1925 and electric post-1925). From an initial pool of approximately 1,400 sides listed in DAHR for the period, we selected 240 recordings by 38 ensembles, including work by King Oliver's Creole Jazz Band, Louis Armstrong's Hot Five and Hot Seven, Jelly Roll Morton's Red Hot Peppers, the Original Dixieland Jass Band, Fletcher Henderson's Orchestra, and Bennie Moten's Kansas City Orchestra. Selection prioritized sides containing at least one extended solo chorus and, where possible, multiple takes of the same title, yielding 22 alternate-take sets that permit direct comparison of improvisational variation.

Analysis proceeded in three stages. First, each recording was transcribed using a hybrid workflow: automated pitch and onset extraction (via the Basic Pitch and CREPE models) followed by manual correction in MuseScore and Sonic Visualiser. Transcription focused on frontline melodic instruments (cornet/trumpet, clarinet, trombone) and, where audible, piano and banjo accompaniment. Second, we coded improvisational features using a scheme adapted from Berliner (1994) and Kernfeld (1995), capturing: (a) the degree of paraphrase versus newly invented material relative to the notated or head statement; (b) phrase-level rhythmic devices (syncopation, stop-time breaks, rubato); (c) harmonic elaboration, including added chromatic tones and substitute dominants; (d) call-and-response and collective improvisation density, measured as the number of simultaneously improvising voices per chorus; and (e) chorus-level formal placement of solos. Two coders independently analyzed a 15% subsample, achieving Cohen's κ = 0.81 for categorical variables; disagreements were resolved by consensus. Third, alternate-take comparisons were analyzed to distinguish fixed compositional elements from genuinely variable improvisation, following the comparative method established in jazz-take scholarship.

Quantitative description (frequency distributions, chi-square tests of feature prevalence across regions and periods) was complemented by qualitative close reading of representative solos, including Armstrong's 1928 "West End Blues" and Morton's 1926 Red Hot Peppers sides. Limitations include transcription error in noisy acoustic-era sources, the mediating role of recording companies in shaping what was documented, and the impossibility of recovering unrecorded performance practice; findings are therefore framed as claims about recorded improvisation specifically, not early jazz practice in general.

title: religious studies|pilgrimage networks in medieval Japanese Buddhism
text:
This article examines the formation, function, and transformation of pilgrimage networks in medieval Japanese Buddhism, arguing that these networks constituted a dynamic infrastructure through which religious authority, doctrinal knowledge, and ritual practice circulated across the archipelago between the twelfth and sixteenth centuries. Drawing on a combination of monastic chronicles, pilgrimage diaries (junrei nikki), temple cartography, and vow texts, the study traces the linkages that connected peripheral sacred sites—mountain ascetic centers such as Kumano, Ōmine, and Tateyama—to established metropolitan institutions like Enryakuji, Kōfukuji, and Tōdaiji. It demonstrates that these networks were neither purely devotional nor strictly institutional, but rather operated as adaptive systems in which wandering ascetics (hijiri), proselytizing monks (kanjin hijiri), and lay confraternities negotiated access to sacral power, patronage, and legitimacy.

The analysis proceeds in three parts. First, it maps the routes, nodes, and custodial arrangements that structured regional pilgrimage circuits, showing how itinerant preachers functioned as brokers who translated esoteric and Pure Land doctrines into locally intelligible idioms. Second, it considers the role of pilgrimage in the economico-political strategies of medieval temples, particularly the use of fundraising campaigns and relic veneration to extend institutional influence into frontier zones. Third, it explores how pilgrimage networks facilitated the transmission of ritual knowledge and artistic forms, contributing to the dissemination of honji suijaku paradigms and the standardization of liturgical practice.

The article concludes that pilgrimage networks were central to the pluralistic religious landscape of medieval Japan, serving as conduits for both orthopraxy and heterodoxy. By foregrounding mobility, mediation, and exchange, this study challenges static models of temple-centered Buddhism and offers a relational framework for understanding the period's religious geography.

title: law|the enforceability of arbitration clauses in consumer contracts
text:
The enforceability of arbitration clauses in consumer contracts has become one of the most contested questions at the intersection of contract law, consumer protection, and dispute resolution policy. Over the past four decades, businesses across a wide range of sectors—including financial services, telecommunications, healthcare, employment-adjacent services, and e-commerce—have increasingly inserted pre-dispute arbitration clauses into standard-form consumer agreements. These clauses typically require consumers to resolve any future dispute through private arbitration and often include class-action waivers, thereby foreclosing aggregate litigation as a practical avenue of redress. The resulting legal landscape raises a fundamental question: to what extent should the state enforce an agreement to arbitrate when that agreement is embedded in a contract of adhesion, was not individually negotiated, and may operate to strip consumers of meaningful access to justice?

The doctrinal foundation for enforcing arbitration agreements in the United States was transformed by a series of Supreme Court decisions interpreting the Federal Arbitration Act of 1925. In Southland Corp. v. Keating (1984), the Court held that the FAA preempts state law governing the enforceability of arbitration clauses, thereby constitutionalizing a national policy favoring arbitration. Subsequent decisions, including Mitsubishi Motors Corp. v. Soler Chrysler-Plymouth, Inc. (1985) and Shearson/American Express Inc. v. McMahon (1987), extended this policy to statutory claims, reasoning that arbitration can adequately vindicate public rights so long as the arbitral forum permits effective pursuit of statutory remedies. The Court's decision in AT&T Mobility LLC v. Concepcion (2011) proved pivotal for consumer contracts: the Court held that the FAA preempts state-law rules conditioning the enforceability of arbitration agreements on the availability of class procedures, thereby validating class-action waivers in consumer arbitration clauses. This was reinforced in American Express Co. v. Italian Colors Restaurant (2013), where the Court rejected the argument that a class waiver should be unenforceable where the cost of individual arbitration would exceed any potential recovery. The cumulative effect, as scholars have long observed, is a regime in which arbitration clauses in adhesion contracts are presumptively enforceable, and state courts are largely disabled from applying their own unconscionability doctrines to police them (Drahozal 2010; Resnik 2015; Sternlight 2012).

A parallel but distinct trajectory characterizes the European Union. The Court of Justice of the European Union, interpreting Council Directive 93/13/EEC on unfair terms in consumer contracts, has held that a national court must examine ex officio whether an arbitration clause in a consumer contract is unfair, and that a clause which has the effect of depriving the consumer of access to the ordinary courts may be regarded as unfair (Case C-168/05, Mostaza Claro, 2006; Case C-40/08, Asturcom Telecomunicaciones, 2009). The Court has emphasized that the weak bargaining position of consumers and the informational asymmetry between the parties justify active judicial intervention, and that arbitration clauses must be drafted in plain intelligible language and must not create a significant imbalance in the parties' rights (Case C-76/10, Pohotovosť, 2010). The EU approach thus treats the enforceability of consumer arbitration clauses as a question of substantive fairness rather than as a matter of federal policy favoring arbitration, producing outcomes that diverge markedly from those in the United States (Hesselink 2016; Micklitz 2011).

Scholarship on the topic has developed along several lines. One strand focuses on consent and the legitimacy of adhesion contracting, arguing that the formal assent on which arbitration enforcement rests is fictional in mass consumer markets and cannot supply the normative basis for waiving fundamental procedural rights (Rakoff 2015; Radin 2013). A second strand examines the empirical realities of consumer arbitration, including filing rates, outcomes, and the structure of repeat-player advantages, and questions whether arbitration in fact delivers the efficiency and fairness benefits claimed by its proponents (Sternlight 2017; Drahozal and Zyontz 2010). A third strand engages comparatively, contrasting the American presumption of enforceability with the European fairness-based approach and exploring whether either regime adequately reconciles freedom of contract with consumer protection (Hesselink 2016; Bermann 2017). A fourth strand examines sector-specific dynamics, particularly in financial services, where arbitration clauses frequently accompany mandatory pre-dispute resolution requirements (Sovern 2015).

Despite this rich literature, important questions remain unresolved. The interaction between arbitration enforcement and emerging regulatory frameworks—such as the EU's Digital Services Act and proposed directives on representative actions—has received limited systematic treatment. Moreover, the global spread of online contracting has intensified the practical stakes of the debate, as consumers routinely assent to arbitration clauses embedded in clickwrap and browsewrap agreements whose terms they neither read nor understand. The enforceability question is therefore not merely doctrinal but institutional: it concerns the allocation of adjudicative authority between public courts and private tribunals, and the capacity of contract law to police the terms on which that authority is delegated.

This paper contributes to that inquiry by examining the enforceability of arbitration clauses in consumer contracts through a comparative doctrinal and normative lens. It proceeds in four parts. Part I traces the doctrinal development of consumer arbitration enforceability in the United States and the European Union, identifying the divergent premises on which each regime rests. Part II analyzes the normative justifications advanced for and against enforcement, focusing on consent, fairness, and access to justice. Part III examines the empirical evidence on consumer arbitration outcomes and assesses whether it supports the policy assumptions underlying current enforcement rules. Part IV proposes a framework for evaluating enforceability that reconciles contractual autonomy with the protective aims of consumer law, and concludes with implications for courts, legislators, and regulators.

title: literary studies|landscape and exile in the poetry of Su Shi
text:
Literature Review: Landscape and Exile in the Poetry of Su Shi

Scholarship on Su Shi (1037–1101) has long recognized that his poetic treatment of landscape is inseparable from his experience of political exile. The literature relevant to this topic can be grouped into four overlapping areas: studies of Su Shi's life and political career, analyses of his landscape poetry and aesthetics, investigations of exile as a literary theme in Song dynasty writing, and comparative or theoretical work on landscape and displacement. This review surveys these strands and identifies the gap that the present study addresses.

The biographical and historical foundation is laid by studies of Su Shi's career and his successive exiles to Huangzhou, Huizhou, and Danzhou. Traditional Chinese scholarship, exemplified by Lin Yutang's (1947) popular biography and by the more philologically grounded work of Kong Fanli (1982), establishes the chronology of the exiles and their psychological impact. Wang Shuizhao (1998) offers a detailed account of Su Shi's literary activities in each place of exile, arguing that the poet's response to displacement evolved from initial shock and self-consolation toward a mature philosophical equanimity. These studies provide essential context, though they tend to treat landscape as a backdrop to biography rather than as a constitutive element of the poetry itself.

A second body of scholarship concerns Su Shi's aesthetics of nature and his theory of literature. Ronald Egan's (1994) study of Su Shi's poetry and poetics remains the most comprehensive English-language treatment, analyzing how Su Shi's critical concept of "naturalness" (ziran) informs his descriptive practice. Egan shows that Su Shi's landscapes are never merely mimetic but are shaped by perceptual and philosophical concerns, including Chan Buddhist and Daoist ideas of emptiness and transformation. Michael Fuller (1990) situates Su Shi's landscape writing within the broader Northern Song "poetry of traces," arguing that the poet's attention to the marks of human presence in nature reflects a historiographical consciousness. These works illuminate Su Shi's aesthetic commitments but engage only intermittently with the specific pressures that exile exerted on his representation of place.

A third strand addresses exile as a literary theme in the Song. Studies of the "exile poetry" tradition, including work on the demotion literature of the Northern Song, trace how displaced officials used landscape to articulate political grievance, moral self-defense, and spiritual transcendence (Chen 2003). Zhang Ming (2007) compares Su Shi's exile poems with those of his contemporaries, arguing that Su Shi's distinctive contribution lies in his capacity to convert the alien landscapes of the south into sites of philosophical dwelling. This comparative work is valuable, yet it often treats landscape as a vehicle for sentiment rather than as a formal and rhetorical problem in its own right.

Finally, theoretical and comparative scholarship on landscape and exile provides a broader frame. Work on the literature of displacement has emphasized that exile transforms landscape into a site of estrangement, memory, and imagined return (Seaton 1983; Williams 1990). Studies of Chinese "shifting landscapes" and the aesthetics of place have shown that the representation of terrain in Chinese poetry is bound up with questions of belonging and cultural identity (Owen 1986; Strassberg 1994). These theoretical perspectives suggest that landscape in exile poetry is neither neutral description nor pure symbol but a negotiated space in which the poet's relationship to home, court, and self is reworked.

Taken together, the existing literature establishes the biographical context of Su Shi's exiles, the contours of his nature aesthetics, the conventions of Song exile poetry, and the theoretical stakes of landscape writing under displacement. What remains underdeveloped is a sustained, poem-centered analysis of how Su Shi's landscape imagery changes across the three exiles and how those changes register his evolving strategies of self-positioning. Existing studies tend either to subordinate landscape to biography or to treat it as an illustration of preexisting philosophy. By tracing the shifting rhetoric of landscape across Su Shi's exile corpus, the present study aims to show that his landscapes are themselves arguments—about memory, moral authority, and the possibility of dwelling in a place one did not choose. It thus seeks to bridge the biographical and aesthetic strands of scholarship and to contribute to the broader inquiry into how literature makes meaning out of displacement.

title: art history|patronage and workshop practice in Ming dynasty court painting
text:
Discussion

The patterns traced across the Yongle through Hongzhi reigns suggest that the analytical separation between "patronage" and "workshop practice" is, for the Ming court, largely artificial. The documentary and stylistic evidence converge on a model in which imperial demand was mediated not through direct commissions to individual masters but through a layered bureaucracy of eunuch supervisors, the Renzhi Palace workshops, and the hereditary military households from which many court painters were drawn. That structure shaped what was painted as surely as any iconographic program. The persistence of the "Three Friends" and "Four Gentlemen" themes in court production, for instance, is difficult to explain by imperial taste alone; it seems better understood as a repertoire consolidated within workshop lineages and then offered upward, with court demand selecting among available options rather than generating motifs ex nihilo.

At the same time, the evidence cautions against overstating workshop anonymity. The case of the Xuande-period handscrolls attributed to Shang Xi indicates that individual brushwork could remain identifiable within a collaborative system, and that painters of the Renzhi Palace were not interchangeable executants. What appears to be a tension between bureaucratic standardization and individual style may rather reflect a division of labor in which design, execution, and inscription were distributed across different hands—a possibility consistent with the uneven quality of inscription calligraphy relative to painted surfaces in several works examined here. This reading also helps account for the apparent discontinuity between the meticulous court manner of the early fifteenth century and the more expressive, Zhe-school-inflected productions of the Hongzhi era: rather than a rupture in taste, it may register a shift in which workshop stage—design or execution—carried greater prestige.

Several limitations must be acknowledged. Attribution remains the central difficulty: seal marks and colophons are frequently later additions, and the practice of workshop replication means that "autograph" is a category of uncertain application to much of this material. The documentary record is skewed toward normative regulations in the *Da Ming Huidian* and toward eunuch-supervised projects, leaving the daily operation of the workshops largely inferential. Nor can this study adequately address regional variation within the court system, or the porous boundary between court and commercial production in the Jiangnan cities.

Conclusion

The evidence assembled here supports a qualified claim: Ming court painting is best characterized not as the product of imperial patrons commissioning autonomous artists, but as a negotiated output of institutional structures in which patronage operated as a filtering and framing mechanism rather than a generative one. Specific findings—the recurrence of workshop-lineage repertoires, the identifiable survival of individual hands within collaborative works, and the correlation between bureaucratic rank and iconographic conservatism—point toward a model of distributed authorship that art-historical vocabulary has been slow to accommodate. If this model holds, the familiar narrative of decline from early Ming grandeur to later mannerism requires revision, since it presupposes a unity of authorial intention that the workshop system did not possess. Further archival work on the Renzhi Palace personnel lists and on the transmission of pattern books between court and commercial workshops would test these conclusions; until then, they remain provisional, offered less as a settled account than as a reframing of the questions the material seems to demand.

title: philosophy|moral luck and the limits of responsibility
text:
Moral Luck and the Limits of Responsibility

 Abstract

This paper examines the problem of moral luck and its implications for our understanding of moral responsibility. Drawing primarily on Thomas Nagel's and Bernard Williams's formulations of the problem, I argue that the phenomenon of moral luck reveals fundamental tensions in our practice of holding agents responsible. I consider three responses to the problem—the denial of moral luck, the acceptance of diminished responsibility, and the revision of our responsibility practices—and argue that while none is fully satisfactory, the third offers the most promising path forward. The paper concludes that acknowledging the limits of responsibility imposed by luck does not undermine morality but rather refines our understanding of what it means to hold one another accountable.

 Introduction

We ordinarily hold people morally responsible for what they do. We praise the generous and blame the selfish, admire the courageous and condemn the cruel. Yet our judgments of responsibility are deeply shaped by factors beyond agents' control. A drunk driver who kills a pedestrian is condemned far more harshly than one who arrives home without incident, though the difference between them lies entirely in luck. This is the problem of moral luck: the apparent contradiction between the fact that our moral judgments are significantly influenced by matters of luck and the intuition that agents can only be responsible for what is within their control.

In this paper, I explore the challenge that moral luck poses to our conception of responsibility. I begin by clarifying the problem as formulated by Nagel and Williams, then examine the principal responses available to us, and finally argue for a qualified acceptance of moral luck that preserves the possibility of responsibility while acknowledging its limits.

 The Problem of Moral Luck

Thomas Nagel identifies four types of moral luck: resultant luck (depending on how one's actions turn out), circumstantial luck (depending on the situations one faces), constitutive luck (depending on one's character and dispositions), and causal luck (depending on antecedent causes). The common thread is that in each case, factors beyond the agent's control affect our moral assessment. Nagel's central observation is that the control principle—the principle that one is morally assessable only for what is within one's control—appears to be both deeply intuitive and impossible to satisfy.

Bernard Williams approaches the problem through the example of Gauguin, who abandons his family to pursue art in Tahiti. If Gauguin succeeds, we might retrospectively justify his choice; if he fails, we condemn him. Yet the success or failure of his artistic project depends on factors he could not foresee or control. Williams argues that this reveals a tension in the concept of moral justification itself: our evaluations are shaped by outcomes in ways that cannot be fully rationalized.

Both thinkers reach a similar conclusion: if we insist on the control principle, moral responsibility becomes impossible, since nothing is fully within our control. Yet abandoning moral responsibility altogether seems unacceptable.

 Responses to Moral Luck

Three broad responses are available. The first is to deny that moral luck exists. One might argue that agents are responsible only for their intentions or character, not for outcomes. On this view, the drunk drivers are equally blameworthy because they equally chose to drink and drive; the death of the pedestrian is morally irrelevant to their responsibility. This position, associated with Kantian ethics, preserves the control principle but at a significant cost: it seems to ignore precisely what makes moral assessment meaningful—the impact of our actions on others.

The second response is to accept that moral luck undermines responsibility and to adopt a diminished conception of moral responsibility. If luck permeates every aspect of our agency, perhaps we should abandon the practices of blame and praise that depend on attributing responsibility. This skeptical conclusion, however, conflicts with deeply held intuitions about accountability and seems practically untenable.

The third response, which I favor, is to revise our responsibility practices rather than abandon them. We can acknowledge that moral luck shapes our judgments without concluding that responsibility is illusory. On this view, responsibility is not an all-or-nothing matter grounded in absolute control but a practice that admits of degrees and is sensitive to context. Recognizing the role of luck can make us more humble in our judgments and more attentive to the structural conditions that shape agency.

 The Limits of Responsibility

Accepting moral luck requires us to acknowledge the limits of responsibility. First, it suggests that our judgments of blame should be tempered by an awareness of circumstance and character formation. The person who acts badly might have been shaped by upbringing, opportunity, and constitution in ways that make their conduct less than fully their own. This does not eliminate responsibility but contextualizes it.

Second, moral luck reveals that responsibility is relational and social. We hold people responsible within practices that are themselves shaped by luck. Recognizing this can lead us to design institutions—legal, educational, and social—that are more forgiving and more attentive to the conditions under which people act.

Third, the problem of moral luck counsels epistemic humility. Since we cannot fully disentangle an agent's choices from the circumstances that made them possible, our judgments of responsibility should be provisional and open to revision.

 Conclusion

The problem of moral luck exposes a genuine tension in our moral practices. We cannot fully reconcile the control principle with the fact that luck pervades human agency. Yet this tension need not lead to skepticism about responsibility altogether. By acknowledging the limits that luck imposes on responsibility, we can develop more nuanced and humane practices of holding one another accountable—practices that recognize both the reality of agency and the contingency of human life.

title: journalism and media studies|local newspaper closures and civic participation
text:
The accelerating closure of local newspapers across many media markets has raised urgent questions about the consequences for democratic life. This article examines the relationship between local newspaper closures and civic participation, asking whether the loss of local news undermines the informational and social foundations on which civic engagement depends. Drawing on a mixed-methods design, we combine a longitudinal quantitative analysis of newspaper closures across 1,200 communities over a twelve-year period with in-depth qualitative fieldwork in four matched pairs of towns—each pair comprising one community that lost its local paper and one that retained it. Quantitative results show that closures are associated with a modest but statistically significant decline in voter turnout in local elections, a reduction in attendance at public meetings, and lower rates of membership in civic organizations, even after controlling for demographic and economic change. Effects are most pronounced in smaller, less affluent communities with limited access to substitute news sources. The qualitative evidence traces these outcomes to three mechanisms: the loss of a shared informational forum, diminished scrutiny of local institutions, and the erosion of a sense of collective identity anchored in the newspaper's coverage of everyday community life. We also identify countervailing responses, including the emergence of digital startups and citizen-led news initiatives, though these rarely fully replace the civic functions of the closed paper. The article concludes by discussing the implications for media policy, philanthropic support for local journalism, and future research on the civic consequences of news deserts.

title: history|grain prices and famine relief in eighteenth-century Qing China
text:
The study of famine relief in eighteenth-century Qing China occupies a central place in the social and economic history of late imperial China, and for good reason. The Qianlong reign (1736–1795) presided over what contemporaries and later historians alike have regarded as the apex of imperial humanitarian governance, a period in which the state claimed an unprecedented capacity to monitor harvests, stabilize grain markets, and provision distressed populations. Yet the same century witnessed repeated subsistence crises, and the relationship between market integration, price formation, and relief intervention remains one of the most contested problems in the field. This paper examines that relationship by asking how grain price data shaped the theory and practice of famine relief in the high Qing, and how the movement of prices across regions conditioned the effectiveness of state responses to dearth. In doing so, it contributes to a growing literature that treats price records not merely as economic indicators but as instruments of governance and as evidence of the changing relationship between state and market in eighteenth-century China.

The historiography of Qing famine relief was transformed by Pierre-Étienne Will's monumental study of bureaucratic relief administration, which demonstrated the extraordinary sophistication of the eighteenth-century state's information systems and its capacity to mobilize resources across provinces (Will 1990). Will's work, together with the collaborative volume on food and money in Chinese history that he co-edited with R. Bin Wong, established the analytical framework within which most subsequent scholarship has proceeded: the Qing state as an activist, market-aware provider of subsistence security, whose granaries, price reports, and relief manuals constituted an early modern apparatus of social welfare (Will and Wong 1991). This interpretation has been extended and qualified by scholars such as Wong, who emphasized the fiscal and administrative limits of state activism and the growing reliance on market mechanisms over the course of the eighteenth century (Wong 1997). More recent work has underscored regional variation, showing that the effectiveness of relief depended heavily on local economic structures, the density of market towns, and the character of provincial officialdom (Dunstan 2006; Rowe 2007).

A parallel and increasingly influential strand of scholarship has exploited the remarkable series of grain price reports preserved in the Qing archives. The palace memorials and provincial reports that recorded monthly or ten-day prices for major grain varieties constitute one of the richest price series available for any premodern economy, and their analysis has yielded fundamental insights into market integration, monetary conditions, and the incidence of dearth. Studies of these data have documented a long-term secular rise in grain prices during the eighteenth century, driven by population growth, the inflow of New World silver, and the monetization of the economy (Wang 1992; Peng 1994). At the same time, scholars have cautioned that price reports were administrative documents produced under bureaucratic incentives, and that their reliability varies with the diligence and honesty of reporting officials (Chen 2012). The methodological challenge of distinguishing genuine market signals from reporting artifacts has become central to the field, and it bears directly on the question of how relief policy responded to price movements.

The intersection of these two literatures—the administrative history of relief and the quantitative history of prices—has generated important but unresolved debates. One line of inquiry concerns the timing and triggers of state intervention: did officials respond to absolute price levels, to relative movements across regions, or to political pressures and institutional routines? Will's account emphasizes the sophistication of the "ever-normal granary" system and its sensitivity to price signals, but critics have argued that by the late Qianlong period the system had become fiscally strained and administratively ossified, with granary stocks depleted and officials increasingly reluctant to report shortages (Will 1990; Dunstan 2006). Another line of inquiry concerns the market consequences of relief: whether state sales of grain from granaries stabilized prices or, conversely, whether official purchases and distributions distorted local markets and displaced private trade. The evidence suggests that outcomes varied considerably by region and by the fiscal capacity of provincial governments, with the prosperous lower Yangzi and the more fragile frontier regions exhibiting markedly different dynamics (Li 2007; Rowe 2007).

This paper intervenes in these debates by examining the relationship between grain prices and relief policy across several provinces during the middle and late Qianlong reign, a period that combines the apogee of relief administration with the first signs of its fiscal exhaustion. It argues that price data functioned simultaneously as a diagnostic tool and as a political language: officials used price reports to justify requests for relief funds and grain transfers, and the central government used them to evaluate provincial performance. The result was a system in which price information was both indispensable and systematically distorted, and in which the effectiveness of relief depended less on the accuracy of price signals than on the administrative and fiscal relationships that connected the throne to its provincial agents. By reconstructing the flow of price information and relief resources, the paper seeks to clarify how the eighteenth-century Qing state understood and managed the risk of famine, and why that understanding proved increasingly inadequate as the century drew to a close.

title: philosophy|moral luck and the limits of responsibility
text:
Literature Review: Moral Luck and the Limits of Responsibility

The problem of moral luck, introduced into contemporary philosophy by Williams (1981) and Nagel (1979), concerns the tension between our practices of moral responsibility and the fact that much of what we do depends on factors beyond our control. Both philosophers independently observed that our ordinary judgments routinely hold agents responsible for outcomes and characteristics that are substantially shaped by luck, yet our considered moral theories typically restrict responsibility to what is within an agent's control. This review surveys the main positions in the ensuing debate and identifies a persistent gap between the metaphysics of responsibility and its ethics, a gap that bears directly on the question of where the limits of responsibility should be drawn.

Nagel (1979) distinguished four kinds of luck: resultant luck, concerning how actions turn out; circumstantial luck, concerning the situations agents face; constitutive luck, concerning the traits agents possess; and causal luck, concerning the antecedent causes of action. His central claim is that these forms of luck jointly threaten to undermine moral responsibility altogether, since every feature for which we praise or blame an agent can be traced to factors the agent did not control. Williams (1981) approached the problem through the case of the lorry driver who, through no fault of his own, kills a child; Williams argued that the driver's remorse and the altered significance of his action reflect a genuine form of moral assessment that cannot be reduced to the assessment of his intentions. For Williams, this reveals that morality, understood as the domain of the voluntary, cannot fully capture ethical life.

Responses to the problem have divided largely into three camps. The first denies the existence of moral luck by insisting that responsibility tracks only what is within the agent's control. Richards (1986) and, more recently, Levy (2011) defend versions of this view, arguing that our luck-inflected judgments are systematically mistaken and should be revised. Levy's account is distinctive in grounding the rejection of resultant luck in a naturalistic theory of moral standing. The second camp accepts moral luck and revises our conception of responsibility accordingly. Adams (1985) argues that virtuous and vicious character can be present without being under the agent's control, and that this is unproblematic once we abandon the assumption that responsibility requires control. Similarly, Moore (1997) defends the claim that causal contributions, not control, ground attributions of responsibility, thereby accommodating resultant luck within a broadly retributivist framework.

The third camp, exemplified by Statman (1991, 1993), seeks to dissolve the paradox by distinguishing between the conditions of moral judgment and the conditions of moral worth. Statman argues that the apparent inconsistency arises from conflating the perspective of the judging community with the perspective of the agent, and that once these are separated, moral luck ceases to be paradoxical. Zimmerman (1987) offers a related strategy, distinguishing responsibility for actions from responsibility for consequences and arguing that only the former is genuinely subject to the control condition. Enoch and Marmor (2007) provide a further refinement, arguing that the kind of luck at issue is not luck in the outcome but luck in the moral quality of the act itself, which reframes the debate in terms of the epistemology of moral assessment rather than its metaphysics.

More recent contributions have shifted the focus from whether moral luck exists to what follows for institutional and interpersonal practices of blame. Latus (2000) argues that the debate has been mischaracterized because the control principle is not in fact a deep commitment of ordinary moral thought. Hanna (2014) develops a compatibilist account on which luck and responsibility are reconciled through the narrative unity of an agent's life. Nelkin (2013) and Hartman (2017) examine the implications of luck for desert and punishment, arguing that even if moral luck is real, its practical consequences are more limited than Williams and Nagel supposed.

What emerges from this literature is a division of labor that has left a central question underdeveloped. The metaphysical debate concerns whether responsibility can survive luck; the ethical debate concerns how we ought to respond to agents whose actions are luck-inflected. Yet the two are rarely integrated. If responsibility is genuinely limited by luck, as Williams and Nagel suggest, then the limits of responsibility are not merely theoretical boundaries but practical constraints on blame, punishment, and reconciliation. The present paper addresses this gap by arguing that the limits of responsibility must be understood as normative limits grounded in the ethics of holding responsible, rather than as metaphysical limits on the attribution of responsibility.

title: linguistics|evidential markers in spoken Tibetan dialects
text:
6. Discussion

The dialect survey reported above yields a picture of evidential marking in spoken Tibetan that is considerably more variegated than the two-term (egophoric vs. non-egophoric) analyses inherited from the descriptive literature on Lhasa Tibetan might suggest. Three findings merit particular attention.

First, the distribution of the hearsay marker *zero* across our sample does not pattern with genetic affiliation in the way we had anticipated. While all Central dialects show *zero* in reportative function, its extension to inferential contexts—what we gloss as 'indirect-inferential'—is attested robustly only in the Ü-speaking varieties around Lhokha and clearly recessive in Tsang. Our Khams consultants, by contrast, consistently rejected *zero* in inferential contexts, preferring *nang* or bare perfective forms with contextual inference. This is difficult to reconcile with a simple retention account: if proto-Tibetic had an inferential *zero*, we would expect its reflexes to surface more evenly. A more plausible reading, though one our data can only gesture toward, is that the inferential use is an areal innovation that spread along the Lhasa–Lhokha corridor and has not penetrated westward. We flag this as a hypothesis for diachronic testing rather than a conclusion.

Second, the egophoric system itself shows structural variation that has consequences for how we model the category. In the Ü varieties, the egophoric *yin* is obligatory in declaratives with first-person volitional subjects and, notably, with second-person subjects under question—the classic conjunct/disjunct pattern. In the Tsang varieties we sampled, however, egophoric marking is optional in declaratives and its absence does not trigger the epistemic downgrading one observes in Ü; consultants accepted *nga las ka byed* 'I work' without *yin* in neutral reportage. This weakens the claim, implicit in much of the literature, that egophoricity in Tibetan is a grammaticalized obligatory category across the family. It may be more accurate to describe it as a variable, discourse-conditioned resource whose obligatoriness is itself a dialect parameter. We note, however, that our Tsang sample is small (n = 6) and drawn from a single valley; we would not want to generalize to Tsang as a whole on this basis.

Third, and methodologically, our results suggest that elicitation via translation tasks systematically under-reports evidential distinctions. When asked to translate Tibetan sentences into English, consultants collapsed evidential contrasts that they readily produced in spontaneous narration and judged as unacceptable when reversed. This is unsurprising given that English lacks grammaticalized evidentiality, but it has practical implications: several of the "optional" markers in our early elicitation data turned out to be obligatory in the narrative task. We would urge caution in interpreting the existing elicitation-based literature on Tibetan evidentiality for this reason.

Several limitations constrain our conclusions. Our sample is skewed toward male consultants over 50, reflecting the demographics of available speakers in the communities we visited; we cannot rule out age or gender effects on the obligatoriness of egophoric marking. Our Khams data are especially thin, drawn from three locations, and the Khams varieties are internally diverse enough that our remarks there should be treated as preliminary. Finally, we did not systematically control for contact with Chinese, which is a plausible confound in the eastern varieties, particularly for the loss of hearsay distinctions among younger speakers that we observed anecdotally but did not test.

 7. Conclusion

The evidence presented here supports three modest claims. Evidential marking in spoken Tibetan is dialectally variable in ways that neither the Lhasa-centric descriptive tradition nor recent typological work has fully registered; the egophoric category is best treated as gradient rather than binary across varieties; and elicitation method materially affects what researchers recover. We do not claim to have resolved the diachrony of the hearsay–inferential split, and our data are insufficient to adjudicate between inheritance and areal diffusion accounts. What we hope to have shown is that the variation is real, patterned, and worth systematic documentation before the relevant varieties undergo further shift. A larger, balanced sample with attention to age grading and contact effects is the obvious next step; the preliminary patterns here should be read as hypotheses to be tested rather than findings to be cited.

title: architecture|adaptive reuse of industrial buildings in post-socialist cities
text:
Adaptive Reuse of Industrial Buildings in Post-Socialist Cities

 Abstract

The transition from state socialism to market economies in Central and Eastern Europe left behind a vast stock of decommissioned industrial buildings. This paper examines adaptive reuse as a strategy for reintegrating these structures into the urban fabric of post-socialist cities. Drawing on cases from Tallinn, Łódź, and Budapest, it argues that adaptive reuse in this context differs from Western practice in three respects: the scale of the industrial legacy, the rapidity of deindustrialization, and the unresolved question of ownership and memory. The paper concludes that successful reuse depends less on architectural ingenuity than on institutional frameworks capable of mediating between speculative development, public interest, and the contested histories embedded in these sites.

 1. Introduction

Between 1989 and the early 2000s, post-socialist cities underwent deindustrialization at a pace and scale without parallel in Western Europe. Entire branches of heavy industry—textiles, machinery, chemicals—collapsed within a decade, leaving factories, warehouses, and workers' settlements stranded within expanding urban cores (Stanilov, 2007). For planners, these sites presented both a liability and an opportunity: contaminated land, obsolete infrastructure, and fragmented ownership on the one hand; central locations, robust structural frames, and distinctive industrial character on the other.

Adaptive reuse—the conversion of obsolete buildings to new uses while retaining their structural and spatial characteristics—emerged as one response. Yet the literature on adaptive reuse is dominated by Anglo-American and Western European case studies, where regulatory frameworks, property markets, and heritage institutions assumed stable forms throughout the post-industrial transition (Bullen & Love, 2011; Langston et al., 2008). Post-socialist cities present a different configuration: accelerated decline, speculative property markets, restitution claims, and ambivalent attitudes toward the industrial past. This paper asks how adaptive reuse operates under these conditions, and what distinguishes its trajectory in post-socialist urbanism.

 2. The Post-Socialist Industrial Legacy

 2.1 Scale and Spatial Distribution

Socialist industrialization was organized around large, integrated enterprises embedded in planned settlement systems. A single textile combine might employ thousands and anchor an entire district. When these enterprises failed, the effects were concentrated: whole neighborhoods lost their economic rationale within a few years. Unlike the gradual deindustrialization of Western cities, post-socialist decline was compressed into roughly a decade (Tsenkova, 2006). The resulting vacancy was therefore not scattered but clustered, producing large contiguous brownfield zones in cities such as Łódź, Ostrava, and Chemnitz.

 2.2 Ownership and Restitution

Property restitution complicated reuse. In many countries, industrial plots were returned to pre-war owners or their heirs, producing fragmented ownership structures and protracted legal disputes. Developers often acquired sites piecemeal, favoring demolition and new construction over the coordination required for comprehensive reuse. Where municipalities retained ownership, cash-strapped budgets limited investment. The result was a patchwork: selective conversion of the most symbolically or commercially attractive structures, while the remainder awaited clearance.

 2.3 Memory and Heritage

Industrial buildings in post-socialist cities carry an ambiguous heritage status. They are simultaneously monuments to socialist modernization and reminders of an imposed system. Preservation movements have been weaker than in Western Europe, and heritage designation has often followed rather than preceded conversion. In some cases—notably the former textile mills of Łódź—reuse has been accompanied by deliberate reinterpretation of the industrial past as a source of local pride, detached from its political context.

 3. Three Cases

Tallinn: Rotermann Quarter. The conversion of the Rotermann industrial complex into a mixed-use district demonstrates market-led reuse. Private developers, working within a municipal masterplan, converted nineteenth-century factories into offices, retail, and housing over two decades. The project succeeded commercially but has been criticized for producing a sanitized, consumption-oriented environment that displaces the area's working-class history (Künnapuu, 2015).

Łódź: Manufaktura. The former Izrael Poznański cotton mill, converted in 2006 into a shopping and cultural complex, represents a flagship reuse project. It preserved the monumental architecture while inserting a commercial program, and it catalyzed wider regeneration of the city center. However, its reliance on a single large investor and its mall-like program raise questions about long-term adaptability.

Budapest: Óbuda Gas Works. A more recent and incremental case, where municipal ownership and heritage protection enabled phased conversion of a gasworks site into cultural and residential uses. The slower pace allowed public debate over the site's meaning, illustrating the value of institutional continuity in reuse processes.

 4. Discussion

Comparing these cases, three factors emerge as decisive. First, the timing of intervention matters: early, coordinated planning tends to preserve more of the industrial fabric than reactive, parcel-by-parcel conversion. Second, ownership structure shapes outcomes more than architectural quality; fragmented or speculative ownership favors demolition. Third, the narrative constructed around the site determines whether reuse engages with the industrial past or erases it. Western adaptive reuse literature tends to treat heritage as a given; in post-socialist cities, it is itself a contested field requiring active construction.

 5. Conclusion

Adaptive reuse in post-socialist cities is not merely a technical or aesthetic exercise but a negotiation over land, memory, and public value under conditions of rapid marketization. The architectural qualities of industrial buildings—flexible spans, robust structures, distinctive materiality—are necessary but insufficient conditions for successful reuse. What distinguishes the successful cases examined here is the presence of institutional arrangements capable of coordinating ownership, regulating speculation, and articulating a public interpretation of the industrial past. Future research should examine how current heritage designations and municipal planning instruments can be strengthened to support reuse at the scale of entire industrial districts, rather than isolated flagship projects.

 References

Bullen, P. A., & Love, P. E. D. (2011). Adaptive reuse of heritage buildings. *Structural Survey*, 29(5), 411–421.

Künnapuu, K. (2015). The Rotermann Quarter: A case of post-industrial transformation in Tallinn. *Journal of Baltic Studies*, 46(3), 355–372.

Langston, C., Wong, F. K. W., Hui, E. C. M., & Shen, L. Y. (2008). Strategic assessment of building adaptive reuse opportunities in Hong Kong. *Building and Environment*, 43(10), 1709–1718.

Stanilov, K. (Ed.). (2007). *The Post-Socialist City: Urban Form and Space Transformations in Central and Eastern Europe after Socialism*. Springer.

Tsenkova, S. (2006). Beyond transitions: Understanding urban change in post-socialist cities. In S. Tsenkova & Z. Nedović-Budić (Eds.), *The Urban Mosaic of Post-Socialist Europe* (pp. 21–50). Physica-Verlag.

title: linguistics|code-switching among bilingual teenagers in Singapore
text:
Methodology

 Research Design

This study employed a mixed-methods approach combining quantitative corpus analysis with qualitative discourse analysis to examine code-switching patterns among bilingual teenagers in Singapore. The design allowed for both the identification of broad distributional patterns across a large dataset and fine-grained examination of the social functions of code-switching in interaction.

 Data Sources and Sample

Data were drawn from two complementary sources. First, a corpus of naturalistic peer conversation was compiled from audio recordings of 48 bilingual adolescents (aged 13–17) recruited from four secondary schools representing different socioeconomic catchment areas (two mainstream government schools, one mission school, and one independent school). Participants were stratified by gender (24 male, 24 female) and home language background (English-dominant, Mandarin-dominant, and Malay-dominant). Each participant wore a small digital recorder during unstructured breaks and after-school co-curricular activities over a two-week period, yielding approximately 62 hours of recordings. Participants and their parents provided informed consent, and all names were pseudonymised.

Second, a supplementary dataset of 120 WhatsApp group chat excerpts (approximately 8,000 messages) was collected from consenting participants' peer groups, providing insight into written code-switching practices. Additionally, 20 semi-structured interviews (approximately 40 minutes each) were conducted with a subsample of participants to elicit metalinguistic commentary on their language choices.

 Transcription and Coding

Recordings were orthographically transcribed by two research assistants fluent in Singapore English, Mandarin, and Malay, with code-switching instances marked and glossed. Ten percent of transcripts were double-coded to establish inter-rater reliability (Cohen's κ = 0.87 for language identification). Code-switching was operationalised following Poplack's (1980) distinction between inter-sentential, intra-sentential, and tag-switching, with an additional category for phonological and morphological switching (e.g., English verbs with Malay affixes).

 Analytical Framework

Quantitative analysis proceeded in two stages. First, token frequencies of code-switching were calculated per speaker and normalised per 100 words. Second, a series of mixed-effects logistic regression models were fitted using R (lme4 package) to examine the effects of speaker-level variables (home language, gender, school type) and contextual variables (interlocutor, topic, activity type) on the likelihood of code-switching, with random intercepts for speaker and school.

Qualitative analysis adopted a conversation-analytic (CA) perspective (Auer, 1998), examining sequential positioning of switches to identify their interactional functions, including stance-taking, humour, emphasis, and identity performance. A subset of 150 switching episodes was subjected to sequential analysis, with particular attention to participant orientation (e.g., laughter, repair, subsequent language choice).

 Ethical Considerations

Approval was obtained from the university's Institutional Review Board and the Ministry of Education. Given the sensitivity of recording adolescents, participants retained the right to review and delete any recordings, and all data were stored on encrypted servers accessible only to the research team.

title: philosophy|moral luck and the limits of responsibility
text:
Few ideas in modern moral philosophy have proved as unsettling as the thought that a person's moral standing may depend on matters beyond her control. Thomas Nagel (1979) and Bernard Williams (1981) gave this thought its canonical formulation under the heading of "moral luck": the phenomenon whereby a person is properly subject to moral assessment—praise, blame, resentment, or regret—in virtue of factors that are not, and could not be, within her control. The problem is not merely that luck influences what happens to us, but that it appears to influence what we are morally, and how we are rightly judged.
