title: psychology|sleep deprivation and emotional regulation in adolescents
text: Sleep deprivation is highly prevalent among adolescents, yet its consequences for emotional functioning remain incompletely understood. The present study examined the relationship between sleep deprivation and emotional regulation in a sample of 248 adolescents (aged 13–18 years; 52% female). Participants were classified into sleep-deprived (n = 121) and adequately rested (n = 127) groups based on self-reported sleep duration and actigraphy data collected over one week. Emotional regulation was assessed using the Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale (DERS) and a laboratory-based emotion induction task in which participants viewed negatively valenced images while subjective emotional intensity and use of cognitive reappraisal were recorded. Sleep-deprived adolescents reported significantly greater difficulties in emotional regulation overall (d = 0.68), with elevations across the impulsivity, clarity, and strategies subscales. During the emotion induction task, sleep-deprived participants reported higher negative emotional intensity (d = 0.54) and demonstrated less frequent spontaneous use of cognitive reappraisal (d = 0.47) compared with adequately rested peers. Mediation analyses indicated that sleep deprivation indirectly predicted poorer emotional regulation through increased daytime sleepiness and heightened negative affectivity. Notably, effects were more pronounced among younger adolescents (13–15 years) than among older participants, suggesting developmental sensitivity during early-to-mid adolescence. These findings indicate that insufficient sleep is associated with both self-reported and laboratory-assessed deficits in emotional regulation, supporting theoretical models implicating sleep in affective functioning. Results underscore the importance of addressing sleep health in interventions targeting adolescent emotional well-being and suggest that school-based sleep education programs may confer benefits for emotion regulation during this developmental period. Longitudinal research is needed to clarify causal direction.

title: religious studies|pilgrimage networks in medieval Japanese Buddhism
text:
The study of pilgrimage in medieval Japanese Buddhism has undergone a substantial transformation over the past four decades, moving from devotional and antiquarian accounts of individual temple traditions toward analyses of mobility, institutional competition, and the circulation of sacral authority across regional and transregional networks. Early foundational work in Western languages, notably by Allan Grapard (1982) and H. Byron Earhart (1989), established that Japanese sacred sites were rarely isolated loci of devotion but were embedded in systems of meaning that linked mountains, temples, and courtly centers into coherent religious topographies. Grapard's concept of the "mandala" as a spatial and institutional logic, and Earhart's comparative attention to the structure of Japanese pilgrimage, together opened the way for scholarship that treats pilgrimage not merely as travel to a destination but as a relational practice constitutive of Buddhist institutions themselves. Building on these foundations, the present article examines the formation and operation of pilgrimage networks in medieval Japanese Buddhism, with particular attention to the eleventh through the sixteenth centuries, a period in which the proliferation of pilgrimage routes, the commercialization of travel, and the competitive management of sacred sites by monastic lineages reshaped the religious landscape of the archipelago.

A central concern of recent scholarship has been the relationship between pilgrimage and institutional power. Japanese researchers such as Hayami Tasuku (1992) and Sasayagi Haruo traced the emergence of the Saikoku and Bandō circuits devoted to Kannon, demonstrating that these routes were not spontaneous expressions of popular piety but were actively promoted by temples seeking to attract patrons and pilgrims. The Saikoku pilgrimage, which by the late medieval period encompassed thirty-three sites in western Japan, exemplifies how a devotional itinerary could function simultaneously as a soteriological technology and as an economic and political instrument. Studies of the Kumano and Ise routes have similarly shown that shrine-temple complexes cultivated pilgrimage traffic through the strategic dissemination of origin narratives (engi), miracle tales (setsuwa), and promotional texts, thereby constructing what has been termed a "pilgrimage economy" in which merit, prestige, and material resources circulated together (Tyler 1990; Moerman 2005). Such work has productively complicated earlier assumptions that pilgrimage represented a form of popular religion distinct from or opposed to elite monastic Buddhism, revealing instead dense entanglements between clerical institutions, aristocratic patrons, and lay travelers.

Parallel to this institutional turn, scholarship has attended to the material and infrastructural dimensions of medieval pilgrimage. The maintenance of routes, the construction of lodging facilities, the role of pilgrimage guides (sendatsu), and the circulation of maps and route descriptions all contributed to the stabilization of networks that spanned provinces. Research on the Ise pilgrimage and its later popularization has illuminated how guides and confraternities (kō) mediated between local communities and distant sacred centers, generating forms of associational religiosity that persisted well into the early modern period (Nakamura 1997; Ambros 2012). Within Buddhist contexts more specifically, the development of the Shikoku henro and analogous circuits tied to Kūkai devotion raises important questions about the relationship between founder cults, hagiography, and the routinization of pilgrimage practice. The figure of the founder as a guarantor of sacral presence along a route underscores how pilgrimage networks were sustained not only by institutional investment but also by narrative and ritual technologies that rendered distant sites mutually referential.

The analytical framework of "networks" adopted here draws on several strands of scholarship. First, it engages with work on medieval Japanese religion that emphasizes horizontal connections among temples, shrines, and confraternities rather than strictly hierarchical models of sectarian organization (Kuroda 1996; Sueki 2002). Second, it incorporates insights from the study of premodern mobility, which has demonstrated that travel in medieval Japan was far more extensive and socially diversified than once assumed, encompassing merchants, artisans, itinerant monks, and female pilgrims alongside elite travelers (Fujii 2003; Goodwin 1994). Third, it attends to the representational strategies through which pilgrimage was imagined and promoted, including illustrated handscrolls, temple legends, and poetic topographies that encoded sacred geography in literary and visual form. By integrating these perspectives, the article treats pilgrimage networks as simultaneously institutional, infrastructural, and imaginative phenomena.

The article's argument proceeds in three parts. The first section examines the institutional strategies by which major monastic centers established and maintained pilgrimage routes, focusing on the competition among temples for control of sacred sites and the resulting proliferation of route narratives. The second section analyzes the role of guides, confraternities, and travel infrastructure in sustaining networks across generations, with attention to the social composition of pilgrim populations. The third section considers the imaginative and ritual dimensions of pilgrimage, arguing that the circulation of engi, setsuwa, and visual representations was integral to the constitution of network coherence. Throughout, the article draws on a combination of primary sources, including temple histories, pilgrimage diaries, and promotional texts, and secondary scholarship in Japanese and English. In doing so, it seeks to contribute to ongoing conversations about the relationship between religion, mobility, and institutional formation in premodern Japan, and to suggest that pilgrimage networks offer a particularly illuminating lens through which to understand the dynamics of medieval Japanese Buddhism as a whole.

title: linguistics|code-switching among bilingual teenagers in Singapore
text:
Literature Review: Code-Switching Among Bilingual Teenagers in Singapore

Code-switching, broadly defined as the alternation between two or more languages or language varieties within a single conversation or utterance, has been extensively studied as a systematic and socially meaningful practice rather than a sign of linguistic deficiency (Gumperz, 1982; Myers-Scotton, 1993). In multilingual Singapore, where English, Mandarin, Malay, and Tamil coexist alongside Singlish and various Chinese dialects, code-switching is a pervasive feature of everyday communication, particularly among adolescents navigating multiple linguistic repertoires. This review synthesises existing research on code-switching among bilingual teenagers in Singapore, focusing on its structural patterns, social functions, and identity-related dimensions, while identifying gaps for future inquiry.

Early foundational work on code-switching established that switching is governed by grammatical constraints and serves important conversational functions. Gumperz (1982) introduced the distinction between situational and metaphorical code-switching, arguing that speakers exploit language alternation to signal shifts in context, topic, or social relations. Myers-Scotton (1993) advanced this line of inquiry with the Markedness Model, proposing that speakers choose codes based on the social meanings associated with them, thereby negotiating rights and obligations in interaction. These frameworks have informed much subsequent research in the Singaporean context, although scholars have also cautioned that models developed in Western bilingual settings require adaptation to postcolonial, multi-ethnic societies (Platt, 1980; Pakir, 1991).

Research specifically addressing Singaporean bilingual teenagers has examined code-switching across several domains, including classroom interaction, peer conversation, and digital communication. Pakir (1991) provided one of the earliest systematic accounts of code-switching in Singapore, documenting how English-educated Chinese Singaporeans alternated between English, Mandarin, and Hokkien in informal talk. She observed that switching was often used to convey affective meanings and to index solidarity within in-group networks. Building on this, Gupta (1994) analysed the pragmatic functions of code-switching among young Singaporeans, noting that switches into Mandarin or dialect were frequently employed for emphasis, humour, or the expression of cultural affiliation, while English remained the default language of formal education and public discourse.

The role of code-switching in educational settings has attracted considerable attention. Teachers and students in Singaporean classrooms frequently engage in translanguaging practices, moving fluidly between Standard English, Singlish, and Mother Tongue languages to facilitate comprehension and manage classroom dynamics (Rubdy, 2007; Vaish, 2008). Vaish (2008) demonstrated that code-switching in English-medium classrooms served both pedagogical and social functions, enabling teachers to clarify content while simultaneously building rapport with students. However, these practices have sometimes been viewed ambivalently by educational authorities, reflecting broader tensions between Singapore's bilingual education policy and the realities of everyday linguistic practice (Gopinathan, 1998; Silver, 2005).

A significant strand of research has explored the relationship between code-switching and identity construction among Singaporean youth. As a generation positioned between the state's bilingual policy and global English-dominated popular culture, teenagers use code-switching to negotiate complex identities (Stroud & Wee, 2007; Wee, 2010). Stroud and Wee (2007) argued that code-switching among Singaporean students functions as a resource for indexing both local affiliation and cosmopolitan orientation, allowing speakers to position themselves simultaneously within and beyond national linguistic categories. Similarly, Wee (2010) examined how Singlish-English code-switching enables young speakers to signal in-group membership while maintaining access to standard English prestige. These findings align with broader sociolinguistic work on youth language practices, which emphasises the agentive and creative dimensions of code-switching (Rampton, 1995; Auer, 1998).

More recent scholarship has turned to digital contexts, where Singaporean teenagers code-switch extensively in text messaging and social media. Studies have documented hybrid linguistic forms that blend English, Mandarin, Malay, and Singlish, reflecting the multimodal and playful nature of online communication (Lee, 2016; Tagg & Seargeant, 2016). Lee (2016) found that WhatsApp exchanges among Singaporean secondary school students exhibited frequent intra-sentential switching, often used to convey stance, humour, and intimacy. Tagg and Seargeant (2016) similarly highlighted how digital code-switching enables young Singaporeans to perform multifaceted identities across linguistic boundaries.

Despite this substantial body of work, several gaps remain. First, much existing research focuses on Chinese Singaporean speakers, with comparatively less attention to code-switching practices among Malay and Tamil teenagers (but see David, 2003, for related Malaysian contexts). Second, longitudinal studies tracking how code-switching patterns evolve across adolescence are scarce. Third, the intersection of code-switching with emerging digital genres and multimodal resources warrants further investigation. Addressing these gaps would enrich understanding of how Singaporean bilingual teenagers deploy their linguistic repertoires to navigate an increasingly complex sociolinguistic landscape.

In summary, research on code-switching among bilingual teenagers in Singapore has moved from descriptive accounts of structural patterns toward socially and identity-oriented analyses. The literature consistently demonstrates that code-switching is a skilled, context-sensitive practice central to peer interaction, classroom communication, and digital self-presentation. Future research should attend more closely to under-represented language communities and to the evolving multimodal dimensions of youth code-switching in Singapore.

title: mathematics education|students' misconceptions about limits in calculus
text:
Discussion

The pattern of errors we observed suggests that students' difficulties with limits are not primarily computational. Few participants in either the procedural or conceptual interview group failed to evaluate the rational functions we presented at points away from the singularity; the breakdown occurred almost exclusively when the task required reasoning about behaviour *near* a point or *at* infinity. This is consistent with Cottrill et al.'s (1996) action–process–object account, though our data complicate a strictly stage-wise reading. Several students who could correctly coordinate a table of values with a graph—arguably evidence of a process conception—nonetheless reverted to substitution-based reasoning when asked to justify a limit symbolically. We interpret this as evidence that process and object conceptions are not merely sequentially acquired but context-sensitive: the same student may operate at different levels depending on representational register, a finding that echoes the register-switching difficulties documented by Duval (2006) in other mathematical domains.

The most persistent misconception in our sample was the treatment of the limit as a value the function *reaches* rather than a value it *approaches*. This manifested in three distinguishable ways: (a) the belief that a limit cannot exist at a point where the function is undefined; (b) the assumption that $f(a)$ and $\lim_{x\to a} f(x)$ must agree whenever both exist; and (c) in the case of limits at infinity, the attribution of a terminal "stopping point" to a graph that in fact continues indefinitely. Category (a) was the most resistant to instruction, surviving even a targeted tutorial session in seven of our twenty-two case-study students. We are cautious about over-interpreting this persistence given the small case-study sample and the single-session design; a longitudinal component would be needed to establish whether this reflects a stable cognitive obstacle or a transient artefact of unfamiliar notation.

A second finding concerns the informal language students bring to the topic. Phrases such as "gets closer and closer" and "never quite reaches" were ubiquitous, and while these formulations are not wrong, our discourse analysis indicates that students often treat them as *definitions* rather than as heuristics pending formalisation. When pressed to produce an $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ argument, students frequently attempted to translate the informal phrasing word-for-word, producing statements that conflated the bound on $|f(x)-L|$ with a bound on $|x-a|$. This suggests that the informal-to-formal transition is not simply a matter of adding rigour to an already-sound intuition but may require restructuring the intuition itself—a claim that warrants direct testing.

Several limitations should be borne in mind. Our participants were drawn from a single institution and were predominantly enrolled in first-year engineering calculus; whether the misconception profile generalises to mathematics majors or to students in other national contexts is an open question. The interview protocol, moreover, relied on a small set of function families (rational, piecewise, and trigonometric), and it is possible that the salience of the "undefined at a point" misconception is partly an artefact of our stimulus selection. Finally, our coding scheme, while subjected to double-coding with acceptable agreement ($\kappa = 0.78$), inevitably imposed categories on responses that were sometimes ambiguous.

 Conclusion

The evidence presented here supports a view of limit misconceptions as structured rather than random: students' errors cluster around a small number of coherent, if incorrect, commitments about what a limit *is*. The pedagogical implication we draw is modest but, we think, actionable. Instruction that merely corrects erroneous answers is unlikely to dislodge these commitments, because the answers are symptoms of a stable underlying model. What appears more promising—though our data speak to this only indirectly—is explicit confrontation with the distinction between value and approach, ideally across multiple representational registers and with deliberate attention to the informal language students use to anchor their reasoning. Whether such an approach produces durable conceptual change is a question our design cannot answer; it would require a controlled intervention with delayed post-testing, which we regard as the natural next step.

title: mathematics education|students' misconceptions about limits in calculus
text:
Here is a course paper on students' misconceptions about limits in calculus, written in English.

---

 Students' Misconceptions About Limits in Calculus: A Persistent Challenge in Mathematics Education

Abstract
The concept of a limit is the foundational pillar of calculus, underpinning the entire edifice of derivatives and integrals. However, for many students, it remains an elusive and profoundly counterintuitive idea. This paper explores the common and persistent misconceptions that students hold regarding the concept of a limit. Drawing on research in mathematics education, it identifies and categorizes several key areas of difficulty, including the conflation of a limit with the function's value at a point, the misunderstanding of the infinite process, and the reliance on informal, dynamic notions of motion at the expense of the formal, static definition. The paper argues that these misconceptions are not merely errors to be corrected but are often logical extensions of a student's prior mathematical experiences. Consequently, it advocates for a pedagogical approach that explicitly confronts these intuitive ideas, promotes a deeper conceptual understanding, and integrates multiple representations of limits to foster a more robust and flexible understanding of this crucial concept.

1. Introduction
Calculus, the mathematics of change, is often perceived as a gateway to advanced studies in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM). At its very heart lies the concept of the limit. The entire structure of calculus—the derivative as a limit of a difference quotient and the integral as a limit of a Riemann sum—is built upon this single, powerful idea. Yet, a vast body of research in mathematics education has consistently shown that students struggle with the formal definition of a limit and frequently develop a range of misconceptions that can impede their understanding of the entire subject.

These misconceptions are not random mistakes; they are often the result of students attempting to reconcile the new, formal language of calculus with their existing, informal intuitions about numbers, functions, and infinity. As educators, it is crucial to understand not only *that* students are wrong, but *why* their reasoning is flawed. This paper will examine some of the most prevalent misconceptions students have about limits, analyze their origins, and discuss the implications for effective teaching practice.

2. The Duality of Limits: Process vs. Object
A fundamental source of student difficulty is the dual nature of the limit concept itself. On one hand, a limit is a dynamic process: the idea of a variable *approaching* a value. On the other, it is a static object: the final, unique value that the function approaches. Students often become stuck in the process-oriented view, failing to make the cognitive leap to the object-oriented view.

This is evident in their struggle with the formal epsilon-delta (ε-δ) definition of a limit. The definition, `lim(x→a) f(x) = L`, is a static statement about a relationship between two arbitrary distances, ε and δ. It does not involve motion or "getting closer." Students who cling to the dynamic "approaching" metaphor find the ε-δ definition abstract, confusing, and disconnected from their intuitive understanding. They may be able to apply limit laws procedurally but fail to grasp the conceptual underpinnings, leaving them unable to handle more complex proofs or theoretical problems.

3. Common Misconceptions and Their Origins
Research has identified several specific and recurring misconceptions about limits.

3.1. The Limit as Function Value
One of the most common misconceptions is the belief that the limit of a function at a point *is* the function's value at that point. Students often conflate `lim(x→a) f(x)` with `f(a)`. This misconception is particularly problematic when dealing with functions that have a discontinuity or are undefined at the point in question. For example, when asked to find the limit of `f(x) = (x² - 1) / (x - 1)` as x approaches 1, many students will first try to substitute x=1, get the indeterminate form 0/0, and conclude that the limit does not exist because the function is undefined there. They fail to understand that the limit is about the behavior *near* the point, not *at* the point.

This error stems from the student's prior experience with continuous functions in algebra and pre-calculus, where evaluation and finding the limit were often the same operation. The concept of a "hole" in a graph is a novel and abstract idea for them.

3.2. The Limit as a "Barrier"
Another related misconception is that a function can never cross its limit. Students may believe that if `lim(x→a) f(x) = L`, then the function's values must always be less than L (or greater than L) as they approach 'a'. While this is true for some functions, it is not a general rule. For instance, the function `f(x) = x * sin(1/x)` as x approaches 0 has a limit of 0, yet the function oscillates infinitely many times and crosses the value of 0 repeatedly. This misconception reveals a misunderstanding of the limit as a boundary or a final destination rather than a value that the function can approach while oscillating around it.

3.3. Misunderstanding Infinity and Asymptotes
The concept of an infinite limit, `lim(x→a) f(x) = ∞`, is particularly fraught with confusion. Students often treat infinity as a very large number rather than a concept describing unbounded growth. They may write "the limit is infinity" and then try to perform arithmetic with it, or they may not understand why a limit "does not exist" in the real number system when it is infinite. Similarly, for limits at infinity, such as `lim(x→∞) f(x) = L`, students may not fully grasp that this describes the long-term, asymptotic behavior of the function.

4. Pedagogical Implications
Addressing these misconceptions requires a shift from a purely procedural approach to one that emphasizes conceptual understanding. Several strategies are promising:

1.  Confront Misconceptions Directly: Teachers should create opportunities for students to explore problems that challenge their intuitive ideas. Using graphing technology to visualize functions like `f(x) = sin(x)/x` near x=0 can help students see that the limit exists even though the function is undefined.

2.  Emphasize Multiple Representations: The limit concept should be explored graphically, numerically, and algebraically. Creating tables of values, analyzing graphs, and manipulating algebraic expressions all contribute to a more robust understanding.

3.  Deconstruct the Formal Definition: The ε-δ definition should not be presented as a magical formula to be memorized. Instead, it should be introduced gradually, using visual aids and guided discovery to help students see it as a precise way of formalizing their intuitive ideas about "closeness."

4.  Focus on the "Why": Students need to understand why the limit concept is necessary in the first place. By starting with problems of instantaneous rate of change and area under a curve, teachers can motivate the need for limits and help students see them as a tool for solving problems, not just an abstract game with symbols.

5. Conclusion
The concept of a limit is a formidable intellectual hurdle for students transitioning from elementary to advanced mathematics. The misconceptions they develop are not simple errors but are often the result of a complex interplay between their prior knowledge, intuitive reasoning, and the abstract nature of the concept itself. The common errors—equating limits with function values, misunderstanding the role of infinity, and struggling with the formal definition—are predictable and well-documented.

For mathematics educators, the key takeaway is that teaching limits requires more than just demonstrating procedures. It demands a pedagogical approach that actively anticipates and addresses student misconceptions, fosters a deep conceptual understanding, and builds bridges between informal intuition and formal rigor. By doing so, we can help students not only to compute limits correctly but also to appreciate the profound and elegant idea that serves as the foundation for all of calculus.
