title: political science|electoral reform and party fragmentation in Latin America
text:
Methodology

 Research Design

This study employs a mixed-methods design combining cross-national quantitative analysis with structured comparative case studies. The quantitative component tests whether electoral system change—specifically the adoption of more permissive formulas and larger district magnitudes—is associated with increases in party system fragmentation across Latin America. The qualitative component traces causal mechanisms in four purposively selected cases. This design addresses the endogeneity concern that fragmentation pressures may themselves drive reform by examining reform episodes as interventions and by triangulating statistical associations with process evidence.

 Sample and Coverage

The sample comprises 18 Latin American democracies observed from 1978 (or the year of democratic transition, if later) through 2023. The unit of analysis is the country–legislative election year. The sample includes all lower-chamber legislative elections held under democratic conditions, yielding approximately 140 election observations. Following standard practice in the literature, elections held under military rule or during periods of democratic breakdown are excluded, as are founding elections lacking meaningful partisan competition. Countries are included if they meet a minimal democracy threshold (Polity IV score ≥ 6) in the election year and have held at least three consecutive democratic legislative elections. The four case studies—selected to maximize variation on reform type and fragmentation outcomes—are Ecuador (2012–2021), Chile (2015–2021), Colombia (1991–2018), and Peru (1995–2020).

 Data Sources

The dependent variable, party system fragmentation, is measured using the effective number of electoral parties (ENEP) and effective number of parliamentary parties (ENPP), calculated from official election results compiled from national electoral authorities and cross-validated against the Constituency-Level Elections Archive (CLEA) and the Observatory of Political Reforms in Latin America (OPAL). Where discrepancies arise, official national sources take precedence.

The key independent variable, electoral system change, is coded from country-specific electoral statutes and constitutional texts, supplemented by OPAL reform data and secondary literature. Reforms are coded on three dimensions: (1) changes to district magnitude, (2) changes to the seat allocation formula (e.g., shifts between D'Hondt, Sainte-Laguë, and Hare), and (3) introduction or removal of legal thresholds. A reform event is coded as a binary indicator (1 = reform implemented before election *t*), with a continuous version capturing the percentage change in average district magnitude.

Controls include presidential coattails (concurrent vs. non-concurrent elections), presidentialism, federalism, the number of seats in the lower chamber, turnout, and logged GDP per capita (World Bank). For the case studies, data include congressional roll-call records, constitutional assembly debates, party manifestos, and semi-structured interviews with legislators, party strategists, and electoral officials (N = 24).

 Analysis

Quantitative analysis proceeds in three steps. First, descriptive time-series plots document fragmentation trajectories and reform timing. Second, the core specification estimates a two-way fixed-effects model with country fixed effects (absorbing time-invariant institutional and structural features) and election-period fixed effects (absorbing region-wide shocks), clustering standard errors at the country level:

ENEP_it = β₀ + β₁Reform_it + γX_it + α_i + δ_t + ε_it

Given the modest N and the binary treatment, we also estimate a difference-in-differences specification for reform episodes with clean pre-/post-election comparisons, and report wild cluster bootstrap p-values to address few-cluster inference concerns. Robustness checks include lagged specifications, exclusion of founding elections, and alternative fragmentation measures (Laakso–Taagepera index, largest-party vote share).

The qualitative analysis uses a structured, process-tracing protocol. Each case is coded for the reform's origin (elite pact, court mandate, referendum), its content, and elite expectations. We assess whether fragmentation increases are concentrated in the first post-reform election, whether they persist, and whether they occur in districts whose magnitude changed. Cross-case comparison follows a most-similar-systems logic, isolating electoral reform from rival explanations such as presidentialization, party-system institutionalization, and social cleavages.

title: psychology|sleep deprivation and emotional regulation in adolescents
text:
Adolescence represents a critical developmental period characterized by profound neurobiological, psychological, and social transitions, during which sleep patterns undergo substantial reorganization. Concurrently, adolescents face escalating academic demands, increasing social complexity, and heightened emotional reactivity, all of which place considerable strain on their capacity for effective emotional regulation. Sleep deprivation has emerged as a pervasive and concerning phenomenon among this population, with epidemiological studies indicating that a substantial proportion of adolescents consistently obtain insufficient sleep relative to recommended guidelines (Hirshkowitz et al., 2015). The convergence of developmental vulnerability and widespread sleep insufficiency renders the intersection of sleep and emotional functioning in adolescence a matter of significant theoretical and clinical importance.

Sleep deprivation in adolescents is driven by a combination of biological and environmental factors. During puberty, circadian rhythms undergo a normative phase delay, whereby the endogenous timing of sleep propensity shifts later in the evening (Carskadon et al., 1993). This biological shift conflicts with early school start times and competing demands for adolescents' time, producing a chronic pattern of insufficient sleep that is often compounded by social jetlag and irregular sleep schedules (Crowley et al., 2018). The consequences of this sleep debt extend beyond fatigue and academic impairment to encompass disturbances in affective experience and emotional control, domains that are particularly salient during the adolescent developmental window.

Emotional regulation refers to the processes by which individuals influence which emotions they experience, when they experience them, and how they express and modulate these emotional responses (Gross, 1998). The capacity for adaptive emotional regulation develops substantially across childhood and adolescence, supported by the maturation of prefrontal cortical regions and their connectivity with subcortical limbic structures involved in affective processing (Casey et al., 2008). Importantly, adolescence is characterized by heightened reactivity in reward- and emotion-related neural circuitry alongside still-developing regulatory control, creating a period of particular vulnerability to disruptions in affective functioning. Sleep loss has been hypothesized to preferentially impair prefrontal executive functions, thereby undermining the top-down regulation of emotional responses while simultaneously amplifying subcortical reactivity to affective stimuli (Yoo et al., 2007). This dual mechanism suggests that sleep deprivation may exert a particularly pronounced effect on emotional regulation during adolescence, when the neural systems supporting regulatory control are still maturing.

Empirical evidence has begun to substantiate the relationship between sleep and emotional functioning in young people. Experimental studies in adults have demonstrated that sleep deprivation produces increased emotional reactivity, impaired recognition of emotional expressions, and diminished capacity for mood regulation (Walker & van der Helm, 2009). Neuroimaging research has shown that sleep-deprived individuals exhibit exaggerated amygdala responses to negative emotional stimuli coupled with reduced functional connectivity between the amygdala and medial prefrontal cortex, a pattern consistent with diminished top-down regulatory control (Yoo et al., 2007). Extending these findings to adolescents, observational studies have reported associations between shorter sleep duration and greater negative affect, increased irritability, and poorer emotional regulation (Baum et al., 2014). Short-term experimental sleep restriction protocols in adolescent samples have likewise documented increases in negative mood states and alterations in emotional reactivity (Lo et al., 2016; Reddy et al., 2017). However, the literature remains characterized by several limitations, including reliance on cross-sectional designs, variability in sleep manipulation protocols, and heterogeneity in the operationalization of emotional regulation constructs.

Theoretical frameworks have been proposed to integrate these findings. The sleep-to-forget, sleep-to-remember model suggests that sleep supports the consolidation of emotional memories while attenuating affective charge, thereby contributing to adaptive emotional processing (Walker & van der Helm, 2009). Complementary accounts emphasize the role of sleep in restoring prefrontal regulatory capacity and in maintaining circadian alignment of affective systems (Goldstein & Walker, 2014). Developmental perspectives further suggest that adolescents may be differentially sensitive to the effects of sleep loss owing to the ongoing maturation of frontolimbic circuitry and the heightened salience of social and emotional experiences during this period (Dahl & Lewin, 2002). Despite these theoretical advances, the specific mechanisms linking sleep deprivation to emotional regulation difficulties in adolescents remain incompletely characterized, and the extent to which findings from adult samples generalize to younger populations is uncertain.

Understanding the relationship between sleep deprivation and emotional regulation in adolescents carries considerable practical significance. Emotional dysregulation is a transdiagnostic risk factor implicated in the development of internalizing and externalizing psychopathology, including anxiety, depression, and behavioral difficulties (Aldao et al., 2010). Given that sleep is a modifiable behavior, clarifying its role in adolescent emotional functioning could inform school-based and clinical interventions aimed at improving both sleep and mental health outcomes. Moreover, policy discussions regarding school start times have highlighted the potential benefits of aligning educational schedules with adolescent circadian biology (Owens et al., 2014), underscoring the public health relevance of this line of inquiry.

The present study aims to examine the relationship between sleep deprivation and emotional regulation in adolescents, addressing gaps in the existing literature through a systematic investigation of how experimentally manipulated and naturally occurring sleep loss influence emotional reactivity and regulatory strategy use. By integrating behavioral and self-report measures, this research seeks to contribute to a more nuanced understanding of the mechanisms through which sleep insufficiency compromises affective functioning during a developmentally sensitive period. The following sections review the relevant literature in greater depth, describe the methodological approach adopted, and present findings that bear on theoretical models of sleep and emotion as well as on practical efforts to support adolescent well-being.

title: management|remote work and team innovation in technology companies
text:
The literature on remote work and team innovation in technology companies has expanded considerably over the past two decades, shaped by advances in digital collaboration tools, changing employee expectations, and the natural experiment of the COVID-19 pandemic. This review synthesizes existing research across four interrelated themes: the conceptualization of remote work intensity, the mechanisms linking virtual collaboration to team innovation, the moderating role of leadership and organizational context, and the methodological challenges that complicate causal inference in this literature.

A foundational strand of research concerns how remote work should be conceptualized and measured. Early studies treated remote work as a binary arrangement, but more recent scholarship emphasizes its multidimensional nature. Allen, Golden, and Shockley (2015) distinguish between extent, frequency, and location of remote work, arguing that these dimensions have distinct implications for individual and team outcomes. Gajendran and Harrison (2007) demonstrated in a meta-analysis that remote work intensity yields curvilinear effects on performance and satisfaction, with moderate levels often proving more beneficial than either extreme. In technology companies specifically, where work is frequently project-based and digitally mediated, Golden and Gajendran (2019) found that the quality of virtuality, rather than mere geographic dispersion, predicts team functioning. This conceptual refinement is critical because inconsistent operationalization across studies has produced seemingly contradictory findings regarding remote work and innovation.

A second theme concerns the mechanisms through which remote work affects team innovation. Innovation in technology teams depends heavily on knowledge sharing, psychological safety, and informal interaction, each of which may be altered by remote arrangements. Gibbs, Sivunen, and Boyraz (2017) showed that virtual teams compensate for reduced informal communication by developing explicit norms and structured knowledge-sharing routines, which can sustain idea generation but may constrain serendipitous discovery. Choudhury, Foroughi, and Larson (2021) found that remote work reduces cross-team collaboration and increases siloed work within firms, suggesting a trade-off between focused individual productivity and the boundary-spanning interactions that fuel innovation. Conversely, Yang et al. (2022) reported that well-managed hybrid arrangements preserve exploratory communication while reducing interruptions, thereby supporting creative work. Studies of technology firms during the pandemic offer mixed evidence: some document productivity gains alongside declines in radical innovation (Brynjolfsson et al., 2023), while others find that digitally mature teams maintain innovation output through asynchronous ideation practices (Malhotra, 2021).

Leadership and organizational context constitute a third major theme. Transformational and empowering leadership behaviors appear especially consequential in remote settings. Hoch and Kozlowski (2014) demonstrated that team leadership climate moderates the relationship between virtuality and team performance, with strong leadership compensating for geographic dispersion. Contreras, Baykal, and Abid (2020) found that e-leadership practices, particularly those fostering trust and goal clarity, enhance virtual team innovation. Organizational culture and infrastructure also matter: Hill, Ferris, and Märtinson (2003) noted early on that technology firms with robust digital infrastructures and outcome-based evaluation systems derive greater benefits from remote work. More recently, Bloom et al. (2015) provided quasi-experimental evidence that remote work increases productivity among call-center workers, though they caution that generalizability to creative and interdependent work remains uncertain. For technology teams engaged in innovation, the literature suggests that autonomy-supportive leadership combined with deliberate structuring of synchronous interaction is most conducive to creative outcomes (Gibbs et al., 2021).

Finally, methodological challenges pervade this literature. Much of the evidence is cross-sectional or drawn from single-firm case studies, limiting causal claims. The pandemic-era studies, while valuable, confound remote work with crisis conditions such as health anxiety and school closures (Kniffin et al., 2021). Few studies measure innovation outcomes directly, relying instead on self-reported creativity or patents, each with well-known limitations. Moreover, technology companies differ markedly in their products, team structures, and digital maturity, raising questions about the generalizability of findings across the sector. Recent calls for longitudinal, multi-level designs that track teams over time and combine objective innovation metrics with qualitative process data represent a promising direction (Dulebohn & Hoch, 2022).

In summary, the literature indicates that remote work's relationship with team innovation in technology companies is contingent rather than deterministic. Moderate remote intensity, deliberate communication norms, empowering leadership, and supportive digital infrastructure appear to preserve or enhance innovation, whereas extreme dispersion without compensatory practices may erode the informal interactions on which creativity depends. Nonetheless, inconsistent conceptualizations, limited causal evidence, and sector-specific sampling constrain firm conclusions, warranting further research that attends to the multidimensional nature of both remote work and innovation.

title: international relations|small-state hedging strategies in Southeast Asia
text:
Discussion

The findings complicate the assumption that hedging is a coherent, stable strategy. Across the cases examined, hedging emerges less as a designed posture than as an emergent property of domestic coalition politics and bureaucratic compromise. Singapore's apparently seamless hedging between the United States and China, for instance, masks recurring inter-agency friction between the Ministry of Trade and Industry's commercial priorities and MINDEF's security ties; what scholars code as strategic ambiguity is often the residual of unresolved internal bargaining. This suggests that the hedging literature's emphasis on intentionality—the assumption that small states calibrate alignments as a unified rational actor—overstates the coherence of the phenomenon. Hedging may be better understood as an institutional equilibrium that holds only so long as external pressure remains below a threshold that would force internal coalitions to resolve their differences.

Second, the cases point to an asymmetry in hedging capacity that the existing literature has not adequately theorized. Vietnam and Indonesia, despite their divergent regime types, both hedge more effectively when they can externalize the costs of ambiguity onto multilateral institutions—ASEAN centrality, the East Asia Summit, the Treaty of Amity and Cooperation. Singapore and, to a lesser degree, Malaysia hedge through bilateral diversification, which is more flexible but also more exposed to sudden shifts in great-power attention. The finding that hedging capacity correlates more strongly with the availability of multilateral cover than with material capabilities runs against balance-of-threat expectations and suggests that ASEAN's institutional architecture functions less as a constraint on great powers than as a subsidy to small-state ambiguity.

Third, the temporal dimension deserves emphasis. The panel data indicate that hedging episodes in the region since 2017 have shortened in duration, from an average of roughly four years to under two, as US-China competition has narrowed the space for ambiguous positioning. This is consistent with the argument that hedging is a luxury good of moderate polarity, but the mechanism appears to be reputational rather than material: small states abandon hedging not when capabilities shift but when the cost of being seen as insufficiently aligned rises. The interviews with Southeast Asian diplomats support this reading; several described a growing "audit" dynamic in which both Washington and Beijing demand clarity on issues—5G procurement, South China Sea patrols, semiconductor export controls—that were previously left deliberately vague.

Several limitations qualify these claims. The case selection, while designed to capture variation in regime type and alliance structure, excludes the region's smallest states—Brunei, Laos, Cambodia—where hedging may operate through different mechanisms or not at all. The temporal analysis relies on event-coding from secondary sources, which likely undercounts low-visibility hedging behavior such as procurement diversification and quiet diplomatic reassurance. Finally, the interview evidence, drawn from 27 mid-level officials and analysts, captures elite perceptions but not the domestic societal pressures that may constrain or enable hedging over longer horizons; future work should incorporate legislative and public-opinion data where available.

Conclusion

This article has argued that small-state hedging in Southeast Asia is best understood as an institutional and coalitional phenomenon rather than a unitary strategic choice, that its viability depends substantially on multilateral cover, and that its temporal horizons have contracted under intensifying great-power competition. These claims are offered as provisional: the evidence supports them for the cases and period examined, but the mechanisms proposed—particularly the reputational audit dynamic—require testing against a broader sample and against cases outside Southeast Asia where hedging has been observed, such as the Gulf states and Central Asia. If the argument holds, it carries an uncomfortable implication for ASEAN-centered institutionalism: the multilateral architecture that has subsidized small-state ambiguity may itself be eroded by the same great-power competition that makes ambiguity valuable. Whether regional institutions can adapt to preserve hedging space—or whether hedging will give way to more explicit alignment choices—is, on the evidence presented here, an open question, and one that the next several years of regional diplomacy will likely answer.

title: history|local militias and state power during the Song–Yuan transition
text:
Here is a course paper in English on the requested topic, structured with an abstract, introduction, body sections, and conclusion, at approximately 900 words.

---

Title: Local Militias and State Power during the Song–Yuan Transition

Abstract
The Song–Yuan transition (13th century) represents a profound rupture in Chinese history, marked by the Mongol conquest of the Southern Song. This paper examines the role of local militias ( *xiangbing* 乡兵 and *minbing* 民兵) during this turbulent period, arguing that they were not merely auxiliary forces but key agents in the reconfiguration of state power. While the Southern Song state increasingly relied on local militarization for survival, this devolution of violence ultimately undermined central authority. The Mongols, in turn, adeptly incorporated these local forces into their own administrative-military structure, the *tumen* system, transforming potentially disruptive militias into instruments of Yuan consolidation. Through an analysis of militia organization, their relationship with Song officials, and their integration into the Yuan military, this paper demonstrates that the transition was characterized not by a simple military conquest, but by a complex negotiation of power between the central state and local militarized elites.

Introduction
The fall of the Southern Song to the Mongols in 1279 was not a sudden event but a prolonged process of military, political, and social transformation. Traditional narratives often focus on the decisive battles and the heroism of Song loyalists. However, a crucial yet understudied dimension is the role of local militias. These forces, rooted in village and clan networks, emerged as significant military actors as the Song state's regular army (the *Jinjun*) proved inadequate against the Mongol threat. This paper asks: How did local militias shape the nature of state power during the Song–Yuan transition? I argue that the relationship between militias and the state was dialectical. For the Southern Song, militias were a necessary but dangerous expedient that accelerated the state's fragmentation. For the Yuan, they were a malleable resource that, once integrated, helped construct a new imperial order. By examining this dual dynamic, we can better understand the transition not just as a change of dynasties, but as a fundamental restructuring of the relationship between the central government and local society.

Body Section 1: The Southern Song and the Devolution of Violence
By the mid-13th century, the Southern Song faced an existential crisis. The Mongol armies, with their superior cavalry and siege technology, repeatedly breached Song defenses. The Song court's response was a policy of local militarization. Local elites were encouraged to raise *xiangbing* (local braves) and *minbing* (people's militia) for self-defense. While this bolstered local resistance, it also devolved military power away from the central government. These militias were loyal first to their localities and commanders, not to the distant Song court. Warlords like Li Tingzhi in the Huai region or the powerful gentry families of Sichuan commanded private armies that often operated with considerable autonomy. The state, desperate for manpower, granted these leaders official titles and resources, effectively legitimizing their private power. This created a paradox: the militias were essential for the Song's survival, yet their very existence eroded the state's monopoly on violence, creating a fragmented political landscape ripe for conquest.

Body Section 2: The Mongol Incorporation and the *Tumen* System
The Mongols, astute observers of the societies they conquered, recognized the potential of these local militias. Rather than simply destroying them, they sought to incorporate them. The key mechanism was the *tumen* (myriad households) system, which reorganized the population for military and administrative purposes. Local militia leaders who submitted to Mongol rule were often confirmed in their positions and granted hereditary command over their units, now integrated into the Mongol military machine. For example, the Han Chinese warlord Zhang Rou and his forces were absorbed into the Yuan army and played a crucial role in the final campaign against the Southern Song. This policy was pragmatic: it utilized existing local power structures, reduced the need for a massive occupying army, and turned potential rebels into stakeholders in the new regime. The militias, once a centrifugal force, were now a centripetal one, helping to pacify and govern the newly conquered territories.

Body Section 3: Negotiation and the Limits of State Power
The relationship between militias and state power was not one of simple domination. It involved constant negotiation. For the Mongols, the challenge was to harness the militias' local knowledge and manpower without allowing them to become too powerful. The Yuan state implemented a dual system: it relied on these local forces but also stationed Mongol and *semu* (Central Asian) troops as a counterbalance. Furthermore, the Yuan government gradually regularized the militias, imposing census registration and bureaucratic oversight. However, local commanders retained significant autonomy, especially in frontier regions. This negotiated settlement meant that Yuan state power was not absolute but was mediated through a patchwork of local militarized elites. The transition, therefore, was not a clean break but a process of adaptation, where the new state had to accommodate, co-opt, and manage the very forces that had emerged from the old order's collapse.

Conclusion
The Song–Yuan transition was a transformative moment in Chinese history, and local militias were central to its unfolding. For the Southern Song, the reliance on these forces was a symptom of state weakness, a devolution of violence that hastened its demise. For the Yuan, the incorporation of militias through systems like the *tumen* was a cornerstone of their successful consolidation, transforming local defenders into agents of conquest and governance. This paper has argued that the relationship between local militias and state power was dynamic and negotiated. The transition was not merely a Mongol victory over a Song state, but a complex realignment of power between the center and the localities. By studying these militias, we gain a more nuanced understanding of how dynastic change occurred on the ground, through the pragmatic and often tense collaboration between imperial ambitions and local interests. The legacy of this period—a state that had to constantly manage and integrate local military power—would continue to shape Chinese political structures for centuries.

title: agronomy|intercropping maize and soybean under drought stress
text:
Methodology

 Study Site and Experimental Design

The experiment was conducted over two consecutive growing seasons (2022 and 2023) at the University of [Name] Experimental Farm (38°12′N, 92°45′W; 215 m a.s.l.). The site experiences a humid continental climate with a mean annual precipitation of 1,020 mm and a mean growing-season temperature of 21.4°C. The soil is a Mexico silt loam (fine, smectitic, mesic Mollic Epiaqualf) with pH 6.4, 2.1% organic matter, and 18 mg kg⁻¹ available phosphorus (Bray-1). Prior to the trial, the field had been under a maize–soybean rotation for five years. Weather data, including daily precipitation, air temperature, and reference evapotranspiration, were obtained from an on-site automatic weather station.

The experiment used a randomized complete block design with a split-plot arrangement and four replications. The main plot factor was water regime: (i) well-watered control, maintained at 60–80% of field capacity via drip irrigation, and (ii) drought stress, imposed from the V6 stage of maize (R1 of soybean) until physiological maturity by withholding irrigation and using rainout shelters to exclude rainfall, targeting 40–50% of field capacity. Soil volumetric water content was monitored at 0–20 and 20–40 cm depths with calibrated capacitance probes (Decagon 5TM) at 48-h intervals to verify stress imposition. The subplot factor was cropping system: (i) sole maize, (ii) sole soybean, and (iii) maize–soybean intercrop in a 2:2 additive series (two maize rows alternating with two soybean rows; maize at 60,000 plants ha⁻¹ and soybean at 200,000 plants ha⁻¹, with intercrop densities equal to 50% of the sole-crop monoculture densities). Subplots measured 6 m × 8 m with a 1.5 m buffer between plots. All treatments received basal fertilization (120 kg N ha⁻¹, 60 kg P₂O₅ ha⁻¹, 40 kg K₂O ha⁻¹) and standard weed and pest management. The same treatments were imposed on the same plots in both years.

 Data Sources and Sampling

Data were drawn from three sources: (1) primary field measurements collected by the research team, (2) sensor-based soil moisture records, and (3) weather station records. Destructive plant sampling was conducted at three growth stages (tasseling/R2, silking/R4, and physiological maturity). At each stage, three representative plants per species per plot were harvested for determination of leaf area index (LI-3100C), aboveground biomass (oven-dried at 70°C to constant weight), and nitrogen concentration (Kjeldahl). At maturity, grain yield was determined from two central rows (3 m length) per plot, adjusted to 14% moisture, and yield components (ears per plant, kernels per ear, 100-kernel weight, pods per plant, seeds per pod) were recorded. Drought tolerance indices were calculated from grain yields, and land equivalent ratio (LER) was computed as the sum of the relative yields of intercrop components. Soil samples (0–20 cm, five cores per plot) were collected before sowing and after harvest for determination of organic matter, total N, and available P. Root samples were taken at silking using a 10-cm-diameter auger to 60 cm depth to estimate root length density.

 Statistical Analysis

Data were analyzed using linear mixed-effects models in R (version 4.3.1) with the lme4 package. Fixed effects were water regime, cropping system, growth stage (where applicable), and their interactions; year, block, and plot were treated as random effects to account for repeated measures and spatial heterogeneity. Normality and homoscedasticity of residuals were verified using Shapiro–Wilk and Levene tests, and data were log-transformed where necessary. Treatment means were separated using Tukey's HSD test at α = 0.05. Partial land equivalent ratios and competitive ratios were calculated to quantify intercrop advantages under stress. Relationships between soil moisture dynamics and yield components were examined using Pearson correlation and multiple regression. A significance level of P < 0.05 was applied throughout, and results are reported as means ± standard error.

title: sociology|intergenerational support among rural migrant families
text:
This study examines the patterns, determinants, and meanings of intergenerational support among rural migrant families in urban China, a population navigating the dual pressures of labor migration and rapid social transformation. Drawing on 42 in-depth interviews and a survey of 316 migrant households, we analyze how material, instrumental, and emotional support flows between generations under conditions of geographic dispersion and institutional exclusion. Findings reveal a pronounced pattern of "reverse intergenerational support": rather than receiving care from adult children, many rural migrant grandparents migrate to cities to provide childcare, enabling younger couples to pursue formal employment while simultaneously reinforcing the grandparents' dependence on their children's precarious urban livelihoods. Financial transfers remain strongly gendered and conditioned by hukou status, with migrant children remitting to rural parents even as they face housing and healthcare insecurity in destination cities. We identify three distinct support regimes—reciprocal, obligation-driven, and need-based—shaped by family migration trajectories, land tenure arrangements, and the availability of urban social services. The study further shows that emotional support operates as a compensatory mechanism when material transfers are constrained, though it cannot fully offset the erosion of traditional filial norms. These findings complicate linear accounts of intergenerational solidarity, suggesting that rural migrant families develop hybrid support arrangements that blend rural-urban resources, formal and informal care, and shifting normative expectations. We argue that migration does not weaken intergenerational ties but reorganizes them, producing new forms of dependency and reciprocity that are inadequately captured by conventional frameworks of filial piety or state welfare. The study contributes to scholarship on family sociology, migration, and care regimes, and offers implications for policies addressing aging and social protection in transitional contexts.

*Keywords:* intergenerational support; rural migrants; family solidarity; care arrangements; hukou; China

title: international relations|small-state hedging strategies in Southeast Asia
text:
The literature on small-state hedging strategies in Southeast Asia has expanded considerably over the past decade, driven by the region's intensifying great-power competition and the reluctance of most Southeast Asian states to choose sides openly. This review synthesises the main contributions, debates, and gaps in this body of work, focusing on how hedging has been conceptualised, why Southeast Asian states hedge, the instruments they employ, and the conditions under which hedging gives way to balancing or bandwagoning.

A first strand of scholarship concerns definition and conceptual boundaries. Kuik (2008) provided one of the earliest systematic treatments, defining hedging as a set of behaviours that sit between balancing and bandwagoning and that seek to avoid clear alignment while preserving autonomy. Lim and Cooper (2015) refined the concept by distinguishing hedging from related strategies such as omni-enmeshment and insurance-seeking, arguing that conceptual precision is essential if the term is not to become a residual category for all non-aligned behaviour. Goh (2016) similarly cautioned against treating hedging as a catch-all, insisting that it involves deliberate ambiguity and mixed signals rather than mere indecision. More recent work has sought to disaggregate hedging into its economic, diplomatic, and military components, with Ciorciari (2022) proposing a typology based on the degree of commitment and reversibility involved in different hedging moves.

A second strand examines the drivers of hedging. Realist accounts emphasise structural pressure: the uncertainty generated by China's rise and the credibility questions surrounding the United States' regional commitments create incentives for Southeast Asian states to avoid premature alignment (Roy 2005; Le Thu 2019). Constructivist and liberal accounts, by contrast, stress the role of ASEAN norms, elite beliefs, and domestic political economy in shaping hedging choices (Ba 2009; Goh 2016). Kuik (2020) offers a useful synthesis, arguing that hedging is best understood as a response to both systemic uncertainty and the desire to preserve the diplomatic centrality and economic openness on which Southeast Asian states depend. Case studies of individual states have enriched this debate: Parameswaran (2014) on Malaysia, Hiep (2020) on Vietnam, and Storey and Thayer (2021) on the Philippines all show that hedging repertoires differ markedly across the region, reflecting variation in threat perception, regime type, and economic dependence.

A third strand analyses the instruments of hedging. Scholars have documented a recurring toolkit: diversified defence procurement, limited and non-binding security cooperation with multiple partners, participation in multilateral fora, and the cultivation of economic ties with both China and the United States (Chung 2004; Kuik 2008; Ciorciari 2022). Le Thu (2019) highlights the growing use of minilateral arrangements and defence diplomacy as hedging devices, while Goh (2016) emphasises the strategic value of ambiguity in declaratory policy. Recent work has also drawn attention to the domestic and institutional constraints on hedging, noting that weak state capacity, bureaucratic fragmentation, and elite competition can undermine the coherence of hedging strategies (Ba 2009; Hiep 2020).

A fourth strand considers the limits and future of hedging. Several scholars argue that intensifying US-China rivalry is narrowing the space for hedging, pushing Southeast Asian states toward more explicit alignment choices (Roy 2005; Storey and Thayer 2021). Others are more optimistic, contending that hedging remains viable because both great powers continue to tolerate ambiguity and because ASEAN-centred institutions provide cover for diversified partnerships (Kuik 2020; Ciorciari 2022). Le Thu (2019) suggests that hedging is becoming more costly and more differentiated, with states hedging harder in some domains while aligning more clearly in others.

Several gaps remain. First, much of the literature is case-study based, and there is limited comparative work testing competing explanations across the region. Second, the relationship between hedging and domestic politics remains under-theorised, particularly regarding how regime legitimacy and elite bargaining shape strategic ambiguity. Third, the literature has yet to fully specify the conditions under which hedging transitions into balancing or bandwagoning, and the empirical record on such transitions is thin. Finally, the implications of hedging for regional order, including its effects on ASEAN cohesion and on the credibility of great-power commitments, remain contested and deserve further attention.

In sum, the literature has moved from broad conceptual debates toward more granular analyses of hedging repertoires, drivers, and limits. Yet the field still lacks a unified theoretical framework capable of explaining variation in hedging behaviour across Southeast Asia and predicting its trajectory under conditions of intensifying great-power competition.

title: psychology|sleep deprivation and emotional regulation in adolescents
text:
Discussion

The present study set out to examine whether experimentally induced sleep restriction would disproportionately impair emotional regulation in adolescents relative to adults, and whether these effects would be moderated by chronotype. Three findings warrant discussion. First, sleep-restricted adolescents reported a 34% greater increase in negative affect following a social exclusion paradigm than did sleep-restricted adults, despite equivalent reductions in sleep duration across groups. Second, this age-dependent effect was partially accounted for by greater amygdala–prefrontal functional connectivity in the adolescent sample during emotion reappraisal, consistent with the interpretation that prefrontal regulatory circuitry is less efficient under conditions of sleep loss in this developmental window. Third, and contrary to our hypothesis, chronotype did not moderate the relationship between sleep restriction and emotional reactivity; evening types did not show larger deficits than morning types once baseline sleep duration was controlled.

The first finding aligns with the broader literature suggesting that adolescence represents a period of heightened vulnerability to sleep loss (Carskadon, 2011; Dahl & Lewin, 2002), though the mechanisms remain contested. One plausible interpretation is that the adolescent brain's ongoing maturation of limbic and prefrontal systems renders it particularly sensitive to the destabilizing effects of sleep restriction. However, we cannot rule out the possibility that adolescents in our sample simply accumulated a greater sleep debt prior to the experimental manipulation, given the well-documented chronic sleep restriction characteristic of this population. Our baseline actigraphy data showed that adolescents averaged 7.1 hours of sleep per night during the week preceding the study, compared with 7.8 hours in adults—a difference that, while statistically controlled, may have amplified the experimental effect.

The absence of a chronotype moderation effect is somewhat surprising given prior work linking eveningness to emotion dysregulation (Randler, 2014). We suspect this null result may reflect a restriction-of-range problem: our sample was predominantly intermediate chronotype, with relatively few extreme morning or evening types. Alternatively, the laboratory-based emotion induction may have been insufficiently sensitive to chronotype-related variation in circadian timing. Future studies employing ecological momentary assessment in naturalistic settings may be better positioned to detect such effects.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. Our sample consisted of university-affiliated adolescents aged 16–18, which may not generalize to younger adolescents or to those from lower socioeconomic backgrounds. The cross-sectional design precludes causal claims about developmental trajectories, and our 24-hour sleep restriction protocol, while ecologically valid, cannot disentangle the effects of sleep loss from those of circadian misalignment. Additionally, the emotion regulation task relied on self-report and a single physiological index (skin conductance); multi-method approaches incorporating neuroimaging during naturalistic emotion provocation would strengthen future work. Finally, our modest sample size (N = 84) limited power to detect small interaction effects, and the null chronotype finding should be interpreted with appropriate caution.

 Conclusion

Taken together, these findings suggest that sleep deprivation may exert a more pronounced effect on emotional regulation in adolescents than in adults, with preliminary evidence implicating developmental differences in prefrontal–limbic circuitry. The absence of chronotype moderation, while not definitive, hints that the sleep–emotion relationship in adolescence may be more universal than previously assumed. Clinically, these results lend cautious support to school-based interventions aimed at protecting adolescent sleep, though our laboratory paradigm cannot speak directly to whether delaying school start times would produce meaningful improvements in emotional functioning. Future longitudinal work tracking sleep, emotional regulation, and neural development across adolescence is needed to clarify whether the effects observed here represent a transient state-dependent phenomenon or a pathway to enduring vulnerability.

title: law|data protection obligations of cross-border e-commerce platforms
text:
Data Protection Obligations of Cross-Border E-Commerce Platforms

 Abstract

Cross-border e-commerce platforms operate at the intersection of multiple legal regimes, processing vast quantities of personal data while simultaneously navigating divergent regulatory frameworks. This paper examines the data protection obligations incumbent upon such platforms, focusing on the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), China's Personal Information Protection Law (PIPL), and the emerging patchwork of national laws governing cross-border data flows. It argues that compliance obligations are not merely formal requirements but substantive duties that shape platform architecture, contractual relationships, and accountability mechanisms. The paper further analyses the tension between data protection and free data flow, and proposes that platforms adopt a "highest common denominator" compliance strategy anchored in accountability and privacy-by-design principles.

 Introduction

The global expansion of e-commerce has produced a class of intermediaries—cross-border platforms—that occupy a structurally distinctive position in the data economy. Unlike domestic merchants, these platforms collect, store, and transfer personal data across jurisdictional boundaries, implicating the privacy interests of consumers in multiple states simultaneously. This position generates a complex web of obligations: platforms may be characterised as data controllers, processors, or both, depending on their relationship to merchants and consumers, and they must reconcile obligations arising under conflicting legal regimes.

This paper proceeds in three parts. Part I maps the principal regulatory frameworks governing cross-border platforms. Part II analyses the substantive obligations—lawful basis, transparency, data subject rights, and cross-border transfer restrictions—that these frameworks impose. Part III considers enforcement and accountability mechanisms, before the conclusion offers recommendations for compliant platform governance.

 I. The Regulatory Landscape

The GDPR establishes the most comprehensive regime. Article 3(2) extends its territorial scope to controllers outside the EU where they offer goods or services to, or monitor the behaviour of, EU data subjects—a provision that captures most cross-border platforms serving European consumers. The GDPR imposes obligations of lawfulness, fairness, and transparency (Article 5), data minimisation and purpose limitation, and mandates a lawful transfer mechanism under Chapter V for data leaving the European Economic Area.

China's PIPL adopts a comparable extraterritorial approach under Article 3(2), applying to overseas processors where they provide products or services to individuals in China or analyse the behaviour of persons within China. The PIPL imposes distinct requirements, including separate consent for sensitive personal information, security assessments for certain cross-border transfers, and the appointment of local representatives. The United States, by contrast, lacks a comprehensive federal statute, relying on sectoral laws and state legislation such as the California Consumer Privacy Act, producing a fragmented compliance environment.

This divergence creates what scholars term the "regulatory trilemma": platforms cannot simultaneously satisfy maximal transparency, minimal data transfer, and global service provision without incurring significant compliance costs.

 II. Substantive Obligations

Lawful basis and consent. Platforms typically rely on contract necessity or consent. The GDPR's standard for valid consent—freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous—is demanding, and the European Data Protection Board has clarified that consent cannot be validly obtained where there is a clear imbalance of power. Cross-border platforms must therefore calibrate consent mechanisms to the strictest applicable standard, as consent valid under one regime may be insufficient under another.

Transparency and information duties. Articles 13 and 14 GDPR require layered privacy notices disclosing purposes, recipients, retention periods, and transfer mechanisms. The PIPL imposes analogous duties under Articles 17 and 39, additionally requiring disclosure of the overseas recipient's identity and purpose. Platforms serving both markets must reconcile these requirements, often through jurisdiction-specific notice layers.

Data subject rights. Platforms must operationalise rights of access, rectification, erasure, restriction, portability, and objection within statutory deadlines. The practical challenge lies in coordinating responses across distributed data systems and third-party processors, and in reconciling the GDPR's one-month deadline with the PIPL's fifteen-day requirement for certain requests.

Cross-border transfer restrictions. This is the most operationally significant obligation. Under the GDPR, transfers require adequacy decisions, standard contractual clauses, or binding corporate rules, following *Schrems II*, supplemented by transfer impact assessments. The PIPL requires one of three mechanisms: security assessment, certification, or standard contracts filed with authorities. Platforms must therefore maintain parallel transfer architectures—a costly but unavoidable consequence of regulatory divergence.

 III. Accountability and Enforcement

Accountability obligations—data protection impact assessments, records of processing, data protection officers, and breach notification—operationalise the substantive duties. Article 33 GDPR requires notification within seventy-two hours; the PIPL requires immediate remedial measures and notification to authorities and affected individuals. Enforcement risk is substantial: GDPR fines reach four percent of global turnover, and the PIPL authorises penalties up to RMB 50 million or five percent of prior-year turnover.

Beyond formal penalties, platforms face reputational and contractual exposure. Merchants increasingly demand data processing agreements that allocate liability, and platforms may be held jointly liable for merchant misconduct under both regimes.

 Conclusion

Cross-border e-commerce platforms bear layered, overlapping data protection obligations that cannot be satisfied through minimal formal compliance. The structural divergence between the GDPR, PIPL, and sectoral regimes requires platforms to adopt a highest-common-denominator strategy: implementing privacy-by-design architecture, harmonising consent and notice standards to the most stringent applicable rule, maintaining parallel transfer mechanisms, and embedding accountability through documented impact assessments and processor oversight. Such an approach converts regulatory fragmentation from a compliance burden into a governance advantage, enhancing consumer trust and reducing enforcement exposure across jurisdictions. Future research should examine the emerging role of mutual adequacy arrangements and international data flow frameworks in reducing these compliance frictions.

title: journalism and media studies|local newspaper closures and civic participation
text:
Methodology

This study employs a longitudinal, quasi-experimental design combining secondary administrative data on local newspaper closures with individual-level survey data on civic participation. The unit of analysis is the county, with individuals nested within counties, allowing us to exploit variation in the timing of newspaper closures across communities.

Data Sources

We draw on three sources. First, newspaper closure data come from the Editor & Publisher International Yearbook and the Alliance for Audited Media, supplemented by LexisNexis searches of trade publications (*Editor & Publisher*, *Nieman Lab*) to identify closures and significant reductions in publication frequency between 2000 and 2022. A closure is coded when a newspaper ceases print publication entirely or shifts to an online-only format with substantially reduced newsroom staff (verified through contemporaneous reporting). Second, civic participation measures come from the Current Population Survey (CPS) Civic Engagement Supplement (2008–2021) and the American National Election Studies (ANES), which provide individual-level indicators of voting, volunteering, group membership, and community meeting attendance. Third, county-level covariates—population, median income, educational attainment, unemployment, and broadband access—are drawn from the American Community Survey and the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

Sample

The analytic sample includes all U.S. counties that had at least one daily or weekly newspaper in 2000 and for which CPS or ANES respondents are available (N = 1,142 counties; approximately 48,000 individual survey respondents across survey waves). Counties are classified into three groups: (1) those experiencing a newspaper closure during the observation window (treated), (2) those with a continuously operating newspaper (comparison), and (3) those never having a local newspaper (excluded from primary analyses). Closure counties (n = 387) are matched to comparison counties using propensity score matching on 2000 baseline characteristics—population size, median household income, education, age structure, and prior voter turnout—to address selection bias in which communities lose newspapers.

Analysis

We estimate two-way fixed-effects models regressing individual civic participation outcomes on an indicator for whether a respondent's county had experienced a newspaper closure by the survey year, including county and year fixed effects and individual-level controls (age, education, income, race/ethnicity, homeownership, length of residence). Standard errors are clustered at the county level. To examine dynamics, we use event-study specifications that trace participation trajectories in the years before and after closure, testing for pre-trends. Given that closure timing may be endogenous to civic decline, we instrument for closure using county-level exposure to national newspaper industry shocks—specifically, declines in newspaper advertising revenue interacted with baseline newspaper market structure—following recent work in media economics. Robustness checks include alternative matching specifications, exclusion of counties with multiple newspapers, and separate models for presidential versus midterm election years. Qualitative data from 24 semi-structured interviews with local officials and civic organization leaders in eight closure counties supplement the quantitative findings, providing mechanism-level evidence on how information loss translates into reduced participation.

title: environmental science|wetland restoration and carbon sequestration
text:
Wetlands are among the most carbon-dense ecosystems on Earth, yet centuries of drainage, conversion, and degradation have transformed many from carbon sinks into net sources of greenhouse gases. Wetland restoration is increasingly promoted as a nature-based climate solution with the potential to recover biodiversity, improve water quality, and sequester atmospheric carbon. However, the magnitude and permanence of carbon benefits remain highly uncertain, varying with wetland type, hydrogeomorphic setting, restoration method, and time since intervention. This review synthesizes current evidence on the relationships between wetland restoration and carbon sequestration, drawing on peer-reviewed studies of freshwater marshes, peatlands, mangroves, and salt marshes. We examine key controlling factors—hydrology, vegetation community composition, soil organic matter dynamics, and methane emissions—that determine whether restored wetlands function as net carbon sinks on management-relevant timescales. Evidence indicates that rewetting drained organic soils can rapidly reduce carbon dioxide emissions, while recovery of the full sequestration capacity often requires decades to centuries, particularly in peatlands. Methane fluxes frequently increase following rewetting, potentially offsetting short-term radiative benefits, though these offsets diminish over time. Mangrove and tidal marsh restoration generally yields more favorable and rapid carbon outcomes. We also assess methodological challenges in quantifying carbon gains, including baseline establishment, spatial variability, and accounting for all greenhouse gases. Finally, we identify research priorities, including long-term monitoring, standardized carbon accounting protocols, and integrated assessment of co-benefits and trade-offs. Restoring wetlands offers substantial, if context-dependent, climate mitigation potential that must be evaluated alongside ecological and social objectives to ensure effective and credible outcomes.

*Keywords:* wetland restoration; carbon sequestration; blue carbon; peatlands; methane; greenhouse gas accounting; nature-based climate solutions

title: history|the role of Venetian merchants in the fourteenth-century spice trade
text:
The fourteenth century represents a pivotal moment in the history of Mediterranean commerce, when the commercial revolution of the High Middle Ages reached its mature form and the Italian maritime republics consolidated their dominance over the long-distance trade in luxury goods. Among these republics, Venice occupies a distinctive position. Its merchant class, operating through a sophisticated network of family firms, state institutions, and colonial outposts, exercised a commanding influence over the flow of spices from the Levant to European markets. This paper examines the role of Venetian merchants in the fourteenth-century spice trade, arguing that their commercial success rested not merely on geographic advantage or naval power but on a flexible combination of institutional innovation, diplomatic engagement with Mamluk and Byzantine authorities, and the integration of family-based commercial networks with the apparatus of the Venetian state. By analyzing the mechanisms through which Venetian merchants acquired, transported, and distributed spices, this study contributes to a broader understanding of how medieval commercial capitalism operated and how the Venetian model shaped the economic landscape of late medieval Europe.

The spice trade of the fourteenth century encompassed a wide range of commodities, including pepper, cinnamon, ginger, cloves, nutmeg, and mace, which reached European markets through a complex chain of intermediaries stretching from Southeast Asia and the Indian Ocean to the ports of the Levant. The fall of Acre in 1291 and the subsequent decline of the Crusader states shifted the focal points of this trade toward Mamluk-controlled Alexandria and Beirut, as well as to the Genoese colony of Caffa on the Black Sea (Abu-Lughod 1989). Venetian merchants adapted rapidly to these changed circumstances, negotiating commercial privileges with the Mamluk sultanate and establishing consular institutions in Alexandria and Damascus that regulated the activities of their compatriots and provided mechanisms for dispute resolution (Ashtor 1983). These institutional arrangements were essential to the stability of long-distance trade, reducing transaction costs and mitigating the risks inherent in cross-cultural commerce.

A central feature of Venetian commercial organization was the integration of private enterprise with public authority. The state supervised the great trading convoys, the mude, which sailed at regular intervals to designated destinations under armed escort, and it required merchants to register their cargoes and pay customs duties at the fondaco dei Tedeschi and other designated points (Lane 1973). At the same time, the Venetian nobility, who constituted the merchant class, organized their affairs through family partnerships known as fraterne and through the commenda, a contractual arrangement in which capital was entrusted to a travelling partner in exchange for a share of profits (Pryor 1988). These instruments allowed Venetian merchants to pool capital, spread risk, and maintain commercial relationships across great distances. The surviving account books and correspondence of families such as the Badoer and the Zibaldone da Canal reveal the day-to-day operations of these networks, including the credit arrangements, insurance practices, and price negotiations that sustained the spice trade (Dotson 1994; Lopez and Raymond 1955).

The comparative dimension of the Venetian achievement becomes clear when set against the experience of Genoa, Pisa, and the Catalan merchants of Barcelona. Genoese merchants, though formidable competitors, concentrated their efforts on the Black Sea route and on the trade in grain and alum, while Venetian merchants specialized to a greater degree in the high-value spice trade and in the Levant markets where pepper and other oriental goods were exchanged for European silver, coral, and textiles (Balard 1983; Epstein 1996). This specialization was reinforced by Venice's diplomatic presence in Cairo and Damascus and by the republic's willingness to conclude commercial treaties with Islamic rulers, a pragmatism that distinguished Venetian policy from the more confrontational stance sometimes adopted by other Christian powers (Jacoby 1997). The Venetian state also invested in the infrastructure of trade, building the Arsenale into the most advanced shipyard in Europe and maintaining a system of state galleys that guaranteed the regular movement of goods between the lagoon and the Levant (Lane 1973).

The significance of the Venetian role in the fourteenth-century spice trade extends beyond the quantification of cargoes and profits. Venetian merchants functioned as cultural brokers as well as economic actors, transmitting not only commodities but also knowledge, techniques, and tastes between the Islamic world and Latin Europe. The commercial practices they developed, including the use of bills of exchange, marine insurance, and double-entry bookkeeping, anticipated features of later financial capitalism (de Roover 1963). Moreover, the wealth generated by the spice trade underwrote the artistic and architectural achievements of fourteenth-century Venice and reinforced the oligarchic political order that governed the republic. Understanding how Venetian merchants organized the spice trade thus illuminates the intersection of commerce, politics, and culture in the late medieval Mediterranean.

This paper proceeds in three parts. The first section examines the institutional framework of Venetian commerce, including the mude system, the consular network, and the legal instruments available to merchants. The second section analyzes the commercial strategies employed by Venetian firms in Alexandria, Beirut, and Constantinople, drawing on surviving merchant correspondence and account books. The third section assesses the impact of the Black Death and the subsequent Venetian-Genoese wars on the spice trade, arguing that Venetian resilience during this period of crisis laid the foundation for the republic's commercial hegemony in the fifteenth century.

title: linguistics|code-switching among bilingual teenagers in Singapore
text:
Discussion

The patterns emerging from the corpus complicate any straightforward account of code-switching as either a marker of limited proficiency or a strategic resource deployed by fully fluent speakers. The 412 switches recorded across roughly nine hours of peer conversation cluster around two functions that are difficult to reconcile within a single framework: clause-internal lexical insertion, predominantly nouns and discourse particles, and clause-external alternation at turn boundaries, often marking shifts in stance or addressee. The first type was overwhelmingly directed at referents with no exact English equivalent—local food items, school-specific terminology, kinship terms—which is consistent with the gap-filling account familiar from earlier Singapore work (Poplack's equivalence constraint was violated in only 6% of intra-sentential cases, all involving tags). The second type is less easily explained by lexical need. Turn-initial switches into Mandarin or Malay frequently preceded disagreement or criticism, a pattern we interpret cautiously: with only 58 such tokens, the association is suggestive rather than robust, and we cannot rule out that the same speakers would produce comparable face-threatening moves in English given a different interlocutor set.

What strikes us as the more consequential finding is the asymmetry across the three focal friendship groups. In the predominantly Chinese-Singaporean group, English-Mandarin switching was frequent (n = 187) and symmetrical, with either language able to serve as matrix; in the Malay-majority group, switching was rarer (n = 64) and almost always English-into-Malay, with Malay functioning as the matrix in 81% of multi-word switches. The Tamil-speaking group occupied an intermediate position, but here our data are thinnest, and the small number of tokens (n = 41) makes any generalization hazardous. One plausible reading is that the matrix-language asymmetry reflects differing degrees of institutional pressure on the heritage language—Malay's status as a national language may afford it a default interactional role that Mandarin, despite its official parity, does not occupy in informal peer talk. We advance this only as a hypothesis; our design cannot adjudicate between language-ideological explanations and more local, network-specific norms, and the group composition was not balanced for socioeconomic background, a variable that has confounded Singapore bilingualism research before.

Two further observations deserve mention. First, switches were overwhelmingly unmarked—no pauses, no repair, no metallinguistic commentary—which supports the view that for these speakers the bilingual repertoire is a single interactional resource rather than two discrete systems called upon in alternation. Second, the one context in which switching all but disappeared was task-focused discussion of schoolwork, where English monolingualism held across all three groups. That the same speakers who switched freely in gossip and banter produced sustained English-only stretches in collaborative task talk suggests register sensitivity of a kind that proficiency-deficit accounts cannot accommodate.

Conclusion

Taken together, the findings argue against treating Singaporean adolescent code-switching as a unitary phenomenon. The data point to at least two distinguishable practices—referent-driven lexical insertion and stance-marking alternation—with different distributions across groups and registers. The group-level asymmetries, while based on a modest sample, indicate that the matrix language in peer interaction is not simply a function of individual fluency but is shaped by community-level norms that future work should examine with larger, balanced samples and, ideally, longitudinal observation. We would also flag the limitations of our elicitation context: the recorded conversations took place in school settings, and the observer's paradox cannot be dismissed, particularly given the near-total absence of switches in task talk, which may reflect self-monitoring under a researcher's gaze rather than a genuine register effect. Replication in unstructured, out-of-school settings is needed before the register finding can be treated as secure.

The practical upshot, stated with due caution, is that classroom policies premised on code-switching as a symptom of weak English are difficult to square with its distribution here—concentrated among fluent speakers, functionally motivated, and register-sensitive. Whether pedagogical embrace of translanguaging would improve outcomes is an empirical question our data cannot answer, and we resist the temptation to extrapolate. What the study does establish is a descriptive baseline: a map of who switches, where, and to what apparent end, against which claims about Singaporean bilingual practice—declinist or otherwise—can at least be checked.

title: education|the effects of formative assessment on secondary school mathematics
text:
The Effects of Formative Assessment on Secondary School Mathematics

 Abstract

Formative assessment has emerged as a central pedagogical strategy in mathematics education, yet its specific effects on secondary school learners remain a subject of ongoing empirical and theoretical inquiry. This paper reviews and synthesizes research on how formative assessment influences students' mathematical achievement, motivation, and self-regulation in secondary school settings. Drawing on both classroom-based studies and larger-scale investigations, the paper argues that formative assessment produces consistently positive—though context-dependent—effects on mathematics learning, particularly when it is embedded in daily instruction, accompanied by substantive feedback, and supported by teachers' assessment literacy. The paper also identifies challenges to implementation, including time constraints, tensions with summative accountability systems, and variability in teacher practice. It concludes by proposing design principles for effective formative assessment in secondary mathematics classrooms.

 1. Introduction

Secondary school mathematics occupies a pivotal position in students' educational trajectories: it shapes access to advanced study, influences career pathways, and often determines students' broader relationship with learning. At the same time, mathematics is frequently reported as a subject in which students experience anxiety, disengagement, and declining confidence during adolescence. In this context, how teachers assess students—and, crucially, how they use assessment to inform teaching and learning—has attracted sustained attention from researchers and practitioners alike.

Formative assessment, broadly defined as the process of gathering and interpreting evidence about student learning in order to adapt instruction and help students advance toward intended learning goals (Black & Wiliam, 1998), stands in contrast to summative assessment, which primarily serves to certify or rank achievement. Over the past three decades, a substantial body of research has examined whether formative assessment "works," for whom, and under what conditions. This paper focuses specifically on secondary school mathematics, asking: What effects does formative assessment have on students' mathematical learning and related outcomes, and what factors mediate these effects?

The paper proceeds in four parts. Section 2 clarifies the conceptual foundations of formative assessment. Section 3 reviews evidence on its effects on achievement, motivation, and self-regulation. Section 4 discusses implementation challenges and conditions for effectiveness. Section 5 offers concluding reflections and design principles.

 2. Conceptual Foundations

Formative assessment is best understood not as a particular technique but as a process involving three key questions: Where is the learner going? Where is the learner now? How can the gap be closed? (Wiliam, 2011). This process encompasses a range of classroom practices, including the elicitation of evidence through questioning and tasks, the provision of feedback, peer- and self-assessment, and the adjustment of instruction in response to evidence.

Two conceptual distinctions are important. First, formative assessment is defined by its *function* rather than its *form*: any assessment activity—a quiz, a homework task, a classroom discussion—can be formative if the evidence it generates is actually used to adapt teaching and learning. Second, in mathematics specifically, formative assessment must attend to the structure of mathematical knowledge. Mathematics is hierarchically organized, with later concepts building on earlier ones; diagnostic information about students' misconceptions and procedural fluency is therefore particularly valuable. This makes mathematics a domain in which formative assessment has strong theoretical promise.

 3. Effects on Learning Outcomes

 3.1 Achievement

The most extensively studied outcome is achievement. Early influential reviews (Black & Wiliam, 1998) reported effect sizes associated with formative assessment interventions that were substantial by educational standards, though subsequent meta-analyses have suggested more modest and variable effects (Kingston & Nash, 2011). In secondary mathematics specifically, studies have found that structured formative assessment—such as regular low-stakes diagnostic quizzes with feedback, "exit tickets" used to plan the next lesson, and classroom questioning that surfaces misconceptions—is associated with improved performance on both proximal and distal measures of mathematical understanding.

Importantly, effects appear strongest when formative assessment is *embedded* in instruction rather than added as an extra activity, and when feedback is specific, timely, and actionable. Feedback that simply reports correctness ("right/wrong") produces weaker effects than feedback that explains *why* an approach is flawed and *what* to do next.

 3.2 Motivation and Attitudes

Secondary students' motivation in mathematics is fragile and declines across adolescence. Formative assessment may support motivation by reducing the stakes of individual tasks, emphasizing mastery rather than performance comparison, and communicating that ability is developable. However, effects on motivation are conditional: if formative assessment is experienced as surveillance or as additional testing, it can heighten anxiety rather than reduce it. The evidence therefore suggests that the *climate* in which formative assessment occurs—whether errors are treated as information or as failure—is decisive.

 3.3 Self-Regulation and Metacognition

A third line of research examines self-regulated learning. Formative assessment practices such as self-assessment checklists, peer feedback protocols, and reflective prompts can help students develop metacognitive awareness of their mathematical thinking. In secondary mathematics, where students must increasingly monitor their own problem-solving strategies, such practices may have lasting value beyond immediate achievement gains, though the evidence base here is smaller and more qualitative.

 4. Implementation Challenges and Conditions

The literature consistently identifies several barriers. First, time: formative assessment requires instructional time for elicitation and feedback, which competes with curriculum coverage pressures. Second, accountability tensions: high-stakes summative examinations can incentivize teaching to the test and discourage the low-stakes exploratory assessment that formative practice requires. Third, teacher assessment literacy: effective formative assessment demands sophisticated skills in interpreting student thinking and designing responsive instruction, which many teachers report lacking in preparation.

These challenges suggest that the effects of formative assessment are not automatic but mediated by teacher knowledge, classroom culture, and institutional support. Professional development that focuses on subject-specific formative assessment in mathematics—rather than generic assessment techniques—appears particularly promising.

 5. Conclusion

The evidence indicates that formative assessment can meaningfully support secondary school students' mathematics learning, with positive effects on achievement, motivation, and self-regulation under favorable conditions. Its effectiveness depends less on adopting specific tools than on embedding evidence-use into daily instruction, providing substantive feedback, and cultivating classroom norms in which errors are treated as learning opportunities. Future research should attend more closely to subject-specific mechanisms in mathematics and to the institutional conditions that enable or constrain formative practice.

References

Black, P., & Wiliam, D. (1998). Assessment and classroom learning. *Assessment in Education*, 5(1), 7–74.

Kingston, N., & Nash, B. (2011). Formative assessment: A meta-analysis and a call for research. *Educational Measurement: Issues and Practice*, 30(4), 28–37.

Wiliam, D. (2011). *Embedded formative assessment*. Solution Tree Press.
