title: history|local militias and state power during the Song–Yuan transition
text:
Methodology

This study examines the relationship between local militia organization and state power in the lower Yangzi and Jiangnan regions during the Song–Yuan transition (roughly 1260–1300). It asks how local armed groups—village defense leagues (*xiangbing*), gentry-led *yibing* (righteous troops), and fortress-community (*baojia*-style) militias—mediated between declining Southern Song authorities and the consolidating Yuan state, and whether militia mobilization expanded or constrained central state capacity. The analysis combines a purpose-built event dataset with close reading of primary sources, using a mixed-methods design that pairs quantitative pattern-finding with qualitative process tracing.

Data sources. Three categories of evidence are used. First, the official corpus: the *Song Shi* and *Yuan Shi* biographies and military treatises, the *Song Huiyao Jigao*, and the *Yuan Dianzhang* (institutional statutes), which record appointments, rewards, and prohibitions concerning militia leaders. Second, local gazetteers (*difangzhi*) from the period and Ming compilations preserving Song–Yuan material, especially for Jiangnan prefectures (Lin'an, Pingjiang, Changzhou, Huzhou, and Shaoxing), which list militia units, fortress construction, and local notables. Third, private writings—literati collections (*wenji*), stele inscriptions (*beiming*), and family genealogies—which supply granular detail on individual militia leaders and their negotiations with successive regimes. All texts are drawn from the Siku Quanshu, Zhonghua Shuju critical editions, and the China Biographical Database (CBDB) for prosopographical linkage. Where gazetteers survive only in later recensions, entries are flagged and source-critical notes recorded.

Sample. The core sample is a set of 214 militia mobilization events (musters, fortress constructions, surrenders, and disbandments) drawn from the above sources for 40 prefectures in the lower Yangzi macro-region, 1260–1300. Events were identified through systematic keyword searches of digitized corpora (兵, 民兵, 義兵, 寨, 堡, 團結, 歸附) and cross-checked against gazetteer chronologies. Inclusion required a dateable event, a locatable jurisdiction, and at least one named actor (official, notable, or unit commander). A purposive subsample of 18 cases—selected for source density and variation in outcome (co-opted, suppressed, or autonomous)—supports the qualitative component. Limitations are acknowledged: surviving sources over-represent literate elite actors and state perspectives, and gazetteer coverage is uneven across prefectures.

Analysis. Quantitative analysis proceeds in three steps. First, events are coded on dimensions including initiator (state, local elite, or hybrid), scale (recorded troop numbers, where given), outcome (incorporation into Yuan military households, disbandment, or persistence), and location. Second, descriptive statistics map the temporal and spatial distribution of mobilization, testing whether militia activity clusters around invasion routes and administrative seats. Third, logistic regression estimates the association between local institutional features (presence of garrison, gentry density proxied by examination success, and pre-existing defense works) and the likelihood of militia co-optation by the Yuan state. Given the small sample and source bias, results are interpreted as suggestive rather than causal.

Qualitative analysis uses process tracing on the 18 cases to reconstruct sequences of negotiation between militia leaders and state agents, identifying mechanisms—honorific appointment, hereditary command, tax exemption, and hostage-taking—through which the Yuan converted local force into fiscal-military capacity. Triangulation across gazetteer, official, and epigraphic sources mitigates single-source bias, and where sources conflict, the discrepancy itself is treated as evidence of competing claims to authority.

title: management|remote work and team innovation in technology companies
text:
The rapid normalization of remote and hybrid work arrangements in technology companies has raised important questions about whether distributed teams can sustain the innovation outcomes traditionally associated with co-located collaboration. This study examines the relationship between remote work intensity and team innovation in technology firms, and investigates the mediating mechanisms and boundary conditions that shape this relationship. Drawing on media synchronicity theory and the input–process–output model of team effectiveness, we propose that remote work affects team innovation indirectly through two competing pathways: knowledge sharing and team creativity-relevant processes, on the one hand, and coordination costs and social isolation, on the other. We further posit that digital collaboration tool usage and transformational team leadership moderate these pathways. Using a multi-source, time-lagged survey design, data were collected from 187 product development teams across 42 technology companies, with team innovation assessed through both supervisory ratings and objective innovation indicators (patent disclosures and implemented product improvements). Results from multilevel structural equation modeling indicate that moderate levels of remote work are associated with higher team innovation, whereas very high remote work intensity (above 80%) is associated with declining innovation, suggesting a curvilinear, inverted U-shaped relationship. Knowledge sharing mediated the positive effect, while coordination costs mediated the negative effect at high intensity. Digital collaboration tool usage and transformational leadership attenuated the negative curvilinear effect. These findings contribute to remote work and team innovation literature by identifying optimal remote work configurations and managerial levers that enable technology companies to harness the innovative potential of distributed teams while mitigating its costs.

*(~250 words)*

title: law|data protection obligations of cross-border e-commerce platforms
text:
The rapid expansion of cross-border electronic commerce has fundamentally reshaped the architecture of international trade, enabling firms of all sizes to reach consumers across jurisdictional boundaries with unprecedented ease. Global retail e-commerce sales have grown at double-digit rates for much of the past decade, and a substantial and increasing share of these transactions involves parties located in different legal systems (UNCTAD 2021). Platform intermediaries—marketplaces, payment processors, logistics coordinators, and advertising networks—sit at the centre of these transactions, aggregating and analysing vast quantities of personal data relating to consumers, merchants, and other participants. This data intensity is not incidental to the cross-border platform business model; it is constitutive of it. Recommendation algorithms, fraud detection, credit scoring, targeted advertising, and logistics optimisation all depend on continuous flows of personal information across borders. As a result, cross-border e-commerce platforms have become among the most significant controllers and processors of personal data in the global economy, and their practices have attracted sustained regulatory and scholarly attention (Zuboff 2019; Citron and Pasquale 2014).

The legal environment in which these platforms operate is, however, deeply fragmented. Since the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) entered into force in 2018, a growing number of jurisdictions have adopted or modernised comprehensive data protection statutes, including Brazil's Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados, China's Personal Information Protection Law, Japan's Act on the Protection of Personal Information, and various state-level privacy laws in the United States (Bradford 2020; Schwartz 2019). These regimes differ not only in their substantive obligations—lawful bases for processing, consent requirements, data subject rights, breach notification duties, and restrictions on automated decision-making—but also in their territorial scope, their mechanisms for regulating transfers of data abroad, and their enforcement postures. The GDPR's extraterritorial reach, combined with its stringent conditions for international transfers following Schrems II, has been particularly consequential for platforms that route personal data through global infrastructure (Kuner 2020; Kuner, Cate, Millard and Svantesson 2023). The result is a regulatory mosaic in which a single platform may be simultaneously subject to overlapping, inconsistent, and occasionally conflicting obligations.

This fragmentation generates distinctive compliance challenges for cross-border e-commerce platforms. Unlike domestic firms operating within a single legal order, platforms must design data governance architectures that satisfy the most demanding applicable regime without thereby violating another. They must determine, often under conditions of legal uncertainty, which jurisdictions' laws apply to which processing activities; how to structure consent and contract mechanisms across diverse populations of users; how to respond to data subject requests that may arrive from anywhere and carry different substantive entitlements; and how to conduct transfers of personal data—including the internal transfers that are intrinsic to multinational corporate structures—in a manner that satisfies transfer restrictions in multiple legal systems simultaneously (Bygrave 2020; Daskal 2018). These difficulties are compounded by the speed of technological change, the opacity of platform data practices, and the asymmetry of information between platforms and both regulators and users.

The scholarly literature has addressed these questions from several angles. A substantial body of work examines the extraterritorial application of data protection law and the conflicts that arise when states assert regulatory authority over data processing occurring abroad (Svantesson 2017; Ryngaert 2015). Another strand focuses on international transfer mechanisms, assessing the adequacy of adequacy decisions, standard contractual clauses, and binding corporate rules as tools for reconciling trade in data with the protection of fundamental rights (Kuner 2020; Yakovleva 2020). A third examines platform accountability more broadly, questioning whether existing regulatory categories—controller and processor, consent and legitimate interest—are adequate to capture the relational and infrastructural power of large platforms (Cohen 2019; Finck 2018). Comparative work has begun to map the convergence and divergence of regional regimes, though much of it predates the most recent legislative developments (Greenleaf 2021).

Nevertheless, important gaps remain. Much of the existing scholarship analyses single jurisdictions or bilateral conflicts, and relatively little work systematically examines the cumulative obligations that bear on cross-border e-commerce platforms as a class of regulated actors. The specific interaction between e-commerce platform architectures—multi-sided markets, integrated payment and logistics services, algorithmic intermediation—and data protection obligations remains underexplored. Furthermore, the enforcement dimension has received insufficient attention: the practical consequences of divergent regulatory interpretations for platform design decisions are poorly understood, as are the strategies platforms deploy to manage regulatory risk across jurisdictions. The question of how platforms should allocate responsibility among their various affiliated entities, contractors, and merchant partners for data protection compliance is likewise unsettled.

This paper addresses these gaps. It asks: what data protection obligations apply to cross-border e-commerce platforms, how do those obligations interact and conflict across jurisdictions, and what compliance strategies are available to platforms seeking to meet them? The analysis proceeds in three parts. It first develops a typology of cross-border platform data processing activities, distinguishing consumer-facing processing, merchant-facing processing, internal corporate transfers, and processing by third-party service providers, and maps the obligations that attach to each. It then examines the principal points of conflict and uncertainty, including conflicting transfer restrictions, divergent rules on consent and lawful basis, and the treatment of automated decision-making. Finally, it evaluates the adequacy of existing compliance mechanisms and considers whether regulatory cooperation, mutual recognition, or harmonisation offers a more coherent path forward. The paper's contribution is to provide a systematic, cross-jurisdictional account of platform data protection obligations and to identify the structural problems that any reform agenda must confront.

title: literary studies|landscape and exile in the poetry of Su Shi
text:
Literature Review: Landscape and Exile in the Poetry of Su Shi

Scholarship on Su Shi (1037–1101) has long recognized that his repeated political exiles shaped both the circumstances and the substance of his poetic production. The relationship between landscape and exile in his work, however, has been approached from several distinct angles, and a review of this literature reveals both substantial consensus and persistent disagreements.

A foundational strand of scholarship treats Su Shi's exile poetry as a record of psychological transformation through engagement with unfamiliar terrain. Yoshikawa (1967) argued that Su Shi's poetry of the Huangzhou period marked a decisive turn toward a more personal, reflective mode, in which the strange landscape of his place of exile became a medium for rethinking his relationship to the state and to himself. This view has been broadly influential. Lin (1972) extended it by tracing a pattern of "spiritual transcendence" across the successive exiles to Huangzhou, Huizhou, and Danzhou, reading the later poems as evidence of increasing equanimity. Both scholars thus treat landscape as a catalyst for inner development rather than as a subject of interest in its own right.

A second body of work foregrounds the rhetorical and representational strategies through which Su Shi constructs landscape in exile. Egan (1994) emphasized Su Shi's intellectual versatility and argued that his exile writings deliberately refashion earlier literary models, including the traditions of the recluse and the banished official, to produce a distinctive voice that neither wholly resists nor wholly accepts displacement. Grant (1998), examining the Huizhou and Danzhou poems, similarly stressed Su Shi's use of local topography and customs as material for a consciously crafted persona, one that converts marginality into a form of authority. These studies share the premise that landscape in Su Shi is never merely observed but always mediated by literary convention and self-presentation.

A third approach situates Su Shi within broader histories of Chinese exile literature. Hawkes (1985) and, more recently, Zhang (2010) have placed Su Shi in a lineage running back to Qu Yuan, arguing that the trope of the loyal official estranged from court provided a template that Su Shi both inherited and revised. Zhang (2010) in particular contends that Su Shi's innovation lay in loosening the association between exile and grievance, allowing landscape to function as consolation rather than merely as a mirror of sorrow. This line of inquiry usefully connects Su Shi to wider traditions, though it has been criticized for smoothing over the heterogeneity of his corpus.

Disagreement centers on the extent and timing of Su Shi's purported equanimity. While Lin (1972) and Zhang (2010) describe a steady movement toward acceptance, Fuller (2006) cautions against reading the poems as straightforward autobiography, noting that expressions of contentment may be rhetorical postures shaped by genre and audience. Similarly, Owen (1996) has questioned the tendency to treat Su Shi's exile poetry as a unified spiritual narrative, arguing that the poems are better understood as occasional responses to specific circumstances. These skeptical readings do not deny the importance of landscape but insist that its significance varies across texts and cannot be reduced to a single developmental arc.

More recent scholarship has begun to address the material and environmental dimensions of Su Shi's exile landscapes. Studies informed by ecocritical and place-based approaches have attended to his representations of local agriculture, climate, and vernacular geography, particularly in the Danzhou poems (Smith 2018; Wang 2020). Wang (2020) argues that Su Shi's attention to the specificities of southern terrain constitutes a form of place-making that complicates any simple opposition between center and periphery. This work is still emerging and has yet to be fully integrated with the older spiritual-biographical tradition.

In summary, the literature converges on the centrality of landscape to Su Shi's exile poetry but diverges on whether that landscape primarily indexes inner transformation, rhetorical self-fashioning, or material embeddedness. The biographical and transcendental readings of Yoshikawa (1967) and Lin (1972) remain influential but have been productively challenged by scholars emphasizing convention and occasion (Fuller 2006; Owen 1996). A gap persists in sustained comparative analysis of how landscape functions differently across the three exile periods, and in work that reconciles the rhetorical and materialist approaches. The present study addresses this gap by examining landscape as a shifting site of negotiation between displacement and belonging across Su Shi's exile corpus.

References

Egan, R. 1994. Word, Image, and Deed in the Life of Su Shi. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press.

Fuller, M. A. 2006. The Road to East Slope: The Development of Su Shi's Poetic Voice. Stanford: Stanford University Press.

Grant, B. 1998. "The Spiritual Geography of Su Shi's Southern Exile." Journal of Chinese Literature and Culture 5(2): 211–238.

Hawkes, D. 1985. The Songs of the South. Harmondsworth: Penguin.

Lin, S. 1972. The Transformation of Su Shih. Princeton: Princeton University Press.

Owen, S. 1996. An Anthology of Chinese Literature: Beginnings to 1911. New York: Norton.

Smith, J. 2018. "Ecologies of Exile in Song Poetry." Chinese Literature: Essays, Articles, Reviews 40: 77–99.

Wang, L. 2020. "Place-Making in Su Shi's Danzhou Poems." T'oung Pao 106(3–4): 355–389.

Yoshikawa, K. 1967. An Introduction to Sung Poetry. Trans. B. Watson. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press.

Zhang, C. 2010. "From Qu Yuan to Su Shi: Traditions of Exile Poetry." Chinese Literature: Essays, Articles, Reviews 32: 45–68.

title: linguistics|code-switching among bilingual teenagers in Singapore
text:
Here is a course paper on the requested topic, structured with an abstract, introduction, body sections, and conclusion, at approximately 900 words.

---

 Code-Switching Among Bilingual Teenagers in Singapore: A Marker of Identity and Linguistic Dexterity

Abstract
This paper explores the phenomenon of code-switching among bilingual teenagers in Singapore, a linguistically diverse nation where English, Mandarin, Malay, and Tamil coexist as official languages alongside a vibrant creole, Singlish. Moving beyond the traditional view of code-switching as a sign of linguistic deficiency, this paper argues that it is a sophisticated communicative strategy. Through an analysis of its forms, social functions, and role in identity construction, the paper demonstrates that code-switching is a central practice through which Singaporean youth navigate their multicultural environment, assert their generational identity, and perform complex acts of belonging.

1. Introduction
Singapore's linguistic landscape is a testament to its multicultural fabric. The government’s bilingual education policy, which mandates the learning of English as a first language and a designated "Mother Tongue" (Mandarin, Malay, or Tamil), has produced a generation of effectively bilingual speakers. Within this context, the informal speech of teenagers is characterized by the fluid and dynamic alternation between these languages, a practice known as code-switching. While often stigmatized in formal educational settings as "half-past six" language or linguistic confusion, linguistic research reveals it to be a rule-governed and purposeful phenomenon. This paper will examine the multifaceted nature of code-switching among Singaporean bilingual teenagers. It will first define the primary forms this switching takes, then analyze its key social functions, and finally, discuss its crucial role as a tool for identity construction in contemporary Singapore.

2. The Forms of Teenage Code-Switching
Code-switching in Singapore is not a monolithic behaviour but manifests in several distinct forms, each with its own characteristics. The most common form is inter-sentential switching, where a speaker alternates between languages across sentence boundaries. A teenager might exclaim in English, "I'm so stressed about this project," and then turn to a friend and add in Mandarin, "怎么办?" ("What should we do?"). This form allows speakers to frame an entire thought or question within the cultural and emotional context of another language.

More intricate is intra-sentential switching, the insertion of words or phrases from one language into a sentence structured in another. This is a hallmark of Singaporean speech, particularly in the use of discourse particles. For instance, a sentence like "Let's go makan *lah*, I'm hungry *already*" seamlessly integrates Malay ("makan" for eat), a quintessential Singlish particle ("lah"), and English. These particles are not random; they carry specific pragmatic meanings, softening commands, adding emphasis, or building rapport. This form of switching requires high proficiency, as speakers must navigate the syntactic rules of both languages simultaneously.

Another pervasive form is tag-switching, where a tag from one language is attached to a monolingual utterance in another. For example, a teenager might say, "This movie is damn good, *kan*?" ("right?"). The use of "kan" (from Malay/ Singlish) is a direct appeal for agreement, a syntactic and social tag that reinforces solidarity. These varied forms demonstrate that code-switching is not a haphazard mixing but a skilled linguistic performance that draws on a deep, integrated bilingual competence.

3. The Social Functions of Code-Switching
For Singaporean teenagers, code-switching serves a range of vital social functions. Firstly, it acts as a solidarity marker, creating an in-group identity. The use of a shared linguistic repertoire, including specific switches and Singlish elements, signals membership in a peer group. This "we-code" strengthens social bonds and fosters a sense of community, differentiating their speech from the more formal "they-code" of teachers or authority figures.

Secondly, code-switching functions as a contextualization cue, signaling shifts in topic, speaker, or social activity. A conversation might begin in standard English about schoolwork, but a switch to a more colloquial mix of English and Mandarin could signal a move to a more personal or gossipy topic. This allows teenagers to manage the flow of conversation and indicate the social footing of the interaction.

Finally, it is a powerful tool for pragmatic effect, such as emphasis or humor. A point made in one language can be reiterated in another for stronger effect. Switching to a Mother Tongue can index cultural values or emotional closeness, while the use of Singlish particles often adds a layer of irony or casualness. Through these functions, code-switching becomes a sophisticated resource for managing social relationships and navigating the complex communicative demands of teenage life.

4. Code-Switching and Identity Construction
Beyond its communicative functions, code-switching is fundamental to how Singaporean teenagers construct and perform their identities. In a society that often emphasizes racial and linguistic categories (CMIO - Chinese, Malay, Indian, Others), young people use code-switching to negotiate these labels. For a Chinese Singaporean, using Mandarin with elders and English with peers is a way of performing both filial piety and modern, global citizenship.

However, their switching is often more nuanced. A Chinese teenager might pepper their English with Hokkien or Malay phrases they've learned from friends, signalling a broader "Singaporean" identity that transcends their official ethnic group. This practice challenges rigid linguistic boundaries and reflects a lived reality of cultural hybridity. Furthermore, the very act of using Singlish, which is deeply embedded with code-switching, is a powerful assertion of a unique, localized Singaporean identity that is distinct from foreign English norms. In this sense, code-switching is not just about language; it is a political and social act of defining oneself in relation to the nation's multicultural and globalized context.

5. Conclusion
The code-switching practices of bilingual teenagers in Singapore are a far cry from linguistic confusion. They represent a dynamic, rule-governed, and highly skilled communicative strategy. From the syntactic integration of intra-sentential switching to the social solidarity forged through shared linguistic cues, this phenomenon is central to teenage interaction. More profoundly, it is a key resource for identity construction, allowing young Singaporeans to navigate their multilingual heritage, assert a unique local identity, and perform their place within a complex, multicultural society. As Singapore continues to evolve, the code-switching of its youth will remain a vital and vibrant reflection of its linguistic and cultural vitality, a testament to the dexterity of its bilingual speakers.

title: chemistry|catalytic conversion of biomass to platform chemicals
text:
Methodology

 Data Sources and Materials

This study employed a combination of primary experimental data and secondary literature data to evaluate the catalytic conversion of lignocellulosic biomass to platform chemicals. Primary experimental data were generated through laboratory-scale catalytic reactions conducted in our research facility. Secondary data were compiled from peer-reviewed literature published between 2015 and 2024, retrieved from Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar databases using search terms including "biomass catalytic conversion," "platform chemicals," "levulinic acid," "5-hydroxymethylfurfural," and "heterogeneous catalysis." Only studies reporting quantitative conversion and selectivity data under well-defined reaction conditions were retained for comparative analysis. Additional reference data on biomass feedstock composition were obtained from the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL) biomass compositional database.

 Sample Preparation and Characterization

Three representative biomass feedstocks were selected: microcrystalline cellulose (Avicel PH-101, Sigma-Aldrich), xylose (≥99%, Sigma-Aldrich), and corn stover obtained from a regional agricultural supplier. Corn stover was milled to a particle size of 0.5–1.0 mm, Soxhlet-extracted with ethanol to remove extractives, and dried at 105 °C for 24 h prior to use. Biomass compositional analysis followed NREL/TP-510-42618 protocols for structural carbohydrates and lignin. Catalyst samples—including sulfonated carbon materials, zeolites (H-ZSM-5, H-Beta), and metal oxide catalysts (Nb₂O₅, TiO₂)—were characterized by X-ray diffraction (XRD), Brunauer–Emmett–Teller (BET) surface area analysis, ammonia temperature-programmed desorption (NH₃-TPD), and Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) to determine crystallinity, porosity, acid site density, and functional groups.

 Experimental Procedure

Catalytic conversion reactions were performed in a 100 mL batch stainless-steel autoclave equipped with a mechanical stirrer and temperature controller. In a typical run, 1.0 g of substrate, 0.1–0.5 g of catalyst, and 20 mL of solvent (water, γ-valerolactone, or water–THF mixtures) were loaded into the reactor. Reactions were conducted at temperatures of 140–200 °C for 30–240 min under nitrogen atmosphere (1–3 MPa). Upon completion, the reactor was cooled, and the reaction mixture was filtered to separate the solid catalyst. Products were quantified using high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC, Agilent 1260) equipped with a refractive index detector and an Aminex HPX-87H column (0.005 M H₂SO₄ mobile phase, 60 °C). Conversion, product yield, and selectivity were calculated on a molar carbon basis. All experiments were performed in triplicate, and mean values with standard deviations are reported.

 Data Analysis

Quantitative analysis of experimental results employed analysis of variance (ANOVA) to assess the statistical significance of differences in conversion and selectivity across catalyst types and reaction conditions (p < 0.05). Response surface methodology (RSM) based on a central composite design was applied to optimize reaction parameters (temperature, time, catalyst loading). Kinetic parameters were estimated by fitting experimental time-course data to first-order and Langmuir–Hinshelwood models using non-linear regression in OriginPro 2022. For the literature dataset, conversion and selectivity values were normalized to consistent units, and meta-analysis was conducted using random-effects models in R (version 4.3.1) to identify overarching trends across catalyst classes. Catalyst stability was evaluated through five consecutive recycle runs, with post-reaction characterization by XRD and BET to detect structural changes. Limitations of the methodology include the inherent variability in biomass feedstock composition and the difficulty of directly comparing data generated under differing analytical protocols across published studies; these factors were mitigated through standardized normalization procedures and strict inclusion criteria.

title: literary studies|landscape and exile in the poetry of Su Shi
text: This article examines the intricate relationship between landscape and exile in the poetry of Su Shi (1037–1101), one of the most prominent literary figures of the Northern Song dynasty. Su Shi’s political exiles to remote regions—Huangzhou, Huizhou, and Danzhou—constitute a defining arc of his life and work, and his poetry from these periods reveals how landscape functions as both a site of displacement and a medium of spiritual and aesthetic transformation. Drawing on close readings of selected poems composed during his banishments, this study argues that Su Shi’s poetic landscapes are not merely descriptive backdrops but dynamic structures through which the poet negotiates loss, alienation, and belonging. The analysis identifies three interrelated modes of landscape representation: the therapeutic, in which natural scenery consoles and reorients the exiled self; the dialogic, in which the poet projects his condition onto the environment and reads his own displacement in its features; and the transcendent, in which landscape becomes a vehicle for philosophical reconciliation, particularly through the poet’s engagement with Buddhist and Daoist thought. Situating these readings within the broader tradition of Chinese exile poetry (bianzhe wenxue), the article contends that Su Shi reworks inherited conventions by refusing both self-pity and mere stoic endurance, instead cultivating an aesthetics of adaptive dwelling. This study contributes to scholarship on Song dynasty poetry and the cultural history of exile by demonstrating how landscape writing enabled Su Shi to convert political marginalization into enduring literary creation.

title: philosophy|moral luck and the limits of responsibility
text:
Few ideas in modern moral philosophy have proved as unsettling as the thought that a person's moral standing may depend on factors beyond her control. Thomas Nagel (1979) and Bernard Williams (1981) gave this thought its canonical formulation under the heading of moral luck: the phenomenon whereby a person is assessed as morally praiseworthy or blameworthy, as responsible or not, partly in virtue of circumstances, consequences, or constitutive features of character that she did not choose and could not have controlled. What makes the phenomenon paradoxical is its tension with a deeply entrenched commitment, namely that responsibility is bounded by control. If two agents are alike in intention, effort, and deliberation, and differ only in some uncontrollable factor, it seems unjust to hold them differentially responsible. Yet our ordinary practices of blame, punishment, praise, and regret routinely do precisely this. The problem of moral luck is thus not a peripheral puzzle but a pressure point at which our conception of moral agency, our practices of accountability, and our sense of justice collide.

The literature has largely organized itself around Nagel's (1979) taxonomy of four kinds of luck: resultant luck, concerning the outcomes of action; circumstantial luck, concerning the situations in which agents find themselves; constitutive luck, concerning the traits and dispositions that make agents who they are; and causal luck, concerning the antecedent causes of action. Williams (1981) approached the same terrain from a different direction, arguing through the figure of the lorry driver who, through no fault of his own, kills a child, that the significance of such events for an agent's life cannot be fully captured by a morality that restricts responsibility to the voluntary. Williams's claim that morality, so conceived, is inadequate to the ethical significance of luck has been as influential as Nagel's paradox, and the two together set the terms of debate for the ensuing four decades.

Responses have clustered into several families. Constitutive luck has been thought by some to threaten the very possibility of responsibility, since if character is substantially a matter of endowment and upbringing, the self that acts may not be attributable in the requisite sense (Strawson 1994; Levy 2011). Others have sought to reconcile responsibility with luck by distinguishing the conditions of responsible agency from the conditions of moral assessment, or by arguing that blameworthiness supervenes on quality of will rather than on outcomes (Scanlon 2008; Talbert 2019). Defenders of outcome-sensitive responsibility have argued that practices of holding responsible serve forward-looking functions, such as deterrence, moral education, and the maintenance of relationships, that justify differential treatment even where desert does not (Dennett 1984; Vargas 2013). Skeptics, by contrast, have pressed the worry that these strategies either abandon the control condition altogether or smuggle it back in under another name (Enoch and Marmor 2007; Hartman 2017).

At stake in these disputes is not only the correct analysis of responsibility but the shape of moral philosophy itself. If luck pervades moral assessment, then a conception of morality as immune to luck, purged of the contingent and the unchosen, may be an illusion, and the attempt to insulate ethics from fortune may distort the phenomena it seeks to explain (Nussbaum 1986; Williams 1981). Conversely, if responsibility can be shown to survive the admission of luck, the result may be a more defensible and humane account of accountability, one that acknowledges the fragility of moral standing without collapsing into skepticism (Nagel 1979; Wolf 2001). The debate thus bears directly on questions of punishment and excuse, on the justification of retributive attitudes, and on the possibility of moral criticism across differences of circumstance and constitution.

This paper contributes to that debate by examining the limits of responsibility in light of moral luck. Its central contention is that the control condition on responsibility cannot be defended in the form in which it is usually assumed, but that this failure does not vindicate global skepticism about responsibility. Rather, the paper argues that responsibility is best understood as a practice whose scope is bounded by normative considerations that are themselves sensitive to luck, and that the limits of responsibility are therefore not fixed once and for all by a metaphysical criterion but are drawn and redrawn in the course of moral life. The argument proceeds in three stages. The first section reconstructs the problem of moral luck and distinguishes its varieties, showing that not all forms of luck pose the same threat. The second section considers and rejects the principal strategies for insulating responsibility from luck, arguing that each either underestimates the pervasiveness of constitutive and circumstantial luck or overstates the resources of a purely quality-of-will account. The third section develops an alternative, practice-based conception of responsibility, according to which the limits of responsibility are set by the demands of justification and answerability within relationships and institutions, and shows how this conception accommodates the insights of both the luck egalitarian and the compatibilist traditions while avoiding their excesses.

The paper's aim is thus both critical and constructive. Critically, it seeks to show that the standard framing of the problem, as a conflict between an uncontroversial control condition and equally uncontroversial practices of blame, rests on an oversimplified picture of both. Constructively, it offers an account of responsibility as bounded, graduated, and socially situated, one that takes seriously the fact that moral agents are vulnerable to fortune without concluding that responsibility is therefore an illusion. If the argument succeeds, the upshot is a conception of the limits of responsibility that is neither a counsel of skepticism nor a license for unlimited blame, but a framework for thinking about when and how we may legitimately hold one another to account.
